content.text:
| Field | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| material_system | str | Material studied (e.g., crystalline Si, crystalline Ge, Si1-xGex alloy, superlattice, nanostructure). Prefer exact wording used in paper. |
| composition_x | str | For Si1-xGex: the x value(s) or composition range (e.g., x=0.2, x=0.5, 0<=x<=1). Null if not applicable/not reported. |
| structure_and_phase | str | Crystal structure and phase info (e.g., diamond cubic, bulk, single crystal, isotopically pure/natural, alloy model type). |
| temperature_points_K | str | Temperatures at which kappa_l is reported (list or range, include units K). If a curve is shown, capture reported range (e.g., 100–1000 K). |
| thermal_conductivity_values | str | Reported lattice thermal conductivity values with units (typically W/m-K) and whether direction-averaged or tensor components; include uncertainties/error bars if given. Prefer tabulated values; otherwise summarize key points (e.g., kappa(300K)=...). |
| kappa_definition_and_components | str | How the paper defines the reported conductivity: lattice-only vs total, inclusion/exclusion of electronic contribution, quantum corrections, decomposition (e.g., harmonic/anharmonic, modal contributions). |
| method_category | str | Primary method used: empirical-potential MD, first-principles PBTE/DFT, hybrid (e.g., DFT IFCs + alloy scattering models), or other. Use the paper's terminology. |
| md_flavor | str | If MD: specify EMD/Green-Kubo, NEMD/direct method, Müller-Plathe, approach-to-equilibrium, transient grating, etc. Null if not MD. |
| interatomic_potential | str | If empirical MD: potential name and parameterization (e.g., Tersoff (which version), Stillinger–Weber, MEAM). For SiGe, include cross-interaction mixing rules if stated. Null if not applicable. |
| emd_gk_details | str | If Green-Kubo/EMD: heat flux definition used, ensemble (NVE/NVT), thermostat scheme (Nosé–Hoover, Langevin) and equilibration/production times, correlation time window, fitting/integration method, multiple time origins, statistical treatment. |
| nemd_details | str | If NEMD/direct: imposed heat flux or temperature gradient method, boundary conditions, thermostat regions, length/area, steady-state criteria, how gradient is computed, contact resistance treatment. |
| simulation_cell_and_convergence | str | System size (number of atoms, dimensions), timestep, run length, number of replicas, finite-size analysis (kappa vs length) and extrapolation method (e.g., 1/kappa vs 1/L). |
| first_principles_details | str | If DFT/PBTE: DFT code and functional (LDA/GGA, etc.), pseudopotentials, plane-wave cutoff, k-point mesh; method to compute IFCs (finite displacement/DFPT), supercell size, order of IFCs (2nd/3rd/4th), q-mesh for BTE, iterative vs RTA solution, smearing parameters. |
| phonon_scattering_mechanisms_included | str | Scattering terms included: 3-phonon, 4-phonon, isotope scattering, alloy/mass-disorder scattering, boundary scattering, impurity/electron-phonon (if any). Note any omissions explicitly stated. |
| alloy_modeling_approach | str | For SiGe: how disorder is modeled (virtual crystal approximation, mass-disorder model, Tamura formula, CPA, explicit random alloy supercells in MD, special quasirandom structures). Include whether force-constant disorder is included vs mass-only. |
| reported_method_comparisons | str | Any explicit comparisons within the paper across methods/potentials (e.g., Tersoff vs SW; GK vs NEMD; DFT-BTE vs MD; RTA vs iterative). Include numerical differences at specific temperatures if reported. |
| agreement_with_experiment | str | Any comparison to experimental thermal conductivity data (which dataset, temperatures, and degree of agreement/discrepancy). Include if the paper claims over/under-prediction and possible reasons. |
| proposed_reasons_for_discrepancies | str | Mechanistic explanations offered for method-dependent differences: e.g., potential inadequacy (phonon dispersion/Grüneisen mismatch), classical vs quantum statistics, finite-size effects, thermostat artifacts, heat-flux definition issues, missing scattering processes (4-phonon), alloy force-constant disorder, etc. |
| notes_on_temperature_dependence | str | Any stated scaling laws or regimes vs temperature (e.g., ~T^-1 at high T, peak near certain T, low-T boundary/isotope limited). Capture qualitative statements and any fitted exponents. |
| key_figures_tables_locations | str | Where the main kappa vs T results appear (figure/table numbers, section). Helps retrieval/verification. |

artifacts.description: Build theories of how the choice of method (Tersoff and Stillinger-Weber empirical potentials in molecular dynamics, Green-Kubo or nonequilibrium MD, first-principles phonon Boltzmann transport with DFT force constants) changes the predicted lattice thermal conductivity of crystalline silicon, germanium and Si1-xGex, as a function of temperature.

s2_metadata.abstract: A computational framework for predicting phonon frequencies, group velocities, scattering rates, and the resulting lattice thermal conductivity is described. The underlying theory and implementation suggestions are also provided. By using input from first principles calculations and taking advantage of advances in computational power, this framework has enabled thermal conductivity predictions that agree with experimental measurements for diverse crystalline materials over a wide range of temperatures. Density functional theory and density functional perturbation theory calculations are first used to obtain the harmonic and cubic force constants. The harmonic force constants are the input to harmonic lattice dynamics calculations, which provide the phonon frequencies and eigenvectors. The harmonic properties and the cubic force constants are then used with perturbation theory and/or phenomenological models to determine intrinsic and extrinsic scattering rates. The full set of phonon properties is then used to solve the Boltzmann transport equation for the mode populations and thermal conductivity. The extension of the framework to include higher-order processes, capture finite temperature effects, and model alloys is described. A case study on silicon is presented that provides benchmarking and convergence data. Available packages that implement the framework are compared.A computational framework for predicting phonon frequencies, group velocities, scattering rates, and the resulting lattice thermal conductivity is described. s2_metadata.abstract: Understanding heat transport in semiconductors and insulators is of fundamental importance because of its technological impact in electronics and renewable energy harvesting and conversion. Anharmonic Lattice Dynamics provides a powerful framework for the description of heat transport at the nanoscale. One of the advantages of this method is that it naturally includes quantum effects due to atoms vibrations, which are needed to compute the thermal properties of semiconductors widely used in nanotechnology, like silicon and carbon, even at room temperature. While the heat transport picture substantially differs between amorphous and crystalline semiconductors from a microscopic standpoint, a unified approach to simulate both crystals and glasses has been devised. Here we introduce a unified workflow, which implements both the Boltzmann Transport equation (BTE) and the Quasi Harmonic Green-Kubo (QHGK) methods. We discuss how the theory can be optimized to exploit modern parallel architectures, and how it is implemented in $\kappa ALDo$: a versatile and scalable open-source software to compute phonon transport in solids. This approach is applied to crystalline and partially disordered silicon-based systems, including bulk silicon and clathrates, and on silicon-germanium alloy clathrates with largely reduced thermal conductivity.

s2_metadata.abstract: While machine learning (ML) has shown increasing effectiveness in optimizing materials properties under known physics, its application in discovering new physics remains challenging due to its interpolative nature. In this work, we demonstrate a general-purpose adaptive ML-accelerated search process that can discover unexpected lattice thermal conductivity ( κ l ) enhancement in aperiodic superlattices (SLs) as compared to periodic superlattices, with implications for thermal management of multilayer-based electronic devices. We use molecular dynamics simulations for high-fidelity calculations of κ l , along with a convolutional neural network (CNN) which can rapidly predict κ l for a large number of structures. To ensure accurate prediction for the target unknown SLs, we iteratively identify aperiodic SLs with structural features leading to locally enhanced thermal transport and include them as additional training data for the CNN. The identified structures exhibit increased coherent phonon transport owing to the presence of closely spaced interfaces.

s2_metadata.abstract: Solid-state thermoelectric devices are currently used in applications ranging from thermocouple sensors to power generators in satellites, to portable air-conditioners and refrigerators. With the ever-rising demand throughout the world for energy consumption and CO2 reduction, thermoelectric energy conversion has been receiving intensified attention as a potential candidate for waste-heat harvesting as well as for power generation from renewable sources. Efficient thermoelectric energy conversion critically depends on the performance of thermoelectric materials and devices. In this review, we discuss heat transfer in thermoelectric materials and devices, especially phonon engineering to reduce the lattice thermal conductivity of thermoelectric materials, which requires a fundamental understanding of nanoscale heat conduction physics.

s2_metadata.abstract: We demonstrate that a high-dimensional neural network potential (HDNNP) can predict the lattice thermal conductivity of semiconducting materials with an accuracy that is comparable to that of density functional theory (DFT) calculation. After a training procedure based on force, the root mean square error between the forces predicted by HDNNP and DFT is less than 40 meV Å−1. As typical examples, we present the results of Si and GaN bulk crystals. The deviation from the thermal conductivity calculated using DFT is within 1% at 200 to 500 K for Si and within 5.4% at 200 to 1000 K for GaN.

s2_metadata.abstract: While machine learning (ML) has shown increasing effectiveness in optimizing materials properties under known physics, its application in challenging conventional wisdom and discovering new physics still remains challenging due to its interpolative nature. In this work, we demonstrate the potential of using ML for such applications by implementing an adaptive ML-accelerated search process that can discover unexpected lattice thermal conductivity ($\kappa_l$) enhancement instead of reduction in aperiodic superlattices (SLs) as compared to periodic superlattices. We use non-equilibrium molecular dynamics (NEMD) simulations for high-fidelity calculations of $\kappa_l$ for a small fraction of SLs in the search space, along with a convolutional neural network (CNN) which can rapidly predict $\kappa_l$ for a large number of structures. To ensure accurate prediction by the CNN for the target unknown structures, we iteratively identify aperiodic SLs containing structural features which lead to locally enhanced thermal transport, and include them as additional training data for the CNN in each iteration. As a result, our CNN can accurately predict the high $\kappa_l$ of aperiodic SLs that are absent from the initial training dataset, which allows us to identify the previously unseen exceptional structures. The identified RML structures exhibit increased coherent phonon contribution to thermal conductivity owing to the presence of closely spaced interfaces. Our work describes a general purpose machine learning approach for identifying low-probability-of-occurrence exceptional solutions within an extremely large subspace and discovering the underlying physics.

s2_metadata.abstract: We present a framework for quantifying the uncertainty that results from the choice of exchange-correlation (XC) functional in predictions of phonon properties and thermal conductivity that use density functional theory (DFT) to calculate the atomic force constants. The energy ensemble capabilities of the BEEF-vdW XC functional are first applied to determine an ensemble of interatomic force constants, which are then used as inputs to lattice dynamics calculations and a solution of the Boltzmann transport equation. The framework is applied to isotopically-pure silicon. We find that the uncertainty estimates bound property predictions (e.g., phonon dispersions, specific heat, thermal conductivity) from other XC functionals and experiments. We distinguish between properties that are correlated with the predicted thermal conductivity [e.g., the transverse acoustic branch sound speed ($R^2=0.89$) and average Gruneisen parameter ($R^2=0.85$)] and those that are not [e.g., longitudinal acoustic branch sound speed ($R^2=0.23$) and specific heat ($R^2=0.00$)]. We find that differences in ensemble predictions of thermal conductivity are correlated with the behavior of phonons with mean free paths between $100$ and $300$ nm. The framework systematically accounts for XC uncertainty in phonon calculations and should be used whenever it is suspected that the choice of XC functional is influencing physical interpretations.

s2_metadata.abstract: The electron-phonon interaction is well known to create major resistance to electron transport in metals and semiconductors, whereas fewer studies are directed to its effect on phonon transport, especially in semiconductors. We calculate the phonon lifetimes due to scattering with electrons (or holes), combine them with the intrinsic lifetimes due to the anharmonic phonon-phonon interaction, all from first principles, and evaluate the effect of the electron-phonon interaction on the lattice thermal conductivity of silicon. Unexpectedly, we find a significant reduction of the lattice thermal conductivity at room temperature as the carrier concentration goes above 10(19)  cm(-3) (the reduction reaches up to 45% in p-type silicon at around 10(21)  cm(-3)), a range of great technological relevance to thermoelectric materials.

s2_metadata.abstract: Parameter-free calculations of lattice dynamics from first principles have achieved significant progress in the past decades, with a wealth of applications in thermodynamics, phase transitions, and transport properties of materials. Current approaches to derive the interatomic force constants (IFCs) of lattice potential become challenging and sometimes infeasible when going beyond third-order anharmonicity, due to the combinatorial explosion in the number of higher-order IFCs. In this work, we present a robust and user-friendly program, , which reliably reconstructs the prescribed potential energy surface of crystalline solids via a Taylor expansion of arbitrarily high order. Given force-displacement datasets, the program enables an efficient and accurate extraction of IFCs using advanced machine-learning algorithms, and further calculates a wide range of harmonic and anharmonic phonon related properties. We show in three prototypical examples how the obtained IFCs have been successfully applied to study anharmonic lattice dynamics and thermal transport. Through these detailed benchmarks, we have also identified the optimal approach for IFC extractions and offered general guidelines for high-fidelity lattice-dynamical simulations, addressing the large uncertainties in the IFCs extracted from existing various schemes. Overall, the project aims to create a phonon code ecosystem that connects diverse phonon simulation platforms and offers access to the broad research community.

s2_metadata.abstract: While using first-principles-based Boltzmann transport equation approach to predict the thermal conductivity of crystalline semiconductor materials has been a routine, the validity of the approach is seldom tested for high-temperature conditions. Most previous studies only focused on the phononic contribution, and neglected the electronic part. Meanwhile, the treatment on phonon transport is not rigorous as a few ingredients, such as four-phonon scatterings, phonon renormalization and thermal expansion, are ignored. In this paper, we present a Boltzmann transport equation study on high-temperature thermal conduction in bulk silicon by considering the effects of both phonons and electrons, and explore the role of the missing parts in the previous studies on the thermal conductivity at elevated temperature. For the phonon transport, four-phonon scattering is found to considerably reduce the thermal conductivity when the temperature is larger than 700 K, while the effects of phonon renormalization and thermal expansion on phononic thermal conductivity are negligible. Bipolar contribution to the electronic thermal conductivity calculated from first-principles is implemented for the first time. More than 25% of heat is shown to be conducted by electrons at 1500 K. The computed total thermal conductivity of silicon faithfully reproduces the measured data. The approach presented in this paper is expected to be applied to other high-temperature functional materials, and the results could serve as benchmarks and help to explain the high-temperature phonon and electron transport phenomena.

s2_metadata.abstract: Various theoretical and experimental methods are utilized to investigate the thermal conductivity of nanostructured materials; this is a critical parameter to increase performance of thermoelectric devices. Among these methods, equilibrium molecular dynamics (EMD) is an accurate technique to predict lattice thermal conductivity. In this study, by means of systematic EMD simulations, thermal conductivity of bulk Si-Ge structures (pristine, alloy and superlattice) and their nanostructured one dimensional forms with square and circular cross-section geometries (asymmetric and symmetric) are calculated for different crystallographic directions. A comprehensive temperature analysis is evaluated for selected structures as well. The results show that one-dimensional structures are superior candidates in terms of their low lattice thermal conductivity and thermal conductivity tunability by nanostructuring, such as by diameter modulation, interface roughness, periodicity and number of interfaces. We find that thermal conductivity decreases with smaller diameters or cross section areas. Furthermore, interface roughness decreases thermal conductivity with a profound impact. Moreover, we predicted that there is a specific periodicity that gives minimum thermal conductivity in symmetric superlattice structures. The decreasing thermal conductivity is due to the reducing phonon movement in the system due to the effect of the number of interfaces that determine regimes of ballistic and wave transport phenomena. In some nanostructures, such as nanowire superlattices, thermal conductivity of the Si/Ge system can be reduced to nearly twice that of an amorphous silicon thermal conductivity. Additionally, it is found that one crystal orientation, 100, is better than the 111 crystal orientation in one-dimensional and bulk SiGe systems. Our results clearly point out the importance of lattice thermal conductivity engineering in bulk and nanostructures to produce high-performance thermoelectric materials. Graphical Abstract

s2_metadata.abstract: While it is well-known that electron-phonon scattering often determines the electron mobility, its impact on lattice thermal conductivity is less clear. Dominant phonon scattering mechanisms that determine the lattice thermal conductivity have been attributed to phonon-phonon and phonon-defect interactions. However, recent studies in silicon have shown that strong electron-phonon interaction can also lead to significant phonon scatterings at high carrier concentrations. Here, we use first-principles simulations to study thermal transport in SiGe alloys and show that the effect of electron-phonon interaction on thermal transport is even more significant than that in Si because mass disorder scattering leaves long mean free path phonons behind, which are more strongly scattered by electrons. At the carrier concentration of 1 × 1020 cm−3, the room temperature lattice thermal conductivity of the Si0.9Ge0.1 alloy including electron-phonon interaction is only 40% of the value without this interaction. The results show that thermal transport in alloys at a high doping level can be significantly impacted by the free carriers, providing important insights into heat conduction mechanisms in thermoelectric materials which are mostly based on heavily doped alloys.

s2_metadata.abstract: Hierarchically nanostructured materials, where disorder is introduced in various length scales (at the atomic scale, the nanoscale, and the mesoscale) is one of the most promising directions to achieve extremely low thermal conductivities and improve thermoelectric performance. Here we theoretically investigate one such system, a nanocrystalline material with nanopores that are introduced between the crystalline regions. We use the Nonequilibrium Green's Function method for electronic transport and Molecular Dynamics for phonon transport.

s2_metadata.abstract: The predictive modeling of lattice thermal conductivity is of fundamental importance for the understanding and design of materials for a wide range of applications. Two major approaches, namely molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and calculations solving approximately the Boltzmann transport equation (BTE), have been developed to compute the lattice thermal conductivity. We present a detailed direct comparison of these two approaches, using as prototypical cases MgO and PbTe. The comparison, carried out using empirical potentials, takes into account the effects of fourth order phonon scattering, temperature-dependent phonon frequencies (phonon renormalization), and investigates the effects of quantum vs. classical statistics. We clarify that equipartition, as opposed to Maxwell Boltzmann, govern the statistics of phonons in MD simulations. We find that lattice thermal conductivity values from MD and BTE show an apparent, satisfactory agreement; however such an agreement is the result of error cancellations. We also show that the primary effect of statistics on thermal conductivity is via the scattering rate dependence on phonon populations.

extracted_data.name_full: An iterative machine learning approach for discovering unexpected thermal conductivity enhancement in aperiodic superlattices
extracted_data.brief_description: Cross-plane lattice thermal conductivity (kappa_l) of Si/Ge binary superlattices and random multilayers (RMLs) computed with classical non-equilibrium MD (NEMD) at 300 K and used to identify RMLs with kappa_l exceeding periodic SLs; modeling choices and simulation details that influence predictions are documented (Tersoff potential, NEMD setup, classical statistics, geometry).
extracted_data.material_system: Si/Ge multilayers (binary Si/Ge superlattices and random multilayers, thin-film geometry)
extracted_data.structure_and_phase: Diamond-cubic unit cells of Si and Ge stacked along [100]; superlattice thin-film (periodic boundary conditions in two lateral directions), smallest layer thickness = 1 UC; equal number of Si and Ge layers; two total lengths studied: 20 UC (≈11 nm) and 40 UC (≈22 nm).
extracted_data.temperature_points_K: 300 K (system temperature); Langevin thermostats applied to reservoir regions at 330 K and 270 K to impose gradient (NEMD).
extracted_data.thermal_conductivity_values: Cross-plane lattice thermal conductivities reported at 300 K. Key values: SL period dependence shows minimum ≈2 W/mK near period ≈2.2 nm (Fig.4a). For 20 UC (total length) 5–5 SL: kappa_l = 2.28 W/mK; an identified 20 UC RML: kappa_l = 2.36 W/mK (≈+3.5% vs SL). CNN predictions and NEMD comparisons span ≈1–2.5 W/mK (parity plot Fig.5b, RMSE ≈0.09 W/mK). For a 40 UC RML identified, kappa_l exceeds corresponding 5–5 SL by ≈5.5% (absolute value not explicitly tabulated). Reported values are averaged over multiple independent runs; no numerical error bars given in text (authors state enhancement is above statistical uncertainty).
extracted_data.kappa_definition_and_components: Reported quantity is cross-plane lattice thermal conductivity (kappa_l) from direct NEMD; electronic contributions are not included. Interface (apparent) thermal resistance R_i is computed as R_i = ΔT_i / q'' and used to decompose total resistance. Discussion separates coherent vs incoherent phonon contributions qualitatively but no modal PBTE decomposition performed in this paper.
extracted_data.method_category: empirical-potential molecular dynamics (classical MD using an empirical interatomic potential).
extracted_data.md_flavor: NEMD (direct non-equilibrium MD) with thermostatted reservoir regions (Langevin thermostats) to impose temperature difference; steady-state heat flux method (compute q'', measure ΔT along length, kappa = q''/(ΔT/L)).
extracted_data.interatomic_potential: Three-body Tersoff potential (Tersoff parameterization commonly used for Si/Ge); authors explicitly set Ge equilibrium lattice constant equal to Si within the Tersoff parameters to remove lattice-mismatch strain in the model.
extracted_data.nemd_details: Procedure: Relaxation 500 ps at 300 K under NPT (periodic BCs all directions), then 250 ps equilibration under NVE; impose non-equilibrium by thermostating bulk Si and Ge reservoir regions (20 UCs each attached to ends of multilayer) at 330 K and 270 K using Langevin thermostats; two UCs of atoms at each end fixed for fixed boundary conditions; allow 500 ps to reach steady state; collect temperature and heat flux averaged for 4 ns; compute kappa_l = q''/(ΔT/L). Temperatures are obtained from atomic velocities in 1D bins along cross-plane direction. No explicit extrapolation (length → ∞) procedure reported for kappa; interfacial thermal resistance extracted from local ΔT at interfaces.
extracted_data.simulation_cell_and_convergence: Cross-section: 6 × 6 unit cells (authors state this is sufficient to converge kappa). Total lengths: 20 UC (≈11 nm) and 40 UC (≈22 nm) studied. Timestep: 0.5 fs. Equilibration: 500 ps (NPT) + 250 ps (NVE); steady-state establishment: 500 ps; production averaging: 4 ns. Number of independent runs: multiple runs used for statistical averaging for key comparisons (exact number not stated). Authors state 6×6 cross-section gives converged kappa; no systematic finite-size (length) extrapolation or kappa vs L plot reported in paper.
extracted_data.phonon_scattering_mechanisms_included: Implicit in classical MD with the chosen empirical potential: anharmonic phonon-phonon scattering and interface scattering are included as described by the potential; quantum statistics not included (classical equipartition). No explicit treatment of 4-phonon processes, isotope scattering, electronic scattering, or first-principles IFC-based scattering rates is reported. Interface-induced coherent/incoherent effects are analyzed qualitatively from atomistic temperature profiles and apparent interface resistances.
extracted_data.alloy_modeling_approach: Not applicable to homogeneous Si1-xGex alloys in this study; authors model explicit layered Si and Ge UCs (atomic arrangement is fully resolved); Ge equilibrium lattice constant forcibly set equal to Si in potential to avoid strain — hence no mass-disorder alloy or virtual-crystal approximation is used.
extracted_data.reported_method_comparisons: Within-paper comparisons: CNN-predicted kappa vs NEMD-validated kappa for RMLs (parity plot, Fig.5b) and ML-accelerated search vs manual random search (computational cost and success rate). The paper cites other literature methods (equilibrium MD, atomistic Green's function, first-principles/Green's-function/BTE studies) but does not present direct numerical comparisons of kappa(T) for bulk Si, Ge or SiGe computed by different methods. No GK vs NEMD numerical comparison for bulk Si/Ge kappa(T) is performed in this work.
extracted_data.agreement_with_experiment: The paper references experimental observations of coherent/incoherent crossover in superlattices ([41]-[44]) but does not perform a direct quantitative comparison between the MD kappa values and bulk experimental kappa(T) for crystalline Si, Ge, or SiGe alloys. Authors state their period-dependent trends are consistent qualitatively with prior theory and experiments on SL period dependence.
extracted_data.proposed_reasons_for_discrepancies: Authors identify mechanistic/modeling sources that affect predictions: (1) coherent vs incoherent phonon transport controlled by interface spacing (period) and layer-thickness randomization; (2) apparent interfacial thermal resistance reduction due to increased coherent phonon contribution in certain RMLs; (3) modeling choices: use of classical MD (no quantum correction), choice and parameterization of interatomic potential (Tersoff) and artificial equalization of Ge lattice constant to Si (removing strain) — each can alter phonon dispersion, interface transmission, and anharmonic scattering; (4) finite simulation cell size, thermostat/reservoir setup, averaging time and steady-state criteria can also influence computed kappa. These are discussed qualitatively as reasons why different computational approaches/potentials could predict different kappa values or trends.
extracted_data.notes_on_temperature_dependence: No temperature-dependent kappa(T) curves for crystalline Si, Ge, or SiGe are reported; all MD predictions and reported values are at 300 K (with reservoir temps 330/270 K for NEMD). Paper discusses regime changes (coherent → incoherent) as a function of superlattice period/layer thickness, not as a function of absolute temperature. No statements of T-scaling laws (e.g., ∼T^-1) for these systems are provided in this work.
extracted_data.key_figures_tables_locations: NEMD simulation protocol: Section 2.2. CNN and iterative search details: Sections 2.3–2.4. kappa vs period and RML vs SL comparisons: Fig.4(a) (Section 3.1–3.2). CNN parity and ML search progress: Fig.5 (a–d). Interface resistances and decomposition: Fig.6 (Section 3.3). Tabulated numeric values appear in text (2.28 W/mK for 5–5 SL, 2.36 W/mK for 20 UC RML example, percent enhancements noted in Section 3.2).

extracted_data.name_full: Crystalline silicon (bulk diamond-cubic Si)
extracted_data.brief_description: First-principles prediction of the lattice thermal conductivity of bulk crystalline silicon at room temperature (300 K) including both intrinsic anharmonic phonon-phonon scattering and electron-phonon interaction (EPI); shows EPI becomes significant for carrier concentrations >10^19 cm^-3 and can reduce lattice κ by up to 45% at 10^21 cm^-3 (p-type).
extracted_data.citation_title: Significant Reduction of Lattice Thermal Conductivity by the Electron-Phonon Interaction in Silicon with High Carrier Concentrations: A First-Principles Study
extracted_data.structure_and_phase: bulk, crystalline (diamond-cubic) silicon; bulk single-crystal context implied
extracted_data.temperature_points_K: 300 K (all calculations reported in this paper are performed at room temperature, 300 K)
extracted_data.thermal_conductivity_values: Numerical W/mK values are not tabulated in the text; reported results summarized as: effect of EPI negligible below 1e18 cm^-3; EPI begins to reduce lattice κ for carrier concentrations >1e19 cm^-3; maximum reported reduction of lattice thermal conductivity up to 45% for p-type Si at carrier concentration ≈1e21 cm^-3. (Exact absolute κ(300 K) values are shown in Fig. 4 of the paper but not given numerically in the text.)
extracted_data.kappa_definition_and_components: Reported conductivity is lattice thermal conductivity (κ_l) only; electronic thermal conductivity is treated separately and not included in κ_l (paper estimates electronic κ_e < ~1 W/mK for n>1e20 cm^-3 using Wiedemann–Franz, but reported κ values are lattice-only). The lattice κ is computed by combining intrinsic phonon-phonon lifetimes (anharmonic) with electron-phonon scattering lifetimes (EPI); lifetimes are defined within a relaxation-time-approximation (RTA) framework for phonon scattering.
extracted_data.method_category: first-principles PBTE/DFT (phonon lifetimes from DFPT/DFT and EPI matrix elements; intrinsic phonon-phonon lifetimes from first-principles anharmonic calculations)
extracted_data.simulation_cell_and_convergence: Not applicable (no empirical MD). Convergence details given for Brillouin-zone sampling: EPI matrix elements originally computed on 12×12×12 k-point mesh and 6×6×6 q-point mesh, then interpolated with EPW to fine meshes; final calculations performed on 60×60×60 k and 60×60×60 q meshes. Brillouin-zone integration performed using a tetrahedra method; convergence of phonon lifetimes with respect to k-mesh density was checked.
extracted_data.first_principles_details: DFT/DFPT calculations performed with Quantum ESPRESSO using a norm-conserving pseudopotential and the Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE) exchange-correlation functional. EPI matrix elements computed via DFPT and interpolated using the EPW code (with modifications to use tetrahedra integration). Initial grids: 12×12×12 k and 6×6×6 q; interpolated to 60×60×60 k and q meshes for final lifetimes. Phonon-phonon (anharmonic) calculations follow methods in Ref. [53] (details of supercell sizes / 3rd-order IFCs / iterative vs RTA solution are referenced to that work and not fully restated in the text). All calculations reported at 300 K.
extracted_data.phonon_scattering_mechanisms_included: Included: intrinsic anharmonic phonon-phonon scattering (phonon-phonon), and electron-phonon interaction (EPI) scattering (both electrons and holes considered). Explicitly not included/omitted or not mentioned: 4-phonon scattering (not discussed), isotope scattering not explicitly mentioned in results, boundary scattering, and impurity/defect scattering (aside from carrier doping which enters via EPI).
extracted_data.reported_method_comparisons: Comparisons performed within the paper: (1) First-principles EPI scattering rates compared to analytic deformation-potential approximation (DPA) asymptotic formulas (Eqs. 3 and 4) for LA and LO modes — good agreement found, with fitted deformation potentials D_A and D_O reported; (2) EPI scattering rates compared to intrinsic phonon-phonon scattering rates (Fig. 3): EPI rates are ≳2 orders of magnitude smaller than phonon-phonon for n<1e18 cm^-3, become comparable in low-frequency region for n>1e19 cm^-3, and exceed phonon-phonon rates for low-frequency phonons at 1e21 cm^-3; (3) holes scatter phonons more efficiently than electrons (numerical comparison shown in figures). The paper does not present a direct comparison between different computational frameworks (e.g., DFT-BTE vs MD) for κ in Si; phonon-phonon calculation procedural details are deferred to Ref. [53].
extracted_data.agreement_with_experiment: No direct quantitative comparison to experiment for the EPI contribution (authors state it is very difficult to isolate EPI contribution experimentally). Qualitative consistency noted: finding that p-type (boron) silicon has lower κ than n-type (phosphorus) at similar doping is consistent with experimental observations (citation [29,65]). Authors estimate electronic κ (via Wiedemann–Franz and experimental σ) to be <~1 W/mK for carrier concentrations above 1e20 cm^-3, and claim this is much smaller than the predicted reduction in lattice κ.
extracted_data.proposed_reasons_for_discrepancies: Explanations offered for observed behavior and differences: (a) anisotropy of conduction-band electron pockets vs isotropic hole pocket leads to electrons being less effective scatterers (intervalley scattering for electrons increases zone-boundary phonon scattering); (b) previous analytic models (Ziman) are insufficient at high carrier concentrations and at higher temperatures; (c) convergence challenges for EPI calculations require very fine k/q meshes — authors used interpolation (Wannier/EPW) and tetrahedra integration to improve convergence; (d) omission of other scattering mechanisms (e.g., 4-phonon, isotope scattering) could affect absolute κ but are not the focus here. The paper does not claim method-inherent artifacts from, e.g., classical vs quantum statistics or MD thermostat artifacts since MD was not used.
extracted_data.notes_on_temperature_dependence: Calculations in this paper are all at 300 K; no explicit κ(T) curves are reported. Analytical asymptotic DPA formulas (Eqs. 3 and 4) include explicit temperature dependence (e.g., ∝(k_B T)^(-3/2) prefactors in nondegenerate regime), and the authors discuss that EPI scattering rates saturate as carrier concentration approaches the degenerate regime. They also note LA-mode EPI scattering rates scale linearly with phonon frequency near the zone center and the slope scales linearly with carrier concentration in the nondegenerate regime.
extracted_data.key_figures_tables_locations: Main results located in: Fig. 1 (EPI scattering rates across Brillouin zone at n=1e21 cm^-3), Fig. 2 (comparison between first-principles EPI scattering rates and DPA asymptotic predictions for LA and LO modes), Fig. 3 (comparison of EPI scattering rates vs intrinsic phonon-phonon scattering rates at 1e21 cm^-3), Fig. 4 (calculated lattice thermal conductivity of silicon as function of carrier concentration at 300 K, showing up to 45% reduction), Fig. 5 (phonon mean free paths with and without EPI at 1e21 cm^-3). Additional methodological details on meshes and interpolation are in the main text; supplemental material [64] contains EPI scattering rates at other carrier concentrations.
extracted_data.additional_notes: EPI matrix elements computed using DFPT and interpolated with maximally localized Wannier functions via EPW; EPW code was modified to use tetrahedra integration for Brillouin-zone integration. Deformation-potential fits extracted: D_A ≈ 2.6 eV (electrons), D_O ≈ 0.5×10^6 eV/cm (electrons), D_A ≈ 2.4 eV (holes), D_O ≈ 5×10^6 eV/cm (holes) — quoted when comparing DPA analytic predictions to first-principles scattering rates.

extracted_data.name_full: Bulk crystalline silicon (diamond cubic) lattice thermal conductivity predicted with Pheasy-extracted IFCs and PBTE (ShengBTE / FourPhonon)
extracted_data.brief_description: First-principles predictions of lattice thermal conductivity (LTC) for bulk silicon across ≈200–1000 K using DFT-derived force constants (IFCs) fitted with Pheasy and transport solved with ShengBTE (3-phonon iteratively, 4-phonon in RTA). The paper reports numerical values (e.g., kappa_3ph(300 K) ≈ 125.4 W m^-1 K^-1 and kappa_3+4ph(300 K) ≈ 115.4 W m^-1 K^-1) and compares levels of theory (HA, 3ph, 3+4ph, SCP, IFCs@T).
extracted_data.structure_and_phase: bulk, crystalline (diamond-cubic) silicon; natural isotopic abundance unless otherwise stated
extracted_data.temperature_points_K: reported curve 200–1000 K (Fig. 1(c)); supplementary tables show values at 200–900 K and specific reported room-temperature (300 K) numbers
extracted_data.thermal_conductivity_values: Representative values at 300 K: 3-phonon (HA+3ph) / PBTE iterative: 125.4 W m^-1 K^-1 (main-text value, also Supplementary Table 1 shows 124.85–125.40 W m^-1 K^-1 for two ensembles); including 4-phonon (HA+3,4ph) reduces to ≈115.4 W m^-1 K^-1 (7.9% drop; Supplementary Table 1 values ≈115.13–115.54 W m^-1 K^-1). Additional rows: SCP+3ph ~122.3–122.5 W m^-1 K^-1; SCP+3,4ph ~112.2–112.5 W m^-1 K^-1; variants with temperature-dependent IFCs (IFCs@T) shown in Supplementary Table 1 (e.g., SCP+3ph+IFCs@T ~124.6–125.9 W m^-1 K^-1). Units: W m^-1 K^-1. Direction: isotropic/averaged bulk value (scalar).
extracted_data.kappa_definition_and_components: Reported quantity is lattice thermal conductivity (LTC) computed from the phonon Boltzmann transport equation (phonon-only, lattice contribution); electronic heat conduction explicitly not included. Calculations include three-phonon scattering (iterative PBTE), optional four-phonon scattering (FourPhonon module in RTA), and isotope scattering (natural abundance). Temperature-dependent phonon renormalization is treated in separate runs (SCP) and temperature-dependent IFCs (IFCs@T) are constructed and tested; decomposition into HA, 3ph, 4ph and temperature-renormalization contributions is reported.
extracted_data.method_category: first-principles PBTE/DFT (DFT-derived IFCs → PBTE with ShengBTE; FourPhonon extension for 4ph)
extracted_data.simulation_cell_and_convergence: IFC extraction: 4x4x4 supercell (128 atoms) used for the silicon Taylor expansion and IFC fitting; initial harmonic IFCs from 5 random displacements (0.01 Å), training ensembles of 64 finite-temperature displaced supercells used for higher-order fits. LTC convergence: phonon q-grid up to 30x30x30 used to converge LTC. DFT supercell electronic sampling: shifted 2x2x2 k-grid for supercell calculations. No MD timesteps; finite-size behavior addressed by q-grid convergence and supercell size for IFCs (4x4x4).
extracted_data.first_principles_details: DFT code: Quantum ESPRESSO; exchange-correlation functional for silicon: PBEsol; plane-wave cutoff: 60 Ry (with stated multiples for charge density expansion); primitive-cell k-grid: 14x14x14; supercell k-grid (supercell calculations): shifted 2x2x2. IFC extraction: Pheasy fitted up to sixth-order Taylor expansion (2nd–6th order IFCs) using adaptive-LASSO (sensing matrix standardization), with cutoffs: 3rd-order up to 5th-nearest neighbor (~6.3 Å), higher orders up to 3rd-nearest (~5.0 Å); some restrictions on many-body rank for 5th/6th orders (max three-body). Phonon renormalization: real-space self-consistent phonons (SCP) including the loop (quartic) self-energy; caution about bubble (cubic) diagram: bubble-corrected frequencies should not be used in PBTE unless self-consistent. PBTE solver: ShengBTE for iterative solution of 3ph; FourPhonon (or ShengBTE extension) for 4ph in RTA; 4ph sampling accelerated using a 1e5-process sampling scheme. Born charges / LO-TO corrections not specifically required for Si (non-polar).
extracted_data.phonon_scattering_mechanisms_included: Three-phonon (3ph) scattering (iterative PBTE), four-phonon (4ph) scattering (included in RTA via FourPhonon extension), isotope (mass-defect) scattering at natural abundance; omitted: electron-phonon scattering, boundary scattering, impurity scattering beyond isotopes (unless specified otherwise).
extracted_data.alloy_modeling_approach: not applicable (pure crystalline silicon only; no SiGe alloy modeling in this paper)
extracted_data.reported_method_comparisons: Explicit comparisons reported: (1) HA+3ph vs HA+3,4ph showing 4ph lowers LTC (7.9% reduction at 300 K); (2) PBTE results using Pheasy-extracted cubic IFCs agree with thirdorder.py/Phonopy third-order IFCs when using consistent DFT parameters (3ph LTC ~124.3 W m^-1 K^-1), validating extraction; (3) levels of theory comparison (HA, 3ph, 3+4ph, SCP, IFCs@T) in Fig.1(d) and Supplementary Table 1: room-temperature LTC is relatively insensitive to inclusion of temperature-dependent IFCs for Si (weakly anharmonic); (4) discussion of theoretical consistency: bubble (cubic) self-energy should not be mixed with perturbative 3ph linewidths unless self-consistently treated; (5) comparisons with experiment (Refs. [88–90]) shown in Fig.1(c). Numerical differences: 3ph ~125 W/mK vs 3+4ph ~115 W/mK at 300 K; SCP variants show small shifts (see Supplementary Table 1).
extracted_data.agreement_with_experiment: Paper compares calculated LTC to experimental datasets (Refs. [88–90] Shanks 1963, Glassbrenner & Slack 1964, Inyushkin et al. 2004). The 3ph PBTE results give overall good agreement across the temperature range in Fig.1(c), but calculations underpredict experimental LTC below ≈400 K; authors attribute the underprediction to the use of the PBEsol exchange-correlation functional rather than methodological transport shortcomings. No detailed experimental error bars given in the text beyond citation of those datasets.
extracted_data.proposed_reasons_for_discrepancies: Authors discuss multiple sources of method-dependent differences: (a) exchange-correlation functional choice (PBEsol leads to underprediction below ~400 K); (b) inclusion or omission of 4-phonon scattering (4ph reduces LTC, effect grows with temperature); (c) incorrect mixing of bubble-corrected phonon frequencies with perturbative 3ph linewidths (theory inconsistency) can produce spurious results; (d) finite supercell size / insufficient q-grid can affect LTC convergence (noted for SrTiO3 example where small supercell underestimates LTC); (e) differences in IFC-extraction flavor (one-shot simultaneous multi-order fitting recommended; cocktail approach with harmonic IFCs fixed can give inconsistent anharmonic IFCs and downstream errors). Classical vs quantum statistics / MD artifacts are not relevant for the PBTE results presented but are discussed generically in the guidelines.
extracted_data.notes_on_temperature_dependence: Phonon frequencies show overall red-shift with increasing temperature (optical modes more affected); 4-phonon scattering increases importance at high temperatures and reduces LTC (e.g., 7.9% decrease at 300 K, larger at higher T). For silicon, authors find weak anharmonicity: inclusion of temperature-dependent IFCs (IFCs@T) makes little difference in room-temperature LTC. No explicit fitted power-law exponent is reported in the text for high-T scaling, but standard high-T trend (decreasing with T) is observed; detailed kappa(T) curves are in Fig.1(c) and Supplementary Table 1.
extracted_data.key_figures_tables_locations: Main-text Fig. 1(c): LTC vs temperature (200–1000 K) compared with experiments; Fig. 1(d): room-temperature LTC under increasing levels of approximation (HA, 3ph, 3+4ph, SCP, IFCs@T); Supplementary Table 1: tabulated LTC numbers for silicon and WS2 for different theory levels (values at 300 K and other temperatures); Supplementary Fig. 1 and Supplementary Fig. 2 show related phonon/transport diagnostics.

extracted_data.name_full: Bulk intrinsic crystalline silicon (diamond cubic)
extracted_data.brief_description: First-principles PBTE/DFT calculation of phononic (lattice) thermal conductivity of naturally occurring bulk Si from 100 K to 1500 K, including 3-phonon, 4-phonon and isotope scattering; additionally calculates electronic thermal conductivity and reports total kappa.
extracted_data.structure_and_phase: diamond cubic, bulk, naturally occurring isotopic composition (g_Si = 2.01e-4)
extracted_data.temperature_points_K: 100–1500 K (continuous curve; specific points discussed: 300 K, 600 K, 800 K, 900 K, 1000 K, 1500 K)
extracted_data.thermal_conductivity_values: Phononic (lattice) results: - Three-phonon only with 0 K IFCs: at 900 K reported as 43 W/mK (stated as ~20% larger than measurement at that T). - Phononic including 3ph + 4ph + isotope + (temperature-dependent IFCs / thermal expansion tested): phononic kappa at 1500 K = 14.2 W/mK. - Room-temperature statements: omission of 4ph overestimates kappa by ~8% at 300 K. Total (phonons + electrons): at 1500 K total kappa = 19.3 W/mK (compared to Glassbrenner & Slack experimental 22.7 W/mK). (Numerical uncertainties: mesh convergence extrapolated via 1/N fit; experimental uncertainty for e-contribution quoted ±0.5 W/mK in ref.)
extracted_data.kappa_definition_and_components: Paper distinguishes phononic (kappa_ph) and electronic (kappa_e) contributions: kappa = kappa_ph + kappa_e. Phononic component computed mode-by-mode (PBTE, RTA) with contributions from 3-phonon, 4-phonon and isotope scattering; electronic component decomposed into polar (electron and hole) and bipolar parts computed from first-principles electron-phonon scattering (EPW). Reported phononic values are lattice-only unless otherwise stated; total kappa includes both components.
extracted_data.method_category: first-principles PBTE/DFT (DFT-derived interatomic force constants + PBTE in RTA)
extracted_data.simulation_cell_and_convergence: Force constants extracted from supercell displacements in 3×3×3 conventional cubic supercells (216 atoms). q-point meshes for BTE zone integration: calculations performed with N = 16, 20, 24, 28 and then linearly extrapolated vs 1/N to obtain mesh-independent kappa (1/N -> 0). Four-phonon scattering computational cost handled by extrapolating 4ph scattering rates from a mesh with N = 12 to larger meshes. No timestep/run-length (MD) because no MD used.
extracted_data.first_principles_details: DFT code: QUANTUM ESPRESSO. Exchange-correlation functional: PBEsol GGA. Plane-wave cutoff: 45 Ry. Force constants: harmonic and anharmonic IFCs extracted by finite-displacement force-displacement fitting in supercells; TDEP used to obtain temperature-dependent effective harmonic and higher-order IFCs. Anharmonic orders included: third-order (3rd) and fourth-order (4th) IFCs. Phonon dynamical properties: DFPT used for electron-phonon properties (separate). BTE solution: relaxation time approximation (RTA) used (iterative solution not used). Brillouin-zone integrations: q-mesh extrapolation described above. Electron transport: EPW used with dense meshes (40×40×40 q mesh for some EPW inputs and 100×100×100 k-mesh for electron-phonon convergence weighting). Band-gap correction: DFT gap (0.75 eV) replaced with temperature-dependent experimental Varshni gap via rigid band shift.
extracted_data.phonon_scattering_mechanisms_included: Included: three-phonon scattering (3ph), four-phonon scattering (4ph), phonon-isotope scattering (Tamura theory). Omitted or not included explicitly for phonon thermal conductivity: phonon-electron (phonon-electron scattering on phonon kappa was not included because considered negligible at intrinsic carrier concentrations in this study), boundary scattering, impurity/extrinsic scattering (beyond natural isotopes).
extracted_data.reported_method_comparisons: Explicit internal comparisons: - 3ph-only (with 0 K IFCs) vs 3ph+4ph: including 4ph significantly reduces kappa above ~500–700 K and brings phononic predictions into agreement with experiment up to ~1000 K; example: at 900 K 3ph-only = 43 W/mK (~20% too high). - 0 K IFCs vs temperature-dependent IFCs (TDEP): temperature-dependent IFCs change phonon frequencies (max freq downshift from 508 to 480 cm^-1 from 300K to 1500K) and lead to net ~+3% difference in kappa (i.e., phonon renormalization minor for Si). - Thermal expansion: changing lattice constant by +0.5% at 1500 K reduces kappa by ~1.5%. - RTA vs iterative: RTA acknowledged to underestimate kappa; previous literature indicates iterative vs RTA difference <4% for Si at RT. Numerical differences summarized above.
extracted_data.agreement_with_experiment: Phononic 3ph-only overpredicts experiment above ~500 K; inclusion of 4ph improves agreement up to ~1000 K. At 1500 K phononic-only theory (even with 4ph etc.) = 14.2 W/mK while experimental total reported by Glassbrenner & Slack is 22.7 W/mK; when electronic contribution (calculated here) is added, total kappa = 19.3 W/mK, closer to experiment but still slightly lower. Authors cite possible reasons: RTA underestimation of phononic kappa and scatter in high-T experimental datasets. Experimental datasets used for comparison: Glassbrenner & Slack (1964), Fulkerson et al. (1968), Shanks et al. (1963).
extracted_data.proposed_reasons_for_discrepancies: Reasons discussed: (1) Missing four-phonon scattering in previous PBTE studies leads to overprediction at high T; (2) RTA solution of PBTE underestimates phononic kappa compared to iterative solution (authors did not perform iterative because of computational cost); (3) phonon-electron scattering negligible under intrinsic carrier concentrations here, so omission not a large source of discrepancy; (4) temperature-dependent IFCs (phonon renormalization) have minor effect in Si but could matter in more anharmonic materials; (5) experimental uncertainty/scatter at T>1000 K; (6) approximations in DFT electronic structure (band-gap underestimation) corrected by empirical Varshni shift for electron transport.
extracted_data.notes_on_temperature_dependence: Key reported dependences: - Three-phonon scattering lifetimes scale roughly as T^-1; four-phonon lifetimes scale roughly as T^-2, so 4ph becomes increasingly important at high T (dominant importance > ~500–700 K). - Inclusion of 4ph makes kappa fall more rapidly with T than 3ph-only. - Phonon renormalization reduces frequencies (group velocities down ~4% from 100 K to 1500 K) and yields slightly longer lifetimes, net small effect (~+3% change in kappa vs 0 K IFCs). - Thermal expansion small effect (~-1.5% kappa at 1500 K for +0.5% lattice expansion). - Electronic contribution becomes significant at high T (electronic kappa ~5.09 W/mK at 1500 K; electrons conduct >25% of heat at 1500 K).
extracted_data.key_figures_tables_locations: Phononic kappa vs T: Fig. 1(a) (Section IV.A). Phonon dispersion and T-dependent frequencies: Fig. 2 (Section IV.A). Phonon lifetimes vs frequency at 300 and 1500 K: Fig. 3 (Section IV.A). Electronic thermal conductivity: Fig. 4 (Section IV.B). Total thermal conductivity (phonons+electrons) vs T: Fig. 6 (Section IV.C).

extracted_data.name_full: Crystalline silicon lattice thermal conductivity predicted by first-principles PBTE/DFT
extracted_data.brief_description: First-principles predictions of the lattice (phononic) thermal conductivity of crystalline silicon using DFT-derived interatomic force constants and solution of the phonon Boltzmann transport equation (both reciprocal-space/DFPT and real-space IFC approaches are discussed). These calculations reproduce experimental kappa(T) trends and absolute values much better than classical empirical-MD for bulk Si.
extracted_data.citation_title: Intrinsic lattice thermal conductivity of semiconductors from first principles.
extracted_data.structure_and_phase: bulk crystalline Si (diamond cubic); natural/isotropic crystal discussed (no special isotopic purity stated for the plotted comparisons)
extracted_data.temperature_points_K: Temperature dependence shown in Fig.10(a) (thermal conductivity versus temperature from first-principles calculations and experiments); key reference point: 300 K (see text and figures). Exact plotted temperature range not numerically listed in text but includes low-T peak and high-T decay regimes (figure).
extracted_data.thermal_conductivity_values: Representative values cited in text: bulk Si thermal conductivity ~150 W m^-1 K^-1 (around 300 K). Fig.10(a) shows first-principles kappa(T) curves that agree with experimental symbols (no tabulated numeric curve values in text).
extracted_data.kappa_definition_and_components: Lattice (phononic) thermal conductivity (kappa_p) only; electronic contribution excluded. First-principles workflow separates harmonic and anharmonic contributions (harmonic eigenmodes from IFCs, anharmonic scattering rates via Fermi's golden rule) and integrates over Brillouin zone to obtain kappa.
extracted_data.method_category: first-principles PBTE/DFT (DFPT reciprocal-space and real-space IFC approaches described)
extracted_data.first_principles_details: Two approaches described: reciprocal-space DFPT (density functional perturbation theory) to obtain force constants (Broido et al. approach), and real-space finite-displacement / polynomial fitting of DFT forces in supercells (Esfarjani et al. approach). Harmonic (2nd) and anharmonic (3rd) IFCs are obtained and used to compute phonon eigenmodes and 3-phonon scattering rates via Fermi's golden rule; solutions obtained either under single-mode relaxation time approximation (RTA) or via iterative (full) solution of the linearized BTE — both approaches are discussed in the review as used in the literature. Exact DFT code, pseudopotentials, cutoffs, q-mesh sizes, supercell sizes are not specified in this review (references cited for details).
extracted_data.phonon_scattering_mechanisms_included: Intrinsic anharmonic 3-phonon scattering (via Fermi's golden rule) is included in the first-principles PBTE calculations; isotope scattering and other perturbative scatterings are discussed as additions in literature, but the review highlights 3-phonon as primary in the cited first-principles works; iterative vs single-mode RTA solution differences are noted.
extracted_data.reported_method_comparisons: The review states that first-principles PBTE (reciprocal-space DFPT and real-space IFC fitting) reproduces experimental kappa(T) for Si very well (cites Broido et al., Esfarjani et al.). It contrasts these successes with discrepancies observed when using empirical interatomic potentials in MD for thermal conductivity predictions (empirical potentials can deviate significantly, see ref.149). The review also notes differences between RTA and iterative BTE solutions (iterative can differ and is sometimes required for accurate results).
extracted_data.agreement_with_experiment: Review reports excellent agreement between first-principles PBTE results and experimental measurements for Si (Fig.10(a) shows lines from first-principles overlaid with experimental symbols). No quantified residuals are given in the review text.
extracted_data.proposed_reasons_for_discrepancies: Where discrepancies occur (mainly with empirical-MD predictions), the review attributes them to: limitations/inaccuracy of empirical interatomic potentials (phonon dispersion and anharmonicity mismatch), classical (non-quantum) statistics in MD leading to errors below Debye temperature, finite-size effects and insufficient convergence in MD, and methodological differences (RTA vs iterative PBTE). For first-principles RTA vs iterative solutions, omission of coupling between modes (i.e., neglect of off-diagonal terms in collision operator) can cause quantitative differences.
extracted_data.notes_on_temperature_dependence: Review summarizes universal behavior: low-T ~ T^3 (boundary-limited/Casimir regime), peak at intermediate T, high-T decreases approximately as T^n with n~1–1.5 due to Umklapp scattering; first-principles calculations reproduce these trends for Si (peak and high-T decay).
extracted_data.key_figures_tables_locations: Fig.10(a) (thermal conductivity versus temperature from first-principles calculations and experimental measurements) and Sect.4.1 (discussion of first-principles PBTE and references to Broido et al. and Esfarjani et al.). Also Fig.10(b) and Fig.11 provide related MFP accumulation and experimental comparisons for Si.

extracted_data.reported_method_comparisons: Review reports that first-principles calculations (reciprocal-space DFPT) reproduce experimental kappa(T) for Ge well (Fig.10(a)). It contrasts these successful ab initio approaches with less successful empirical-MD approaches in other systems.
extracted_data.agreement_with_experiment: Described as excellent agreement (Fig.10(a) shows first-principles lines and experimental symbols overlapping for Ge). No numerical error bars reported in the review.
extracted_data.proposed_reasons_for_discrepancies: Noted general reasons for discrepancies between methods: empirical potentials may poorly capture dispersion and anharmonicity; MD is classical and requires quantum corrections at low T; omission of certain scattering mechanisms or use of approximate solutions (RTA) can lead to differences.
extracted_data.notes_on_temperature_dependence: Same universal trends as for Si: low-T boundary-limited T^3, intermediate-peak, high-T decay roughly T^-1 to T^-1.5 due to Umklapp processes; first-principles captures these features for Ge.
extracted_data.key_figures_tables_locations: Fig.10(a) (thermal conductivity versus temperature from first-principles calculations and experimental measurements) and Sect.4.1 (discussion of first-principles PBTE and references to Broido et al.).

extracted_data.name_full: Lattice thermal conductivity predictions for Si1-xGex alloys (Si-Ge alloys)
extracted_data.brief_description: Discussion of computational predictions for Si1-xGex alloy lattice thermal conductivity: empirical-MD NEMD studies have shown large discrepancies with experiment, whereas first-principles force constants combined with virtual-crystal/alloy scattering models (DFPT + VCA/Tamura/Abeles-type treatments) (e.g., Garg et al.) reproduce experimental kappa(T). The review contrasts modeling approaches and highlights modeling choices that explain differences.
extracted_data.citation_title: Role of Disorder and Anharmonicity in the Thermal Conductivity of Silicon-Germanium Alloys: A First-Principles Study.
extracted_data.material_system: Si1-xGex alloy (Si-Ge alloy), various compositions discussed generally; specific experimental composition example: Si0.8Ge0.2 noted elsewhere in paper but alloy discussion treats 0<=x<=1
extracted_data.composition_x: general 0 <= x <= 1 (text mentions Si1-xGex alloys and specific commonly-used composition Si0.8Ge0.2 in other contexts); review cites experimental Si1-xGex thermal conductivity falling below ~10 W m^-1 K^-1 (reference 48) for alloy mixtures.
extracted_data.structure_and_phase: substitutional solid-solution (alloy) modeled via virtual crystal / average-crystal approaches in many theoretical treatments; disorder (mass and possibly force-constant disorder) discussed. Crystal structure assumed same as parent (diamond cubic) in virtual-crystal treatments.
extracted_data.temperature_points_K: Temperature dependence of alloy kappa discussed qualitatively (figures for related materials shown in Fig.10(a) for pure materials; alloy experimental values cited at 300 K in text). Review does not provide explicit numeric kappa(T) curves for Si1-xGex in text, but states measured thermal conductivity can fall to below ~10 W m^-1 K^-1 (300 K).
extracted_data.thermal_conductivity_values: Experimental statement: measured thermal conductivity of Si1-xGex can sharply fall down to below ~10 W m^-1 K^-1 (cited ref.48). The review states that Garg et al. (DFPT + virtual crystal) were able to reproduce experimental thermal conductivity of Si1-xGex; NEMD with empirical potentials gave large discrepancies (ref.189). No explicit numerical DFT curve values are tabulated in the review text.
extracted_data.kappa_definition_and_components: Lattice thermal conductivity (kappa_p) of the alloy; electronic contribution not primary focus here. In virtual-crystal treatments kappa is computed using modified dispersion and added impurity scattering terms (mass-disorder scattering), typically combined via Matthiessen's rule with anharmonic scattering.
extracted_data.method_category: hybrid: first-principles force constants (DFPT) + virtual crystal/alloy scattering models (Garg et al.); also empirical-potential MD (NEMD) studies are discussed and contrasted.
extracted_data.md_flavor: NEMD (nonequilibrium MD) with empirical interatomic potentials; review notes these NEMD simulations yielded large discrepancies with experiments for SiGe alloys (ref.189).
extracted_data.interatomic_potential: For the empirical-MD studies the review does not list a specific potential name in the text for the Si-Ge NEMD discrepant studies, only that empirical potentials were used and caused deviations; the review references Skye & Schelling (ref.189) for MD on Si-Ge alloys where potentials are used.
extracted_data.nemd_details: Review remarks general NEMD drawbacks: finite simulation size potentially shorter than relevant phonon MFPs, artificial size effects from heat reservoirs, and use of large temperature differences across small domains; these methodological issues can cause discrepancy in predicted kappa for alloys when using NEMD with empirical potentials.
extracted_data.simulation_cell_and_convergence: Review highlights that NEMD suffers from finite-size effects and that MD-accessible sizes are limited; specific cell sizes, timesteps, run lengths not provided in the review (see cited MD papers).
extracted_data.first_principles_details: Garg et al. used DFPT-derived force constants in combination with a virtual crystal model to compute phonon dispersions and anharmonic scattering rates; mass-disorder scattering and alloy disorder treated perturbatively (Abeles-style/ Tamura-type approaches) and included alongside intrinsic anharmonic scattering to obtain alloy kappa. The review notes real-space fitting and DFPT reciprocal approaches as two ways to obtain IFCs; specific computational parameters (codes, cutoffs, meshes) are not listed in the review itself.
extracted_data.phonon_scattering_mechanisms_included: Intrinsic anharmonic (3-phonon) scattering plus alloy impurity/mass-disorder scattering treated perturbatively (Rayleigh-type low-frequency limit, Tamura model that incorporates DOS) in the DFPT+VCA studies; other terms (e.g., force-constant disorder beyond mass-only, multiple-scattering/dependent scattering) are discussed as potentially important but not always included.
extracted_data.alloy_modeling_approach: Virtual crystal approximation (VCA) / Abeles-type approach: form a new 'average' crystal with averaged masses and force constants, compute modified dispersion, then add mass-disorder scattering as a perturbation (Rayleigh-like or Tamura formalism). Garg et al. used DFPT force constants + virtual crystal model; the review notes questions about the validity of perturbative (first-order) impurity scattering in the non-dilute limit and about whether only mass disorder vs force-constant disorder is sufficient.
extracted_data.reported_method_comparisons: Explicit comparisons noted: empirical-potential NEMD studies gave large discrepancies with measured values for SiGe alloys (ref.189), while DFPT + virtual-crystal approach (Garg et al.) reproduced experimental thermal conductivity successfully. The review emphasizes that hybrid first-principles + alloy-scattering modeling matched experiment better than direct empirical-MD for SiGe alloys. Shiomi et al. are mentioned as performing EMD using first-principles-derived force constants for other alloyed systems and obtaining reasonable agreement.
extracted_data.agreement_with_experiment: The review reports that DFPT+VCA (Garg et al.) reproduces experimental thermal conductivity of Si1-xGex; conversely, NEMD with empirical potentials showed significant deviations from experiments (Skye & Schelling ref.). Experimental data quoted: Si1-xGex kappa falls to below ~10 W m^-1 K^-1 at 300 K.
extracted_data.proposed_reasons_for_discrepancies: Review lists reasons for method-dependent differences: empirical potentials may not capture accurate phonon dispersions and anharmonicity for alloys; MD is classical and misses quantum occupation effects (important below Debye temperature); perturbative impurity-scattering models (Rayleigh/Tamura) may be invalid at high frequencies or in non-dilute alloys; force-constant disorder (changes in IFCs due to substitution) may be important but is not always included (VCA often treats mass-only disorder); dependence of scattering on whether impurity frequencies fall inside/outside host phonon bands; finite-size effects and thermostat/large gradient artifacts in NEMD; insufficient treatment of dependent scattering and localization effects.
extracted_data.notes_on_temperature_dependence: Review reiterates general crystalline trends (low-T boundary-limited, intermediate peak, high-T ~ T^-1 to T^-1.5). For alloys, strong suppression of kappa at room temperature is emphasized (down to <~10 W m^-1 K^-1 for SiGe alloys); no explicit fitted temperature exponents for alloys are provided in the review text.
extracted_data.key_figures_tables_locations: Alloy discussion in Sect.5.1 (Alloy) and references therein; the success of DFPT+VCA is mentioned in Sect.5.1 with citation to Garg et al. (ref.155). Discrepancies of empirical NEMD are mentioned in same section (ref.189). General temperature-vs-kappa comparisons for pure materials are in Fig.10(a).

extracted_data.name_full: Equilibrium Molecular Dynamics (Green–Kubo) lattice thermal conductivity predictions for crystalline silicon (this paper)
extracted_data.brief_description: Lattice thermal conductivity of pristine and nanostructured crystalline Si (grain-boundary 'superlattice' and nanopores) computed by equilibrium MD using the Green–Kubo HCACF method with a force-matched Stillinger–Weber potential in LAMMPS; reported at 300 K and compared to literature values at 350 K.
extracted_data.material_system: Si (crystalline; pristine and nanostructured: superlattice grain boundaries and pores)
extracted_data.structure_and_phase: Diamond cubic silicon (8-atom unit cell); simulated supercells with rotated grains producing grain boundaries; some local amorphicity near grain-boundary contacts after annealing noted
extracted_data.temperature_points_K: 300 K (MD simulations equilibrated at 300 K); literature comparisons referenced at 350 K and broader ranges in cited experimental works
extracted_data.thermal_conductivity_values: Pristine (EMD-GK, 300 K): 207.41 ± 11.51 W m^-1 K^-1; Superlattice (grain boundaries, 300 K): 41.99 ± 2.47 W m^-1 K^-1 (~5× reduction vs pristine MD); Pores (4.6% porosity, 300 K): 29.14 ± 2.48 W m^-1 K^-1 (~7.1× reduction vs pristine MD); SL + pores (300 K): 12.10 ± 1.33 W m^-1 K^-1 (~17.1× reduction vs pristine MD). Literature experimental baseline used: ~101.5 W m^-1 K^-1 (350 K).
extracted_data.kappa_definition_and_components: Lattice thermal conductivity computed from equilibrium MD Green–Kubo via integration of the heat-current autocorrelation function (HCACF); reported values are lattice-only (no separate electronic contribution); classical MD was used and no quantum correction is reported.
extracted_data.method_category: empirical-potential MD
extracted_data.interatomic_potential: Stillinger–Weber (SW) potential with force-matched parameter set optimized to DFT-GGA (Lee & Hwang, 2012)
extracted_data.emd_gk_details: Procedure reported: relax structure with conjugate-gradient; NPT run at 300 K for 125 ps with 0.5 fs timestep (allows thermal expansion); anneal near grain-boundary contacts; NVE equilibration 125 ps; NVE production 10 ns with 2 fs timestep while recording HCACF; HCACF (non-normalized) integrated per Green–Kubo to obtain kappa_xx; periodic boundary conditions in all directions; sets of 10 independent calculations performed for each geometry. The paper does not explicitly state the exact heat-flux definition used, the correlation-time cutoff/integration window, use of multiple time origins, or fitting procedures.
extracted_data.simulation_cell_and_convergence: Simulation cell: 184 × 14 × 10 supercells of Si (diamond-cubic 8-atom unit cell) => 184*14*10*8 = 206,080 atoms; periodic boundary conditions in all directions; timestep: 0.5 fs during NPT, 2 fs during NVE production; production length: 10 ns; number of replicas: 10 independent runs per geometry; authors state the pristine system has been converged for size but no detailed size-extrapolation (e.g., kappa vs 1/L) or systematic finite-size extrapolation is presented.
extracted_data.phonon_scattering_mechanisms_included: Anharmonic phonon-phonon scattering is included implicitly by classical MD to all orders; boundary scattering from explicit pores and grain boundaries included via atomistic geometry; isotope scattering and electron-phonon scattering are not explicitly modeled/separated; no explicit treatment of 3- vs 4-phonon processes as MD treats anharmonicity implicitly classically.
extracted_data.reported_method_comparisons: Direct comparisons reported: MD-pristine kappa (207.4 W/mK at 300 K) vs literature experimental kappa (~101.5 W/mK at 350 K) showing MD overprediction; authors quantify reductions due to nanostructures (SL ~5×, pores ~7.1×, combined ~17.1×). They also compare expected Matthiessen's-rule combined value (1/k_SL+pores ≈ 1/k_SL + 1/k_pores giving ~17.2 Wm^-1K^-1) and note the actual combined MD value (12.1 Wm^-1K^-1) gives a larger reduction than that simple estimate.
extracted_data.agreement_with_experiment: MD pristine kappa is significantly higher than the literature experimental value used (207.4 W/mK MD at 300 K vs ~101.5 W/mK experimental at 350 K). The authors explicitly note that the MD thermal conductivity is higher than experimentally realized and attribute this primarily to the choice of interatomic potential.
extracted_data.proposed_reasons_for_discrepancies: Authors state the main cause of MD overprediction is the choice/parameterization of the interatomic potential (SW force-matched parameters still overpredict kappa). They also note annealing introduced some amorphicity near grain-boundary contacts (which would tend to reduce kappa), but the explicit reason given for the MD-experiment discrepancy is the potential; other possible sources (classical vs quantum statistics, HCACF integration/windowing, finite-size effects) are not explicitly discussed in detail.
extracted_data.notes_on_temperature_dependence: Simulations were performed at a single temperature (300 K). The paper does not present kappa(T) predictions or scaling laws; it instead cites experimental kappa(T) datasets (Stranz et al. 2013 up to 900 K and Carruthers 1957 from 2–300 K) for context and uses a 350 K literature data point for ZT baseline.
extracted_data.key_figures_tables_locations: MD method and parameters described in Methods (Section II). Results and all reported kappa values are in Results (Section III) and summarized in Table 1. No figures present kappa as a function of temperature in this paper.

extracted_data.name_full: crystalline silicon (bulk)
extracted_data.brief_description: Lattice thermal conductivity of bulk Si computed by anharmonic lattice dynamics / phonon BTE using both DFT-calculated and HDNNP-predicted interatomic forces; reported κ(300 K)=112.1 W/m·K (DFT) and κ(300 K)=110.4 W/m·K (HDNNP), with HDNNP within 1% of DFT across 200–500 K.
extracted_data.structure_and_phase: bulk, diamond-cubic (conventional unit cell used); DFT/MD training unit cell size for snapshots: 64 atoms; second-/third-order IFC supercells: 2×2×2 conventional cell
extracted_data.temperature_points_K: Comparison/accuracy quoted for 200–500 K; explicit value reported at 300 K; κ(T) curve shown in Figure 3(a) (temperature axis in K).
extracted_data.thermal_conductivity_values: HDNNP: κ(300 K) = 110.4 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹; DFT: κ(300 K) = 112.1 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹. Paper states deviation between HDNNP and DFT is within 1% over 200–500 K. Full κ(T) curve appears in Figure 3(a).
extracted_data.kappa_definition_and_components: Lattice-only thermal conductivity computed from phonon Boltzmann transport equation (linearized BTE) using phonon lifetimes from third-order anharmonic (three-phonon) processes; electronic contribution not included. Single-mode relaxation time approximation (RTA) used to compute κ.
extracted_data.method_category: anharmonic lattice dynamics (ALD) / first-principles PBTE (DFT IFCs) and hybrid approach (HDNNP used to predict forces/IFCs as surrogate for DFT).
extracted_data.interatomic_potential: High-dimensional neural network potential (HDNNP) trained to DFT forces; classical Stillinger–Weber potential (SW) was used only to generate MD snapshots for HDNNP training (MD snapshots: SW in LAMMPS at several temperatures).
extracted_data.simulation_cell_and_convergence: Second-order IFC supercell: 2×2×2 conventional cell (Si); Third-order IFC supercell: 2×2×2 conventional cell (Si); Brillouin-zone sampling for BTE: 11×11×11 q-point mesh; DFT displacement patterns (Si): total of 111 displacement patterns noted; MD snapshots for training: unit cell size = 64 atoms, classical MD 10,000 steps with 0.001 ps timestep used to generate configurations.
extracted_data.first_principles_details: DFT code: VASP (PAW). Exchange–correlation: LDA used for Si. Plane-wave cutoff energy = 550 eV. IFCs obtained by finite-displacement approach via phonopy/phono3py. BTE solved within single-mode RTA (not iterative).
extracted_data.phonon_scattering_mechanisms_included: Three-phonon scattering (third-order anharmonicity) included. Isotope scattering, four-phonon scattering, boundary scattering, and electron–phonon scattering are not mentioned (i.e., not included). Non-analytic LO–TO correction was not included in GaN phonon dispersion calculations (not directly affecting Si).
extracted_data.reported_method_comparisons: Direct within-paper comparison of κ computed using forces from HDNNP versus forces from DFT (VASP) within same ALD/phonon-BTE workflow (phono3py). Numerical comparison for Si: κ_HDNNP(300K)=110.4 W/m·K vs κ_DFT(300K)=112.1 W/m·K; deviation ≤1% over 200–500 K. Computational cost comparison: DFT force evaluations for 111 displacements required 24 CPUs × 4.5 h; HDNNP required 1 CPU × 10 s for same displacement evaluations.
extracted_data.agreement_with_experiment: The paper compares HDNNP results to DFT results (target is reproducing DFT). Phonon dispersions are plotted with experimental data for reference (Fig.2), but no direct experimental κ vs T comparison for Si thermal conductivity is discussed in the text.
extracted_data.proposed_reasons_for_discrepancies: Differences between HDNNP and DFT are attributed to training/force-prediction errors (training optimized to minimize force RMSE). HDNNP model neglects long-range electrostatics (stated as a model choice), which could affect polar materials but is less critical for Si. Additional sources of discrepancy in other materials (GaN example) include small IFC supercell sizes; also the use of single-mode RTA (instead of full iterative solution) can introduce differences relative to more complete treatments.
extracted_data.notes_on_temperature_dependence: Paper reports HDNNP reproduces DFT κ(T) within 1% for 200–500 K for Si; explicit κ values provided at 300 K. No explicit fitted temperature-scaling law (e.g., T⁻¹) is given in the text.
extracted_data.key_figures_tables_locations: Figure 3(a) shows thermal conductivity vs temperature for Si; phonon/IFC details in Methods and Supplementary; force RMSE and training details in main text and Figures 1–3 and Supplementary Materials.
