theory-3.name: Disorder-Representation Dominance (DRD) Theory for SiGe
theory-3.description: In Si1-xGex, once alloy disorder is appreciable, the primary driver of differences in predicted lattice thermal conductivity (κ) across computational studies is not the transport solver (Green–Kubo/Einstein EMD, NEMD, PBTE-RTA, PBTE-iterative), but the representation of disorder itself: (i) periodic small-cell substitution patterns vs large, explicitly random supercells (long-range disorder); (ii) mass-disorder-only (e.g., VCA+Tamura/Abeles) vs models that also include force-constant disorder and non-perturbative multiple scattering; (iii) whether the model permits the emergence of non-propagating/weakly propagating excitations where heat transport is controlled by generalized diffusivity (velocity-like matrix elements) rather than by well-defined phonon group velocities. DRD asserts a characteristic signature: periodic “substituted” alloy cells yield much higher κ than truly random alloys at the same composition, potentially by orders of magnitude, because long-range randomness strongly suppresses generalized velocities/diffusivity of low-frequency heat-carrying excitations even when DOS and linewidth/lifetime trends appear similar. Consequently, solver differences become second-order only after remaining mean free paths are shorter than simulation length scales and after finite-size artifacts are controlled.
theory-3.theory_query: Build theories of how the choice of method (Tersoff and Stillinger-Weber empirical potentials in molecular dynamics, Green-Kubo or nonequilibrium MD, first-principles phonon Boltzmann transport with DFT force constants) changes the predicted lattice thermal conductivity of crystalline silicon, germanium and Si1-xGex, as a function of temperature, based on the following results.

components.theory_name_plain_language: For SiGe alloys, how you model disorder dominates the answer
components.theory_description: In Si1-xGex, once alloy disorder is appreciable, the primary driver of differences in predicted lattice thermal conductivity (κ) across computational studies is not the transport solver (Green–Kubo/Einstein EMD, NEMD, PBTE-RTA, PBTE-iterative), but the representation of disorder itself: (i) periodic small-cell substitution patterns vs large, explicitly random supercells (long-range disorder); (ii) mass-disorder-only (e.g., VCA+Tamura/Abeles) vs models that also include force-constant disorder and non-perturbative multiple scattering; (iii) whether the model permits the emergence of non-propagating/weakly propagating excitations where heat transport is controlled by generalized diffusivity (velocity-like matrix elements) rather than by well-defined phonon group velocities. DRD asserts a characteristic signature: periodic “substituted” alloy cells yield much higher κ than truly random alloys at the same composition, potentially by orders of magnitude, because long-range randomness strongly suppresses generalized velocities/diffusivity of low-frequency heat-carrying excitations even when DOS and linewidth/lifetime trends appear similar. Consequently, solver differences become second-order only after remaining mean free paths are shorter than simulation length scales and after finite-size artifacts are controlled.
components.theory_description_plain_language: In SiGe alloys, simplified or periodic disorder models can drastically overpredict thermal conductivity compared to truly random alloys; this modeling choice often matters more than whether you use GK, NEMD, or BTE.

law.statement_name: Long-range randomness can suppress generalized diffusivity far beyond periodic substituted-cell predictions
law.theory_statement: For substitutional Si–Ge alloys (and closely related group-IV alloys) at fixed composition x, an explicitly random, sufficiently large supercell representation of disorder predicts substantially lower κ than a small periodically repeated substituted-cell model at the same x when long-range disorder is strong enough to reduce generalized heat-carrying velocities/diffusivities. This reduction can occur even when vibrational DOS and three-phonon linewidth/lifetime trends are broadly similar between the two representations, because long-range randomness primarily suppresses transport through reduced generalized velocity (off-diagonal heat-current/velocity matrix elements) and associated diffusivity of low-frequency excitations.
law.theory_statement_plain_language: A truly random alloy can conduct heat far worse than a small repeating ‘ordered alloy pattern’, mainly because long-range randomness destroys how vibrations carry energy across the structure.
law.domain_scope: Applies to substitutional Si–Ge alloy-like disorder where (a) disorder is not extremely dilute and (b) long-wavelength/low-frequency modes would otherwise dominate κ. Most directly supported here for real-space QHGK/ALD formalisms on explicit large supercells, but intended to generalize to any method whose disorder model can be toggled between periodic and truly random realizations (e.g., explicit-supercell PBTE, GK-MD). Not intended for perfectly periodic superlattices/multilayers where interfaces, coherence length, and band folding dominate rather than random-alloy disorder.
special_cases: Dilute limit: for very small x (or 1-x), a small periodic substitution may approximate a random alloy more closely (difference between periodic and random realizations shrinks).

Mass-disorder-only models (e.g., VCA+Tamura/Abeles) may miss force-constant disorder and multiple-scattering/localization-like effects; they may therefore deviate in either direction depending on frequency range and composition.
Short simulation cells or insufficient configurational averaging can mask this effect by introducing additional finite-size/statistical bias.

supporting_evidence.text: For nominally identical composition Si0.85Ge0.15 (clathrate), a periodically replicated substituted-cell model yields κ≈31 W/mK (QHGK on a 5×5×5 replicated supercell of the 136-atom substituted cell), while a truly random 17000-atom alloy realization yields κ≈1.7 W/mK; the authors attribute the large difference mainly to strong suppression of generalized diffusivity/velocities (especially for <3 THz modes), with DOS and lifetimes not changing comparably.

The same study reports that the periodically substituted 15% Ge case has κ≈33 W/mK from BTE-RTA on the 136-atom substituted cell, and κ≈31 W/mK from QHGK on its periodic replica, indicating that the very low κ (1.7 W/mK) is specifically tied to long-range randomness rather than solver choice for the periodic model.

novelty_evaluation.what_already_exists: It is well-established that alloy disorder lowers κ and that small periodic models can misrepresent disorder; diffuson/localization-style pictures and the importance of non-propagating contributions in disordered solids are known broadly.
novelty_evaluation.what_is_novel: A method-selection-oriented, alloy-specific dominance claim: for SiGe-like alloys, long-range randomness primarily suppresses generalized velocities/diffusivity of low-frequency heat carriers, producing potentially order-of-magnitude κ differences between periodic substituted cells and explicit random realizations, often exceeding solver-to-solver differences once finite-size issues are controlled.
novelty_evaluation.classification_explanation: The underlying physics (disorder reducing transport beyond lifetimes) is related to existing disorder theories, but DRD reframes it as the leading axis of cross-method disagreement for SiGe and emphasizes generalized diffusivity suppression as the discriminator even when DOS/lifetimes appear similar.
references: Garg (2011) Role of disorder and anharmonicity in the thermal conductivity of silicon-germanium alloys [DFPT+VCA/Tamura; highlights alloy-scattering modeling importance]
Allen (1993) Thermal conductivity of disordered solids [diffusons/localization; disorder-suppressed diffusivity beyond simple phonon picture]
QHGK/real-space ALD literature (various) [generalized velocities/diffusivities in disordered systems]

law.statement_name: In strong-disorder alloys, disorder-model uncertainty can exceed solver-choice uncertainty
law.theory_statement: In Si1-xGex at moderate-to-high disorder strength (x away from 0 and 1, especially near the κ minimum region), the spread in predicted κ attributable to the disorder model (explicit random vs periodic substituted vs VCA/mass-only perturbative alloy scattering; inclusion/exclusion of force-constant disorder) is expected to exceed the spread attributable to the transport-solver choice (EMD-GK/Einstein vs NEMD vs PBTE-RTA vs PBTE-iterative), provided (i) the simulation/Brillouin-zone sampling is sufficiently converged for the remaining mean free paths and (ii) the method uses the same underlying interatomic forces/IFCs. Mechanistically, once disorder truncates mean free paths and suppresses coherence/hydrodynamic normal-process effects, solver-level differences (e.g., iterative vs RTA corrections) become secondary relative to the physics omitted or misrepresented by simplified disorder treatments.
law.theory_statement_plain_language: For strongly alloyed SiGe, whether you model real atomic randomness (and force-constant disorder) matters more than whether you compute κ with GK, NEMD, or BTE.
law.domain_scope: Bulk substitutional diamond-like Si1-xGex alloys (not superlattices) in the regime where alloy scattering is strong enough that long-MFP contributions are heavily suppressed and remaining transport is not sensitive to hydrodynamic normal-process corrections. Applies to comparisons using the same underlying force model (same potential or same DFT/ML-derived IFCs). Does not apply when (a) NEMD finite-length effects dominate, (b) coherent transport in periodic layering dominates, or (c) potentials differ substantially (then potential error may dominate).
special_cases: If NEMD cells are too short or temperature gradients too large, solver artifacts (finite-size/nonequilibrium bias) can again dominate and violate the statement.
Near end members (x→0 or x→1), disorder is weak and intrinsic anharmonicity/normal-process physics can re-elevate solver differences (e.g., iterative vs RTA).

If disorder is modeled in ways that intentionally remove strain or modify lattice mismatch (e.g., enforced equal lattice constants in multilayers), the relative dominance between disorder representation and solver choice may change.

supporting_evidence.text: A review/discussion of Si/Ge/SiGe methods notes: (i) pure Si and Ge can show consistency between GK-MD and BTE in prior work, but (ii) BTE becomes problematic for Si–Ge alloys, pointing to alloy/disorder treatment—not merely solver choice—as a key divergence source.

Another review discussion states that empirical-potential NEMD studies can show large discrepancies with experiment for SiGe alloys, while DFPT+VCA/Tamura-type approaches (e.g., Garg et al.) can reproduce experiments, highlighting disorder-model adequacy as a controlling factor in alloys.

In explicit-disorder calculations (QHGK) at fixed composition, switching only the disorder realization from periodic substituted to truly random changes κ from ~31 W/mK to ~1.7 W/mK, dwarfing the difference between BTE-RTA and QHGK for the periodic substituted model (~33 vs ~31 W/mK).

Classical MD with explicit alloying (Tersoff EMD) reports very strong κ suppression and in some strongly suppressed nanowire/superlattice cases nearly temperature-independent κ over 200–500 K, consistent with a regime where detailed solver refinements are less influential than the presence of strong disorder/interface scattering; while these are nanostructured cases, they illustrate the broader ‘strong scattering reduces solver sensitivity’ mechanism.

novelty_evaluation.what_already_exists: It is known that alloy modeling is challenging for PBTE and that disorder strongly reduces κ; it is also known that solver approximations (RTA vs iterative) can matter in crystals, especially at low T.
novelty_evaluation.what_is_novel: A dominance ordering tailored to SiGe alloys: once disorder is strong and finite-size issues are controlled, the principal uncertainty axis shifts from solver choice to disorder representation (randomness length scale and inclusion of force-constant disorder), enabling a practical hierarchy for interpreting cross-method disagreements.
novelty_evaluation.classification_explanation: This is a synthesis/ordering principle rather than a new scattering theory; it is not stated explicitly in the provided sources as a ranked rule, though it is consistent with their qualitative claims about alloy difficulty and disorder sensitivity.
references: Garg (2011) Role of disorder and anharmonicity in the thermal conductivity of silicon-germanium alloys [importance of alloy/disorder treatment in PBTE]
Review literature on Si/Ge/SiGe transport methods (various) [notes BTE difficulties for alloys; solver vs model considerations]
Allen (1993) Thermal conductivity of disordered solids [disorder regime where phonon picture and solver nuances are less central]

new_predictions_likely: For bulk diamond Si1-xGex near x≈0.5, keeping the same interatomic model (e.g., one empirical potential or one DFT/ML force model), κ computed for (i) a periodic small-cell substitution pattern (or its periodic replicas) will exceed κ computed for (ii) a large explicitly random alloy supercell with converged disorder correlations, even when using the same transport solver.

If two studies use the same solver (e.g., PBTE-RTA) but one uses VCA+mass-disorder (Tamura/Abeles) and the other uses an explicit-disorder supercell including force-constant disorder, the explicit-disorder result will generally produce lower κ at intermediate compositions, with the largest deviation coming from low-to-mid frequency contributions.
new_predictions_unknown: In diamond SiGe, there exists a temperature/composition window where force-constant disorder (beyond mass disorder) changes κ by >2× relative to mass-only models; the window shifts with T because increasing anharmonic broadening partially masks disorder-induced diffusivity suppression.

A convergence criterion based on a disorder correlation length (from pair/multisite correlations of alloy configurations) will predict when periodic alloy models approach random-alloy κ; for SiGe at 300 K this length may exceed typical MD-accessible cells, implying many published MD results are effectively ‘short-correlation’ disorder models.
negative_experiments: Compute κ for a sequence of SiGe explicit-alloy models with increasing supercell size and increasingly randomized correlations (e.g., SQS-like to fully random) using identical solver and identical force model; if κ converges quickly to the periodic-substitution value rather than decreasing toward a lower random-alloy value, DRD’s long-range-randomness dominance is weakened for diamond SiGe.

For the same harmonic spectrum, compare PBTE(VCA+Tamura mass disorder) to an explicit-disorder PBTE/QHGK that includes force-constant disorder; if they agree closely across x at 300 K (within ~10–20%), then DRD overstates the importance of force-constant/long-range disorder for diamond SiGe (even if it remains true for clathrates).

unaccounted_for.text: The clearest quantitative evidence for the ‘periodic substituted vs truly random’ order-of-magnitude κ gap is for a SiGe clathrate alloy rather than diamond SiGe; the magnitude of the effect could be smaller in diamond-structure SiGe alloys.

special_cases: Periodic superlattices/multilayers: coherence and interface physics dominate; DRD is aimed at substitutional random alloys, not designed layered systems.

If a model intentionally removes lattice-mismatch strain (e.g., forcing Ge lattice constant equal to Si in some MD multilayer setups), disorder/strain interplay is altered and DRD predictions may need modification.
When potential quality dominates (different empirical potentials or DFT functionals), potential error can swamp disorder-representation effects.

references: Garg (2011) Role of disorder and anharmonicity in the thermal conductivity of silicon-germanium alloys [DFPT+VCA/Tamura alloy-scattering modeling; related but not a dominance-ordering principle]
Allen (1993) Thermal conductivity of disordered solids [diffuson/localization framework; related mechanism for diffusivity suppression in disorder]
QHGK/real-space ALD literature (various) [generalized velocities/diffusivities; provides formalism underlying the mechanism]
existing_theory.what_already_exists: General understanding that alloy disorder reduces κ and that VCA/Tamura models approximate disorder scattering; awareness that alloys and disorder can challenge PBTE and that explicit disorder can matter.
existing_theory.what_is_novel: A ranked, method-selection theory for SiGe asserting that, once disorder is strong and finite-size issues are controlled, disorder representation (randomness length scale; mass vs force-constant disorder; nonperturbative effects) is the dominant determinant of cross-method κ variation, with generalized diffusivity suppression of low-frequency carriers as the key mechanism.
existing_theory.classification_explanation: The mechanism is grounded in existing disorder transport concepts, but the explicit dominance ordering and its practical implication for interpreting solver-to-solver differences in SiGe is a novel synthesis relative to the provided evidence.

theory-4.name: Tersoff Bulk-Si Overconductivity Law (with Temperature Amplification)
theory-4.description: This theory explains (and predicts) systematic method-dependent bias in bulk crystalline silicon lattice thermal conductivity when using the Tersoff-1989 empirical potential in MD (EMD/GK/Einstein or homogeneous NEMD) relative to first-principles phonon Boltzmann transport (PBTE) based on DFT interatomic force constants (IFCs). The proposed mechanism is that Tersoff-1989 parameterization yields an effectively under-damped phonon gas in bulk Si: (i) harmonic properties (dispersion/group velocities) and/or (ii) anharmonic scattering strengths derived from the potential produce phonon lifetimes that are too long compared to DFT, yielding inflated κ. At elevated temperatures (≈800–1200 K and above), first-principles references that include four-phonon (4ph) scattering predict a steeper reduction of κ with T than 3ph-only models; if Tersoff does not reproduce the correct magnitude/temperature scaling of higher-order anharmonicity, the bias relative to such 4ph-inclusive references is expected to persist and often exceed ±30%. The theory explicitly recognizes that MD flavors (homogeneous NEMD vs EMD) can introduce finite-size/gradient artifacts that may partially cancel intrinsic potential bias, so the observed direction/magnitude depends on convergence (especially length in NEMD).

components.theory_name_plain_language: Tersoff tends to give too-high thermal conductivity for bulk silicon, and the mismatch tends to worsen at high temperature

The theory explicitly recognizes that MD flavors (homogeneous NEMD vs EMD) can introduce finite-size/gradient artifacts that may partially cancel intrinsic potential bias, so the observed direction/magnitude depends on convergence (especially length in NEMD).
components.theory_description_plain_language: Tersoff-1989 makes heat-carrying vibrations in bulk silicon scatter too weakly, so κ comes out too large versus DFT-based BTE, and the gap can grow at high temperature when four-phonon scattering matters in the DFT reference. NEMD size/gradient artifacts can sometimes hide part of that overprediction.

law.statement_name: Room-temperature bulk Si: Tersoff IFC-based transport overestimates κ by ~2× vs DFT PBTE (anchor law)
law.theory_statement: For defect-free bulk diamond-cubic Si near 300 K, lattice-dynamics/BTE calculations that use IFCs derived from a Tersoff empirical potential can yield κ that is ~2× larger than DFT-based PBTE solutions (direct inversion) for the same material class, indicating that (absent strong finite-size artifacts) Tersoff-1989-based bulk-Si MD is predisposed to overpredict κ relative to DFT-PBTE benchmarks.
law.theory_statement_plain_language: Around 300 K, using Tersoff for bulk silicon tends to give about twice the thermal conductivity that DFT-based BTE gives.
law.domain_scope: Bulk, crystalline, defect-free diamond-cubic Si at or near room temperature (~300 K). Applies to comparisons where the Tersoff side uses the same potential to generate harmonic + anharmonic IFCs for ALD/PBTE, and the reference side is DFT-derived PBTE (ideally iterative/inversion) with comparable included scattering physics (at least intrinsic 3-phonon; isotope/4-phonon may differ and should be accounted for when interpreting ratios). Used as a predictive prior for Tersoff-1989 MD (EMD or homogeneous NEMD) bias direction when cell sizes are sufficiently converged.
special_cases: If the MD implementation is not size-converged (especially homogeneous NEMD with too-short length), κ may be suppressed and the overprediction can be partially or fully canceled.
Different Tersoff parameter sets (not strictly the original 1989 set) may differ; the evidence does not cover every parameterization.
Solver differences (RTA vs inversion) can shift DFT PBTE reference values by several percent (e.g., ~5% for Si at 300 K in one dataset), but this is far smaller than the ~2× gap anchored here.

supporting_evidence.text: DFT PBTE (direct inversion, quantum statistics) for diamond Si reports κ(300 K)=147 W/mK; the same study reports Tersoff-based ALD/BTE κ_Q(300 K)=305 W/mK (and κ_classical=260 W/mK), i.e., ≈2.1× higher than DFT inversion at 300 K.
The same DFT PBTE study shows RTA vs inversion differences are modest at 300 K (quantum: 140 vs 147 W/mK; ~5%), implying the ≈2× Tersoff-vs-DFT gap is not explainable by RTA vs inversion alone.

A separate first-principles PBTE/DFT workflow (phono3py, RTA) gives κ(300 K)=112.1 W/mK for Si, further indicating that first-principles PBTE values cluster far below ~300 W/mK at 300 K; Tersoff ≈305 W/mK is therefore an outlier high relative to multiple DFT-based PBTE pipelines.

Another first-principles PBTE/DFT study for bulk Si (iterative 3ph with isotopes; optional 4ph) reports κ_3ph(300 K)≈125.4 W/mK and κ_3+4ph(300 K)≈115.4 W/mK, again far below ~300 W/mK and consistent with Tersoff-based transport being high relative to DFT-based transport at 300 K.

A first-principles uncertainty-quantification study reports a range of DFT-PBTE κ(300 K) values depending on XC functional (e.g., PBE 154, PBEsol 128, LDA 122 W/mK; BEEF-vdW best-fit 171 W/mK for isotopically pure Si with only 3ph). Even the high end of these DFT predictions is well below 260–305 W/mK from Tersoff transport, supporting the conclusion that Tersoff is systematically high at 300 K versus DFT PBTE.

novelty_evaluation.what_already_exists: It is broadly known that empirical potentials can mispredict κ in Si because they may not reproduce phonon dispersions and anharmonicity accurately, and that Tersoff can be problematic for thermal transport.
novelty_evaluation.what_is_novel: This statement formalizes an operational, quantitatively anchored prior (~2× at 300 K) to forecast the direction and rough magnitude of Tersoff-1989 bulk-Si MD bias relative to DFT-PBTE baselines in unseen comparisons (e.g., GPUMD homogeneous NEMD vs almaBTE).
novelty_evaluation.classification_explanation: The phenomenon is not new, but the theory statement is a scenario-targeted, quantitative law anchored to a specific cross-method data point and used predictively for unseen method comparisons.
references: Tersoff (1989) New empirical approach for the structure and energy of covalent systems [origin of the potential class used in MD/ALD comparisons]
Broido et al. (2007) Intrinsic lattice thermal conductivity of semiconductors from first principles [DFT-PBTE benchmark framework for Si/Ge]
Esfarjani et al. (2011) Heat transport in silicon from first principles [DFT PBTE benchmarks; establishes typical κ scale near 300 K]
Garg et al. (2011) Role of disorder and anharmonicity in the thermal conductivity of silicon-germanium alloys [DFT-based transport as reference class for Si/SiGe]

law.statement_name: High-temperature amplification: 4-phonon-aware DFT references reduce κ faster with T than Tersoff-1989 is expected to (categorical forecast at ~1100 K)
law.theory_statement: In bulk crystalline Si at high temperatures (roughly ≥800 K up to ~1500 K), four-phonon (4ph) scattering contributes substantially to total resistive scattering, lowering κ relative to 3ph-only PBTE and steepening the κ(T) decay. Therefore, when comparing Tersoff-1989-based homogeneous NEMD (or other classical MD with that potential) to a DFT-PBTE reference that includes 4ph (and isotopes), the ratio κ_Tersoff/κ_DFT,4ph is expected to remain >1 and, under size-converged NEMD conditions, is likely to exceed 1.3 around ~1100 K (i.e., “Tersoff higher by more than 30%”), unless NEMD finite-length/gradient artifacts suppress κ sufficiently to bring the ratio into the ±30% band.
law.theory_statement_plain_language: At ~1100 K, a DFT reference that includes four-phonon scattering drops κ strongly; Tersoff-1989 MD is therefore expected to come out noticeably higher (often >30% higher) unless the NEMD setup artificially lowers κ.
law.domain_scope: Bulk, defect-free crystalline diamond Si at high temperature (~800–1500 K), comparing (A) Tersoff-1989 classical MD (especially homogeneous NEMD) and (B) DFT-derived PBTE that includes at least 3ph+4ph+isotope scattering (as in modern almaBTE-like workflows when 4ph is enabled/available). This statement is about method+physics mismatch: the reference includes explicit 4ph/isotopes; MD includes only what the empirical potential generates (no quantum statistics).
special_cases: If the DFT reference omits 4ph at 1100 K, the expected method gap shrinks; the >30% categorical forecast is specifically for 4ph-inclusive references.

If homogeneous NEMD length is insufficient (ballistic truncation) or the imposed gradient is too large, κ_Tersoff can be biased downward, potentially producing apparent agreement within 30% even if the intrinsic potential bias is upward.
At very high T where electronic thermal conductivity becomes non-negligible in experiment, comparisons must ensure both sides are lattice-only (the statement concerns lattice κ).

supporting_evidence.text: A first-principles Si study spanning 100–1500 K reports that omitting 4ph overestimates κ by ~8% at 300 K and that 4ph becomes increasingly important above ~500–700 K; at 900 K, 3ph-only κ is reported as 43 W/mK and is ~20% larger than measurement, implying that 4ph-inclusive κ is substantially lower at high T than 3ph-only.

The same first-principles high-T study states (as a mechanistic scaling rule) that 3ph lifetimes scale roughly ~T^-1 while 4ph lifetimes scale roughly ~T^-2, indicating an accelerating relative importance of 4ph with increasing temperature.

Independent first-principles PBTE for Si at 300 K shows 4ph reduces κ from ~125.4 to ~115.4 W/mK (~7.9%), consistent with the claim that 4ph corrections are non-negligible already at 300 K and grow with T.

Tersoff-based ALD/BTE for diamond Si at 300 K strongly overpredicts κ relative to DFT inversion (305 vs 147 W/mK), supporting the premise that the potential can yield insufficient effective resistive scattering and/or inflated transport quantities; this provides the abductive anchor that the bias remains upward unless canceled by NEMD artifacts.

General methodological discussion notes empirical-potential MD results can be strongly affected by interatomic potential quality and MD finite-size effects, consistent with the stated caveat that NEMD artifacts can move comparisons toward apparent agreement.

This statement was logically inferred (abduction) by combining: (i) evidence that Tersoff produces large upward bias at 300 K in bulk Si transport (Tersoff ALD/BTE vs DFT PBTE), and (ii) evidence that DFT PBTE κ decreases more strongly with T when 4ph scattering is included (increasingly important at high T).

novelty_evaluation.what_already_exists: It is established that 4ph scattering reduces κ at high temperature in Si and that empirical potentials can introduce bias; it is also well known that NEMD can suffer from finite-size effects.
novelty_evaluation.what_is_novel: A concrete, scenario-specific categorical prediction for the H5-like comparison at ~1100 K: that size-converged Tersoff-1989 homogeneous NEMD will most likely be >30% higher than a 4ph-inclusive DFT PBTE reference.
novelty_evaluation.classification_explanation: The underlying mechanisms are known, but using them to produce an explicit categorical forecast for an unseen benchmark (Tersoff-1989 homogeneous NEMD vs almaBTE-like 4ph-inclusive reference) is a new, operational theory statement.
references: Feng & Ruan (2016–2018) Four-phonon scattering and high-T κ in Si [establishes growing 4ph importance with T]
McGaughey & Kaviany / Turney et al. (various) MD vs lattice dynamics for κ and size/statistics issues [context for MD artifacts and classical-statistics limits]
Broido et al. / Esfarjani et al. PBTE benchmarks for Si [establishes expected κ(T) behavior for DFT PBTE references]

new_predictions_likely: H5 @300 K: For size-converged bulk Si, κ_Tersoff-1989(homogeneous NEMD)/κ_almaBTE(3ph/4ph+isotopes as implemented) will be >1.0; a plausible prior range is ~1.3–2.1, with the upper end corresponding to the ≈2× Tersoff-vs-DFT transport anchor (305 vs 147 W/mK).

H5 @1100 K: If the almaBTE reference includes strong high-T resistive physics (especially 4ph), then the comparison category is most likely “Tersoff higher by more than 30%”, unless NEMD length/gradient artifacts reduce κ_Tersoff.
new_predictions_unknown: If a carefully converged homogeneous NEMD calculation with Tersoff-1989 at 1100 K produces κ within 30% of a 4ph-inclusive DFT PBTE reference, it would imply a strong, temperature-dependent cancellation between (i) Tersoff’s intrinsic overconductivity and (ii) NEMD finite-size/nonequilibrium artifacts, suggesting that method agreement can be accidental rather than indicating correct physics.

If replacing Tersoff-1989 with a DFT-trained ML potential (or force-matched empirical potential) and then running homogeneous NEMD yields κ close to 4ph-inclusive DFT PBTE at 1100 K, it would support the claim that the dominant error source is the potential’s anharmonic coefficients rather than NEMD methodology itself.
negative_experiments: Perform homogeneous NEMD with Tersoff-1989 for bulk Si at 300 K and 1100 K while systematically increasing sample length and cross-section; if κ converges to within ±30% of the DFT PBTE reference at both temperatures, the claimed intrinsic Tersoff overconductivity prior is weakened.

Compute ALD/PBTE for bulk diamond Si using Tersoff-1989 IFCs but compare RTA vs full inversion; if full inversion reduces κ by a factor comparable to the observed ~2× gap to DFT, then solver approximation (not potential) would be the main driver—contradicting the theory’s emphasis on potential-derived scattering/dispersion errors.

Extract effective Grüneisen parameters and phonon lifetimes from Tersoff-1989 (via ALD) and from DFT IFCs and test whether Tersoff systematically yields longer lifetimes for heat-carrying acoustic modes; absence of such lifetime inflation would undermine the “underdamped phonon gas” mechanism.

unaccounted_for.text: No direct bulk diamond Si κ(T) dataset from Tersoff-1989 MD (EMD or homogeneous NEMD) is provided in the evidence; the anchor is Tersoff ALD/BTE at 300 K, not MD, and not specifically labeled as Tersoff-1989 in that source entry.

An SW force-matched potential used with EMD-GK for pristine Si yields κ(300 K)=207±12 W/mK, showing that not all empirical potentials underpredict scattering; however, this theory is about Tersoff-1989 specifically and does not model SW behavior.

conflicting_evidence.text: A methods discussion summary reports that some literature found GK-MD and BTE consistent for pure Si and Ge, suggesting that MD is not intrinsically biased high for pure crystals and that potential choice and convergence can flip outcomes; this does not directly contradict the Tersoff-specific claim but limits generality.

special_cases: If the comparison reference (almaBTE or similar) uses only 3ph scattering (no 4ph) at 1100 K, then the expected discrepancy with Tersoff-1989 may be smaller and could fall within ±30% depending on NEMD suppression.

If the MD result includes additional effective scattering due to defects, isotope disorder, or interface/boundary scattering not present in the DFT bulk reference, κ_MD can be lower even with the same potential; the theory assumes pristine bulk Si.
At temperatures far below the Debye temperature, classical MD occupation errors (equipartition) can qualitatively change κ(T); this theory is aimed at ~300 K and above, not cryogenic regimes.

existing_theory.what_is_novel: A quantitatively anchored, Tersoff-specific prior (~2× at 300 K in bulk Si transport) combined with a high-T categorical forecast (>30% high at ~1100 K versus 4ph-inclusive DFT references) tailored to predict outcomes for unseen GPUMD homogeneous NEMD vs almaBTE comparisons.
existing_theory.classification_explanation: Mechanisms are established, but the explicit operationalization into a scenario-targeted predictive law (with a quantitative anchor and a categorical 1100 K forecast) goes beyond standard general statements, while still being grounded in known physics.

theory-5.name: Small-Supercell/RTA Depresses DFT-PBTE κ Baseline Law (revised)
theory-5.description: This theory explains within-first-principles spread in predicted lattice thermal conductivity κ(T) for bulk Si/Ge (and by extension SiGe workflows) that arises before any comparison to MD. It identifies two systematic downward-bias mechanisms that can depress a DFT-PBTE baseline: (1) using a single-mode relaxation-time approximation (SMRTA/RTA) instead of an iterative or direct-inversion solution of the linearized PBTE, which neglects mode-coupling (off-diagonal) terms and thus tends to underpredict κ when normal scattering is non-negligible; and (2) using insufficient real-space range for harmonic/anharmonic IFCs (too-small finite-displacement supercells or too-short neighbor cutoffs), which distorts key dispersion features (notably TA near zone edges) and/or the phase space/matrix elements for scattering, potentially lowering κ. The theory is intended to forecast method-to-method ratios (e.g., MD vs almaBTE) by clarifying when the DFT-PBTE reference itself may be systematically low, and how that depends on temperature and convergence settings.

components.theory_name: Small-Supercell/RTA Depresses DFT-PBTE κ Baseline Law (revised)
components.theory_name_plain_language: Some DFT-based BTE workflows can predict too-low κ because of solver and convergence choices
components.theory_description: This theory explains within-first-principles spread in predicted lattice thermal conductivity κ(T) for bulk Si/Ge (and by extension SiGe workflows) that arises before any comparison to MD. It identifies two systematic downward-bias mechanisms that can depress a DFT-PBTE baseline: (1) using a single-mode relaxation-time approximation (SMRTA/RTA) instead of an iterative or direct-inversion solution of the linearized PBTE, which neglects mode-coupling (off-diagonal) terms and thus tends to underpredict κ when normal scattering is non-negligible; and (2) using insufficient real-space range for harmonic/anharmonic IFCs (too-small finite-displacement supercells or too-short neighbor cutoffs), which distorts key dispersion features (notably TA near zone edges) and/or the phase space/matrix elements for scattering, potentially lowering κ. The theory is intended to forecast method-to-method ratios (e.g., MD vs almaBTE) by clarifying when the DFT-PBTE reference itself may be systematically low, and how that depends on temperature and convergence settings.
components.theory_description_plain_language: Even if you use DFT and BTE, choices like RTA (instead of a full PBTE solver) and too-small supercells for force constants can make κ come out artificially low, which then changes MD-vs-DFT comparisons.

law.statement_name: SMRTA/RTA bias: κ_RTA ≤ κ_iter/inv, with a temperature-dependent gap
law.theory_statement: For bulk crystalline Si (and similar phonon-dominated crystals) when κ is computed from perturbative three-phonon scattering using the linearized PBTE, the single-mode relaxation time approximation (SMRTA/RTA) yields κ values that are systematically lower than direct inversion or iterative PBTE solutions because SMRTA neglects off-diagonal mode-coupling in the collision operator. The relative bias (κ_iter/inv − κ_RTA)/κ_iter/inv is modest near 300 K for Si (order of a few percent in the provided evidence) but is expected to grow as temperature decreases into regimes where normal processes and hydrodynamic-like transport make mode-coupling more important; at sufficiently high temperatures where resistive (Umklapp and higher-order) scattering dominates, the bias tends to remain small.
law.theory_statement_plain_language: Using RTA instead of a full PBTE solution usually makes κ a bit too small; the difference is small near room temperature for Si but gets larger at lower temperatures.
law.domain_scope: Bulk crystalline group-IV semiconductors (Si, Ge) and similar nonpolar/weakly polar crystals, in first-principles (or first-principles-like) PBTE calculations where three-phonon scattering is treated perturbatively and the PBTE is solved either in SMRTA/RTA or by iterative/direct inversion; excludes cases dominated by extrinsic scattering (boundaries/defects) or where κ is computed by classical MD rather than PBTE.
special_cases: If off-diagonal couplings are intrinsically weak for a given material/temperature (collision operator nearly diagonal), SMRTA and inversion/iterative solutions can agree to within ~1%.

At very high T where strong resistive scattering dominates (including 4-phonon if present), the incremental correction from going beyond SMRTA may stay small even though absolute κ changes strongly with T.
In strongly hydrodynamic regimes (low T, high purity), SMRTA can be qualitatively inadequate; the bias can exceed 'few percent'.

supporting_evidence.text: For bulk diamond Si at 300 K, a DFT PBTE calculation reports κ_Q,Inv = 147 W/mK (direct inversion with quantum statistics) and κ_Q,RTA = 140 W/mK, i.e., RTA is ~5% lower than inversion at the same IFC level.

A separate first-principles Si study (including 3ph, 4ph, isotopes) states that prior literature indicates the iterative vs RTA difference is <4% for Si at room temperature (consistent with a modest systematic underestimation from RTA near 300 K).

A review of first-principles PBTE notes that iterative solutions can differ from RTA and that RTA neglect of coupling between modes can cause quantitative differences; this frames the mechanism as general across PBTE implementations.

novelty_evaluation.what_already_exists: SMRTA/RTA underestimation relative to iterative/direct PBTE is a well-established feature of phonon BTE theory, especially where normal processes matter.
novelty_evaluation.what_is_novel: The novel contribution is the explicit use of SMRTA-vs-iterative bias as a 'baseline depression' mechanism that can systematically inflate apparent MD/DFT ratios, and the explicit prediction of when (in temperature space) that baseline shift will matter most for method comparisons in Si/Ge benchmarking workflows.
novelty_evaluation.classification_explanation: The transport mechanism is established, but framing it as a predictable baseline shift affecting cross-method comparisons (rather than merely a solver choice) is a new applied-theory emphasis supported by the within-DFT numerical gap shown for Si.
references: Omini & Sparavigna (1995) Beyond the isotropic-model approximation in the theory of thermal conductivity [iterative solution of phonon BTE; establishes SMRTA limitations]
Broido et al. (2007) Intrinsic lattice thermal conductivity of semiconductors from first principles [PBTE framework; discusses solution methods]
Esfarjani et al. (2011) Heat transport in silicon from first principles calculations [PBTE solution approaches; iterative vs RTA context]

law.statement_name: Finite-displacement IFC range/supercell inadequacy can bias κ downward via dispersion and scattering errors
law.theory_statement: In PBTE workflows where harmonic and anharmonic IFCs are obtained from finite-displacement supercells (DFT or DFT-surrogate forces), insufficient real-space range—either by too-small supercell, too-short neighbor cutoff, or otherwise underconverged IFC extraction—can underestimate κ by (i) distorting harmonic phonon dispersions (group velocities and density of states) and/or (ii) distorting three-phonon matrix elements and phase space, thereby changing lifetimes. A key mechanistic indicator of this sensitivity in Si/Ge is the known difficulty of accurately capturing the transverse-acoustic (TA) branch near the X-point and its dependence on the number of neighbor shells retained; if TA(X) is mispredicted, the low-frequency/heat-carrying acoustic landscape is altered and κ can shift. The magnitude and direction of the bias are material- and workflow-dependent, but when the extracted IFCs are underconverged, κ is expected to be systematically low relative to a well-converged PBTE baseline.
law.theory_statement_plain_language: If the force-constant supercell or cutoff is too small, the phonon dispersion and scattering will be wrong and κ often comes out too low.
law.domain_scope: Crystalline bulk (Si, Ge, and related) PBTE calculations using real-space finite-displacement IFC extraction (including phono3py/phonopy-style workflows and ML-surrogate force providers), where IFC cutoffs/supercells may truncate relevant interactions; excludes reciprocal-space DFPT calculations where the dominant convergence knob is instead the q-mesh and perturbation sampling (though those can have other convergence issues).
special_cases: For very simple nonpolar crystals (e.g., Si) the required IFC range may be relatively short, so κ may be less sensitive once modest supercells are used; the effect can still appear through TA-edge sensitivity.
For polar/complex crystals (e.g., GaN example), small supercells can cause larger κ errors; Si/Ge may show smaller but nonzero sensitivity.
If the PBTE solution is dominated by added extrinsic scattering (e.g., isotope/defect/boundary terms), moderate harmonic-dispersion errors may have reduced impact on total κ.

supporting_evidence.text: A phono3py PBTE study explicitly reports that small IFC supercell sizes can underestimate κ (discussed for GaN: using a 32-atom cell vs 108-atom in a prior study, with underestimation attributed to supercell size). This provides direct evidence that IFC supercell inadequacy can depress κ in finite-displacement PBTE workflows.

Uncertainty-quantification work notes that predicting TA branch frequencies near the X-point is challenging for both Si and Ge and that the discrepancy has been ascribed to the number of neighbor shells included in harmonic force-constant calculations—linking IFC range/cutoff choices mechanistically to dispersion errors that can shift κ.

A first-principles uncertainty study for isotopically pure Si shows κ at 300 K depends strongly on DFT functional and correlates with TA[100] sound speed and TA X-point frequency (R^2=0.77 for TA X-point frequency correlation), supporting the claim that errors in TA-branch characteristics (which can arise from underconverged IFC range) propagate into κ variability.

A first-principles PBTE study for Si emphasizes careful convergence practices (large supercells, q-grids up to 30x30x30) and highlights that insufficient convergence (supercell/q-grid) can affect κ; while not isolating supercell-size error numerically for Si, it supports the general necessity of converged IFC extraction to avoid κ bias.

novelty_evaluation.what_already_exists: It is well known that PBTE results require convergence with respect to IFC supercell size/cutoff, and that inaccurate phonon dispersions lead to inaccurate κ.
novelty_evaluation.what_is_novel: The novel aspect is elevating TA(X)/neighbor-shell sensitivity (explicitly noted for Si/Ge) as a mechanistic diagnostic for when IFC-range truncation is likely to cause a systematic κ underestimation, and tying that directly to baseline shifts relevant for cross-method comparisons (DFT-vs-MD and DFT-vs-DFT-workflow).
novelty_evaluation.classification_explanation: This extends standard convergence wisdom by proposing a specific, physically interpretable predictor (TA-edge sensitivity) for κ bias risk in Si/Ge finite-displacement workflows, rather than treating supercell convergence as a purely numerical checklist.
references: Jain & McGaughey (2015) Thermal conductivity predictions from first principles: dependence on phonon dispersion and scattering [convergence and sensitivity context]
Tadano & Tsuneyuki (2015) Self-consistent phonon/finite-displacement IFC practices [IFC extraction and convergence]
ShengBTE and phono3py method papers/documentation [finite-displacement IFC extraction; convergence dependence]

new_predictions_likely: For bulk Si near 300 K, a PBTE workflow that switches from SMRTA/RTA to iterative or direct inversion while holding the same IFCs fixed will increase κ by a few percent (order 3–6%), consistent with the 147 vs 140 W/mK evidence gap.

At temperatures below ~200 K in high-purity bulk Si (where normal processes are more influential), the relative increase κ_iter/inv − κ_RTA will be larger than at 300 K (directionally: RTA becomes progressively less accurate).

If two DFT-PBTE workflows differ mainly by underconverged IFC real-space range (smaller supercells/cutoffs) versus converged IFC range, the underconverged workflow will tend to predict lower κ for Si/Ge, with the discrepancy correlating with errors in TA branch features (e.g., TA X-point frequency).
new_predictions_unknown: For bulk Ge, correcting harmonic IFC range (more neighbor shells / larger supercell) will change κ more strongly than for Si (because of potentially greater TA-edge sensitivity), possibly changing the ordering of which DFT functional appears 'best' against experiment once convergence is enforced.

In explicit-supercell PBTE modeling of Si1-xGex (not VCA), insufficient supercell size will not only depress κ but also alter the apparent composition dependence by artificially suppressing long-wavelength contributions, potentially shifting the κ(x) minimum away from x≈0.5 in a size-dependent way.
negative_experiments: For a fixed bulk-Si DFT IFC set, compute κ(T) using both SMRTA/RTA and direct inversion/iterative PBTE across a temperature sweep. If κ_RTA exceeds κ_iter/inv at any temperature with identical inputs, the assumed systematic directionality (RTA underestimation) would be called into question (suggesting inconsistent scattering implementation or numerical issues).

Within a finite-displacement PBTE workflow for Si or Ge, vary harmonic/anharmonic IFC supercell sizes and neighbor cutoffs while keeping q-mesh convergence tight. If κ is invariant within ~1% across these changes and TA(X) frequencies are also stable, the proposed IFC-range-driven κ underestimation mechanism is likely negligible for that workflow/material.

unaccounted_for.text: No provided evidence gives a direct numerical example (for bulk Si or Ge) where a too-small IFC supercell quantitatively lowers κ; the explicit documented magnitude example is for GaN, so the size of this bias for Si/Ge remains uncertain from the current evidence set.

special_cases: In some materials/temperatures the collision operator is nearly diagonal (weak mode coupling), making SMRTA effectively exact and eliminating solver-induced baseline shifts.

If κ is dominated by extrinsic scattering (grain boundaries, pores, strong disorder, boundaries), differences between SMRTA and iterative PBTE may be masked by added resistive channels; likewise, modest dispersion errors from IFC truncation may have reduced effect on total κ.

Reciprocal-space DFPT approaches avoid real-space supercell truncation but have their own convergence sensitivities (e.g., q-mesh, interpolation); this theory focuses on finite-displacement IFC range effects.

references: Omini & Sparavigna (1995) Beyond the isotropic-model approximation in the theory of thermal conductivity [iterative PBTE vs RTA solver theory]
Broido et al. (2007) Intrinsic lattice thermal conductivity of semiconductors from first principles [PBTE methodology and solution choices]
Esfarjani et al. (2011) Heat transport in silicon from first principles calculations [PBTE and sensitivity to inputs/solutions]
existing_theory.what_already_exists: Solver-choice effects (RTA vs iterative/inversion) and IFC convergence requirements are established in PBTE practice.
existing_theory.what_is_novel: A focused, predictive 'baseline depression' framing for benchmarking/ratio questions: it treats solver choice and IFC-range underconvergence as systematic, directionally consistent biases that can shift the DFT reference used in MD-vs-DFT comparisons, and proposes TA(X)/neighbor-shell sensitivity as a practical diagnostic for the IFC-range mechanism in Si/Ge.
existing_theory.classification_explanation: The underlying physics is not new, but the theory formalizes it as a benchmarking law with explicit temperature dependence and a mechanistic diagnostic (TA-edge sensitivity) to anticipate when first-principles baselines will be depressed.

metadata.title: Computational prediction of lattice thermal conductivity: A comparison of molecular dynamics and Boltzmann transport approaches
metadata.abstract: The predictive modeling of lattice thermal conductivity is of fundamental importance for the understanding and design of materials for a wide range of applications. Two major approaches, namely molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and calculations solving approximately the Boltzmann transport equation (BTE), have been developed to compute the lattice thermal conductivity. We present a detailed direct comparison of these two approaches, using as prototypical cases MgO and PbTe. The comparison, carried out using empirical potentials, takes into account the effects of fourth order phonon scattering, temperature-dependent phonon frequencies (phonon renormalization), and investigates the effects of quantum vs. classical statistics. We clarify that equipartition, as opposed to Maxwell Boltzmann, govern the statistics of phonons in MD simulations. We find that lattice thermal conductivity values from MD and BTE show an apparent, satisfactory agreement; however such an agreement is the result of error cancellations. We also show that the primary effect of statistics on thermal conductivity is via the scattering rate dependence on phonon populations.

metadata.title: An Iterative Machine Learning Approach for Discovering Unexpected Thermal Conductivity Enhancement in Aperiodic Superlattices

tldr.text: This work implements an adaptive ML-accelerated search process that can discover unexpected lattice thermal conductivity enhancement instead of reduction in aperiodic superlattices (SLs) as compared to periodic superLattices by using a convolutional neural network to identify previously unseen exceptional structures.

metadata.abstract: While machine learning (ML) has shown increasing effectiveness in optimizing materials properties under known physics, its application in challenging conventional wisdom and discovering new physics still remains challenging due to its interpolative nature. In this work, we demonstrate the potential of using ML for such applications by implementing an adaptive ML-accelerated search process that can discover unexpected lattice thermal conductivity ($\kappa_l$) enhancement instead of reduction in aperiodic superlattices (SLs) as compared to periodic superlattices. We use non-equilibrium molecular dynamics (NEMD) simulations for high-fidelity calculations of $\kappa_l$ for a small fraction of SLs in the search space, along with a convolutional neural network (CNN) which can rapidly predict $\kappa_l$ for a large number of structures. To ensure accurate prediction by the CNN for the target unknown structures, we iteratively identify aperiodic SLs containing structural features which lead to locally enhanced thermal transport, and include them as additional training data for the CNN in each iteration. As a result, our CNN can accurately predict the high $\kappa_l$ of aperiodic SLs that are absent from the initial training dataset, which allows us to identify the previously unseen exceptional structures. The identified RML structures exhibit increased coherent phonon contribution to thermal conductivity owing to the presence of closely spaced interfaces. Our work describes a general purpose machine learning approach for identifying low-probability-of-occurrence exceptional solutions within an extremely large subspace and discovering the underlying physics.

metadata.title: Significant reduction of lattice thermal conductivity by the electron-phonon interaction in silicon with high carrier concentrations: a first-principles study.

tldr.text: Unexpectedly, a significant reduction of the lattice thermal conductivity at room temperature as the carrier concentration goes above 10(19)  cm(-3) is found, a range of great technological relevance to thermoelectric materials.

metadata.abstract: The electron-phonon interaction is well known to create major resistance to electron transport in metals and semiconductors, whereas fewer studies are directed to its effect on phonon transport, especially in semiconductors. We calculate the phonon lifetimes due to scattering with electrons (or holes), combine them with the intrinsic lifetimes due to the anharmonic phonon-phonon interaction, all from first principles, and evaluate the effect of the electron-phonon interaction on the lattice thermal conductivity of silicon. Unexpectedly, we find a significant reduction of the lattice thermal conductivity at room temperature as the carrier concentration goes above 10(19)  cm(-3) (the reduction reaches up to 45% in p-type silicon at around 10(21)  cm(-3)), a range of great technological relevance to thermoelectric materials.

| agreement_with_experiment | No direct quantitative comparison to experiment for the EPI contribution (authors state it is very difficult to isolate EPI contribution experimentally). Authors estimate electronic κ (via Wiedemann–Franz and experimental σ) to be <~1 W/mK for carrier concentrations above 1e20 cm^-3, and claim this is much smaller than the predicted reduction in lattice κ. |
| proposed_reasons_for_discrepancies | Explanations offered for observed behavior and differences: (a) anisotropy of conduction-band electron pockets vs isotropic hole pocket leads to electrons being less effective scatterers (intervalley scattering for electrons increases zone-boundary phonon scattering); (b) previous analytic models (Ziman) are insufficient at high carrier concentrations and at higher temperatures; (c) convergence challenges for EPI calculations require very fine k/q meshes — authors used interpolation (Wannier/EPW) and tetrahedra integration to improve convergence; (d) omission of other scattering mechanisms (e.g., 4-phonon, isotope scattering) could affect absolute κ but are not the focus here. They also note LA-mode EPI scattering rates scale linearly with phonon frequency near the zone center and the slope scales linearly with carrier concentration in the nondegenerate regime. |
| key_figures_tables_locations | Main results located in: Fig. 1 (EPI scattering rates across Brillouin zone at n=1e21 cm^-3), Fig. 2 (comparison between first-principles EPI scattering rates and DPA asymptotic predictions for LA and LO modes), Fig. 3 (comparison of EPI scattering rates vs intrinsic phonon-phonon scattering rates at 1e21 cm^-3), Fig. 4 (calculated lattice thermal conductivity of silicon as function of carrier concentration at 300 K, showing up to 45% reduction), Fig. 5 (phonon mean free paths with and without EPI at 1e21 cm^-3). metadata.title: First-principles phonon physics using the Pheasy code
metadata.abstract: Parameter-free calculations of lattice dynamics from first principles have achieved significant progress in the past decades, with a wealth of applications in thermodynamics, phase transitions, and transport properties of materials. Current approaches to derive the interatomic force constants (IFCs) of lattice potential become challenging and sometimes infeasible when going beyond third-order anharmonicity, due to the combinatorial explosion in the number of higher-order IFCs. In this work, we present a robust and user-friendly program, , which reliably reconstructs the prescribed potential energy surface of crystalline solids via a Taylor expansion of arbitrarily high order. Given force-displacement datasets, the program enables an efficient and accurate extraction of IFCs using advanced machine-learning algorithms, and further calculates a wide range of harmonic and anharmonic phonon related properties. We show in three prototypical examples how the obtained IFCs have been successfully applied to study anharmonic lattice dynamics and thermal transport. Through these detailed benchmarks, we have also identified the optimal approach for IFC extractions and offered general guidelines for high-fidelity lattice-dynamical simulations, addressing the large uncertainties in the IFCs extracted from existing various schemes. Overall, the project aims to create a phonon code ecosystem that connects diverse phonon simulation platforms and offers access to the broad research community.

metadata.title: Uncertainty quantification in first-principles predictions of phonon properties and lattice thermal conductivity
metadata.abstract: We present a framework for quantifying the uncertainty that results from the choice of exchange-correlation (XC) functional in predictions of phonon properties and thermal conductivity that use density functional theory (DFT) to calculate the atomic force constants. The energy ensemble capabilities of the BEEF-vdW XC functional are first applied to determine an ensemble of interatomic force constants, which are then used as inputs to lattice dynamics calculations and a solution of the Boltzmann transport equation. The framework is applied to isotopically-pure silicon. We find that the uncertainty estimates bound property predictions (e.g., phonon dispersions, specific heat, thermal conductivity) from other XC functionals and experiments. We distinguish between properties that are correlated with the predicted thermal conductivity [e.g., the transverse acoustic branch sound speed ($R^2=0.89$) and average Gruneisen parameter ($R^2=0.85$)] and those that are not [e.g., longitudinal acoustic branch sound speed ($R^2=0.23$) and specific heat ($R^2=0.00$)]. We find that differences in ensemble predictions of thermal conductivity are correlated with the behavior of phonons with mean free paths between $100$ and $300$ nm. The framework systematically accounts for XC uncertainty in phonon calculations and should be used whenever it is suspected that the choice of XC functional is influencing physical interpretations.

metadata.title: Thermal conductivity of intrinsic semiconductor at elevated temperature: role of four-phonon scattering and electronic heat conduction
metadata.abstract: While using first-principles-based Boltzmann transport equation approach to predict the thermal conductivity of crystalline semiconductor materials has been a routine, the validity of the approach is seldom tested for high-temperature conditions. Most previous studies only focused on the phononic contribution, and neglected the electronic part. Meanwhile, the treatment on phonon transport is not rigorous as a few ingredients, such as four-phonon scatterings, phonon renormalization and thermal expansion, are ignored. In this paper, we present a Boltzmann transport equation study on high-temperature thermal conduction in bulk silicon by considering the effects of both phonons and electrons, and explore the role of the missing parts in the previous studies on the thermal conductivity at elevated temperature. For the phonon transport, four-phonon scattering is found to considerably reduce the thermal conductivity when the temperature is larger than 700 K, while the effects of phonon renormalization and thermal expansion on phononic thermal conductivity are negligible. Bipolar contribution to the electronic thermal conductivity calculated from first-principles is implemented for the first time. More than 25% of heat is shown to be conducted by electrons at 1500 K. The computed total thermal conductivity of silicon faithfully reproduces the measured data. The approach presented in this paper is expected to be applied to other high-temperature functional materials, and the results could serve as benchmarks and help to explain the high-temperature phonon and electron transport phenomena.

Authors cite possible reasons: RTA underestimation of phononic kappa and scatter in high-T experimental datasets. Experimental datasets used for comparison: Glassbrenner & Slack (1964), Fulkerson et al. (1968), Shanks et al. (1963). |
| proposed_reasons_for_discrepancies | Reasons discussed: (1) Missing four-phonon scattering in previous PBTE studies leads to overprediction at high T; (2) RTA solution of PBTE underestimates phononic kappa compared to iterative solution (authors did not perform iterative because of computational cost); (3) phonon-electron scattering negligible under intrinsic carrier concentrations here, so omission not a large source of discrepancy; (4) temperature-dependent IFCs (phonon renormalization) have minor effect in Si but could matter in more anharmonic materials; (5) experimental uncertainty/scatter at T>1000 K; (6) approximations in DFT electronic structure (band-gap underestimation) corrected by empirical Varshni shift for electron transport. |
| notes_on_temperature_dependence | Key reported dependences: - Three-phonon scattering lifetimes scale roughly as T^-1; four-phonon lifetimes scale roughly as T^-2, so 4ph becomes increasingly important at high T (dominant importance > ~500–700 K). - Inclusion of 4ph makes kappa fall more rapidly with T than 3ph-only. - Phonon renormalization reduces frequencies (group velocities down ~4% from 100 K to 1500 K) and yields slightly longer lifetimes, net small effect (~+3% change in kappa vs 0 K IFCs). - Thermal expansion small effect (~-1.5% kappa at 1500 K for +0.5% lattice expansion). - Electronic contribution becomes significant at high T (electronic kappa ~5.09 W/mK at 1500 K; electrons conduct >25% of heat at 1500 K). |
| key_figures_tables_locations | Phononic kappa vs T: Fig. 1(a) (Section IV.A). Phonon dispersion and T-dependent frequencies: Fig. 2 (Section IV.A). Phonon lifetimes vs frequency at 300 and 1500 K: Fig. 3 (Section IV.A). Electronic thermal conductivity: Fig. 4 (Section IV.B). Total thermal conductivity (phonons+electrons) vs T: Fig. 6 (Section IV.C). |

metadata.title: A Comprehensive Review of Heat Transfer in Thermoelectric Materials and Devices
metadata.abstract: Solid-state thermoelectric devices are currently used in applications ranging from thermocouple sensors to power generators in satellites, to portable air-conditioners and refrigerators. With the ever-rising demand throughout the world for energy consumption and CO2 reduction, thermoelectric energy conversion has been receiving intensified attention as a potential candidate for waste-heat harvesting as well as for power generation from renewable sources. Efficient thermoelectric energy conversion critically depends on the performance of thermoelectric materials and devices. In this review, we discuss heat transfer in thermoelectric materials and devices, especially phonon engineering to reduce the lattice thermal conductivity of thermoelectric materials, which requires a fundamental understanding of nanoscale heat conduction physics.

| name_full | Crystalline silicon lattice thermal conductivity predicted by first-principles PBTE/DFT |
| brief_description | First-principles predictions of the lattice (phononic) thermal conductivity of crystalline silicon using DFT-derived interatomic force constants and solution of the phonon Boltzmann transport equation (both reciprocal-space/DFPT and real-space IFC approaches are discussed). These calculations reproduce experimental kappa(T) trends and absolute values much better than classical empirical-MD for bulk Si. |
| citation_title | Intrinsic lattice thermal conductivity of semiconductors from first principles. |
| mention_or_use | mention |
| material_system | Si (crystalline, bulk) |
| composition_x | None |
| structure_and_phase | bulk crystalline Si (diamond cubic); natural/isotropic crystal discussed (no special isotopic purity stated for the plotted comparisons) |
| temperature_points_K | Temperature dependence shown in Fig.10(a) (thermal conductivity versus temperature from first-principles calculations and experiments); key reference point: 300 K (see text and figures). Exact plotted temperature range not numerically listed in text but includes low-T peak and high-T decay regimes (figure). |
| thermal_conductivity_values | Representative values cited in text: bulk Si thermal conductivity ~150 W m^-1 K^-1 (around 300 K). Fig.10(a) shows first-principles kappa(T) curves that agree with experimental symbols (no tabulated numeric curve values in text). |
| kappa_definition_and_components | Lattice (phononic) thermal conductivity (kappa_p) only; electronic contribution excluded. First-principles workflow separates harmonic and anharmonic contributions (harmonic eigenmodes from IFCs, anharmonic scattering rates via Fermi's golden rule) and integrates over Brillouin zone to obtain kappa. |
| method_category | first-principles PBTE/DFT (DFPT reciprocal-space and real-space IFC approaches described) |
| md_flavor | None |
| interatomic_potential | None |
| emd_gk_details | None |
| nemd_details | None |
| simulation_cell_and_convergence | None |
| first_principles_details | Two approaches described: reciprocal-space DFPT (density functional perturbation theory) to obtain force constants (Broido et al. approach), and real-space finite-displacement / polynomial fitting of DFT forces in supercells (Esfarjani et al. approach). Harmonic (2nd) and anharmonic (3rd) IFCs are obtained and used to compute phonon eigenmodes and 3-phonon scattering rates via Fermi's golden rule; solutions obtained either under single-mode relaxation time approximation (RTA) or via iterative (full) solution of the linearized BTE — both approaches are discussed in the review as used in the literature. Exact DFT code, pseudopotentials, cutoffs, q-mesh sizes, supercell sizes are not specified in this review (references cited for details). |
| phonon_scattering_mechanisms_included | Intrinsic anharmonic 3-phonon scattering (via Fermi's golden rule) is included in the first-principles PBTE calculations; isotope scattering and other perturbative scatterings are discussed as additions in literature, but the review highlights 3-phonon as primary in the cited first-principles works; iterative vs single-mode RTA solution differences are noted. |
| alloy_modeling_approach | None |
| reported_method_comparisons | The review states that first-principles PBTE (reciprocal-space DFPT and real-space IFC fitting) reproduces experimental kappa(T) for Si very well (cites Broido et al., Esfarjani et al.). It contrasts these successes with discrepancies observed when using empirical interatomic potentials in MD for thermal conductivity predictions (empirical potentials can deviate significantly, see ref.149). The review also notes differences between RTA and iterative BTE solutions (iterative can differ and is sometimes required for accurate results). |
| agreement_with_experiment | Review reports excellent agreement between first-principles PBTE results and experimental measurements for Si (Fig.10(a) shows lines from first-principles overlaid with experimental symbols). No quantified residuals are given in the review text. |
| proposed_reasons_for_discrepancies | Where discrepancies occur (mainly with empirical-MD predictions), the review attributes them to: limitations/inaccuracy of empirical interatomic potentials (phonon dispersion and anharmonicity mismatch), classical (non-quantum) statistics in MD leading to errors below Debye temperature, finite-size effects and insufficient convergence in MD, and methodological differences (RTA vs iterative PBTE). For first-principles RTA vs iterative solutions, omission of coupling between modes (i.e., neglect of off-diagonal terms in collision operator) can cause quantitative differences. |
| notes_on_temperature_dependence | Review summarizes universal behavior: low-T ~ T^3 (boundary-limited/Casimir regime), peak at intermediate T, high-T decreases approximately as T^n with n~1–1.5 due to Umklapp scattering; first-principles calculations reproduce these trends for Si (peak and high-T decay). |
| key_figures_tables_locations | Fig.10(a) (thermal conductivity versus temperature from first-principles calculations and experimental measurements) and Sect.4.1 (discussion of first-principles PBTE and references to Broido et al. and Esfarjani et al.). Also Fig.10(b) and Fig.11 provide related MFP accumulation and experimental comparisons for Si. |

| name_full | Lattice thermal conductivity predictions for Si1-xGex alloys (Si-Ge alloys) |
| brief_description | Discussion of computational predictions for Si1-xGex alloy lattice thermal conductivity: empirical-MD NEMD studies have shown large discrepancies with experiment, whereas first-principles force constants combined with virtual-crystal/alloy scattering models (DFPT + VCA/Tamura/Abeles-type treatments) (e.g., Garg et al.) reproduce experimental kappa(T). The review contrasts modeling approaches and highlights modeling choices that explain differences. |
| citation_title | Role of Disorder and Anharmonicity in the Thermal Conductivity of Silicon-Germanium Alloys: A First-Principles Study. |
| mention_or_use | mention |
| material_system | Si1-xGex alloy (Si-Ge alloy), various compositions discussed generally; specific experimental composition example: Si0.8Ge0.2 noted elsewhere in paper but alloy discussion treats 0<=x<=1 |
| composition_x | general 0 <= x <= 1 (text mentions Si1-xGex alloys and specific commonly-used composition Si0.8Ge0.2 in other contexts); review cites experimental Si1-xGex thermal conductivity falling below ~10 W m^-1 K^-1 (reference 48) for alloy mixtures. |
| structure_and_phase | substitutional solid-solution (alloy) modeled via virtual crystal / average-crystal approaches in many theoretical treatments; disorder (mass and possibly force-constant disorder) discussed. Crystal structure assumed same as parent (diamond cubic) in virtual-crystal treatments. |
| temperature_points_K | Temperature dependence of alloy kappa discussed qualitatively (figures for related materials shown in Fig.10(a) for pure materials; alloy experimental values cited at 300 K in text). Review does not provide explicit numeric kappa(T) curves for Si1-xGex in text, but states measured thermal conductivity can fall to below ~10 W m^-1 K^-1 (300 K). |
| thermal_conductivity_values | Experimental statement: measured thermal conductivity of Si1-xGex can sharply fall down to below ~10 W m^-1 K^-1 (cited ref.48). The review states that Garg et al. (DFPT + virtual crystal) were able to reproduce experimental thermal conductivity of Si1-xGex; NEMD with empirical potentials gave large discrepancies (ref.189). No explicit numerical DFT curve values are tabulated in the review text. |
| kappa_definition_and_components | Lattice thermal conductivity (kappa_p) of the alloy; electronic contribution not primary focus here. In virtual-crystal treatments kappa is computed using modified dispersion and added impurity scattering terms (mass-disorder scattering), typically combined via Matthiessen's rule with anharmonic scattering. |
| method_category | hybrid: first-principles force constants (DFPT) + virtual crystal/alloy scattering models (Garg et al.); also empirical-potential MD (NEMD) studies are discussed and contrasted. |
| md_flavor | NEMD (nonequilibrium MD) with empirical interatomic potentials; review notes these NEMD simulations yielded large discrepancies with experiments for SiGe alloys (ref.189). |
| interatomic_potential | For the empirical-MD studies the review does not list a specific potential name in the text for the Si-Ge NEMD discrepant studies, only that empirical potentials were used and caused deviations; the review references Skye & Schelling (ref.189) for MD on Si-Ge alloys where potentials are used. |
| emd_gk_details | None |
| nemd_details | Review remarks general NEMD drawbacks: finite simulation size potentially shorter than relevant phonon MFPs, artificial size effects from heat reservoirs, and use of large temperature differences across small domains; these methodological issues can cause discrepancy in predicted kappa for alloys when using NEMD with empirical potentials. |
| simulation_cell_and_convergence | Review highlights that NEMD suffers from finite-size effects and that MD-accessible sizes are limited; specific cell sizes, timesteps, run lengths not provided in the review (see cited MD papers). |
| first_principles_details | Garg et al. used DFPT-derived force constants in combination with a virtual crystal model to compute phonon dispersions and anharmonic scattering rates; mass-disorder scattering and alloy disorder treated perturbatively (Abeles-style/ Tamura-type approaches) and included alongside intrinsic anharmonic scattering to obtain alloy kappa. The review notes real-space fitting and DFPT reciprocal approaches as two ways to obtain IFCs; specific computational parameters (codes, cutoffs, meshes) are not listed in the review itself. |
| phonon_scattering_mechanisms_included | Intrinsic anharmonic (3-phonon) scattering plus alloy impurity/mass-disorder scattering treated perturbatively (Rayleigh-type low-frequency limit, Tamura model that incorporates DOS) in the DFPT+VCA studies; other terms (e.g., force-constant disorder beyond mass-only, multiple-scattering/dependent scattering) are discussed as potentially important but not always included. |
| alloy_modeling_approach | Virtual crystal approximation (VCA) / Abeles-type approach: form a new 'average' crystal with averaged masses and force constants, compute modified dispersion, then add mass-disorder scattering as a perturbation (Rayleigh-like or Tamura formalism). Garg et al. used DFPT force constants + virtual crystal model; the review notes questions about the validity of perturbative (first-order) impurity scattering in the non-dilute limit and about whether only mass disorder vs force-constant disorder is sufficient. |
| reported_method_comparisons | Explicit comparisons noted: empirical-potential NEMD studies gave large discrepancies with measured values for SiGe alloys (ref.189), while DFPT + virtual-crystal approach (Garg et al.) reproduced experimental thermal conductivity successfully. The review emphasizes that hybrid first-principles + alloy-scattering modeling matched experiment better than direct empirical-MD for SiGe alloys. Shiomi et al. are mentioned as performing EMD using first-principles-derived force constants for other alloyed systems and obtaining reasonable agreement. |
| agreement_with_experiment | The review reports that DFPT+VCA (Garg et al.) reproduces experimental thermal conductivity of Si1-xGex; conversely, NEMD with empirical potentials showed significant deviations from experiments (Skye & Schelling ref.). Experimental data quoted: Si1-xGex kappa falls to below ~10 W m^-1 K^-1 at 300 K. |
| proposed_reasons_for_discrepancies | Review lists reasons for method-dependent differences: empirical potentials may not capture accurate phonon dispersions and anharmonicity for alloys; MD is classical and misses quantum occupation effects (important below Debye temperature); perturbative impurity-scattering models (Rayleigh/Tamura) may be invalid at high frequencies or in non-dilute alloys; force-constant disorder (changes in IFCs due to substitution) may be important but is not always included (VCA often treats mass-only disorder); dependence of scattering on whether impurity frequencies fall inside/outside host phonon bands; finite-size effects and thermostat/large gradient artifacts in NEMD; insufficient treatment of dependent scattering and localization effects. |
| notes_on_temperature_dependence | Review reiterates general crystalline trends (low-T boundary-limited, intermediate peak, high-T ~ T^-1 to T^-1.5). For alloys, strong suppression of kappa at room temperature is emphasized (down to <~10 W m^-1 K^-1 for SiGe alloys); no explicit fitted temperature exponents for alloys are provided in the review text. |
| key_figures_tables_locations | Alloy discussion in Sect.5.1 (Alloy) and references therein; the success of DFPT+VCA is mentioned in Sect.5.1 with citation to Garg et al. (ref.155). Discrepancies of empirical NEMD are mentioned in same section (ref.189). General temperature-vs-kappa comparisons for pure materials are in Fig.10(a). |

metadata.title: Transport simulations in hierarchically disordered nanostructures for thermoelectric material design

journal.name: 2018 IEEE 13th Nanotechnology Materials and Devices Conference (NMDC)

metadata.abstract: Hierarchically nanostructured materials, where disorder is introduced in various length scales (at the atomic scale, the nanoscale, and the mesoscale) is one of the most promising directions to achieve extremely low thermal conductivities and improve thermoelectric performance. Here we theoretically investigate one such system, a nanocrystalline material with nanopores that are introduced between the crystalline regions. We use the Nonequilibrium Green's Function method for electronic transport and Molecular Dynamics for phonon transport.

| thermal_conductivity_values | Pristine (EMD-GK, 300 K): 207.41 ± 11.51 W m^-1 K^-1; Superlattice (grain boundaries, 300 K): 41.99 ± 2.47 W m^-1 K^-1 (~5× reduction vs pristine MD); Pores (4.6% porosity, 300 K): 29.14 ± 2.48 W m^-1 K^-1 (~7.1× reduction vs pristine MD); SL + pores (300 K): 12.10 ± 1.33 W m^-1 K^-1 (~17.1× reduction vs pristine MD). Literature experimental baseline used: ~101.5 W m^-1 K^-1 (350 K). |
| kappa_definition_and_components | Lattice thermal conductivity computed from equilibrium MD Green–Kubo via integration of the heat-current autocorrelation function (HCACF); reported values are lattice-only (no separate electronic contribution); classical MD was used and no quantum correction is reported. |
