| md_flavor | Equilibrium MD (Green–Kubo HCACF integration) |
| interatomic_potential | Stillinger–Weber (SW) potential with force-matched parameter set optimized to DFT-GGA (Lee & Hwang, 2012) |
| emd_gk_details | Procedure reported: relax structure with conjugate-gradient; NPT run at 300 K for 125 ps with 0.5 fs timestep (allows thermal expansion); anneal near grain-boundary contacts; NVE equilibration 125 ps; NVE production 10 ns with 2 fs timestep while recording HCACF; HCACF (non-normalized) integrated per Green–Kubo to obtain kappa_xx; periodic boundary conditions in all directions; sets of 10 independent calculations performed for each geometry. The paper does not explicitly state the exact heat-flux definition used, the correlation-time cutoff/integration window, use of multiple time origins, or fitting procedures. |
| nemd_details | None |
| simulation_cell_and_convergence | Simulation cell: 184 × 14 × 10 supercells of Si (diamond-cubic 8-atom unit cell) => 184*14*10*8 = 206,080 atoms; periodic boundary conditions in all directions; timestep: 0.5 fs during NPT, 2 fs during NVE production; production length: 10 ns; number of replicas: 10 independent runs per geometry; authors state the pristine system has been converged for size but no detailed size-extrapolation (e.g., kappa vs 1/L) or systematic finite-size extrapolation is presented. |
| first_principles_details | None |
| phonon_scattering_mechanisms_included | Anharmonic phonon-phonon scattering is included implicitly by classical MD to all orders; boundary scattering from explicit pores and grain boundaries included via atomistic geometry; isotope scattering and electron-phonon scattering are not explicitly modeled/separated; no explicit treatment of 3- vs 4-phonon processes as MD treats anharmonicity implicitly classically. |
| alloy_modeling_approach | None |
| reported_method_comparisons | Direct comparisons reported: MD-pristine kappa (207.4 W/mK at 300 K) vs literature experimental kappa (~101.5 W/mK at 350 K) showing MD overprediction; authors quantify reductions due to nanostructures (SL ~5×, pores ~7.1×, combined ~17.1×). They also compare expected Matthiessen's-rule combined value (1/k_SL+pores ≈ 1/k_SL + 1/k_pores giving ~17.2 Wm^-1K^-1) and note the actual combined MD value (12.1 Wm^-1K^-1) gives a larger reduction than that simple estimate. |

| proposed_reasons_for_discrepancies | Authors state the main cause of MD overprediction is the choice/parameterization of the interatomic potential (SW force-matched parameters still overpredict kappa). metadata.title: Simulating lattice thermal conductivity in semiconducting materials using high-dimensional neural network potential
metadata.abstract: We demonstrate that a high-dimensional neural network potential (HDNNP) can predict the lattice thermal conductivity of semiconducting materials with an accuracy that is comparable to that of density functional theory (DFT) calculation. After a training procedure based on force, the root mean square error between the forces predicted by HDNNP and DFT is less than 40 meV Å−1. As typical examples, we present the results of Si and GaN bulk crystals. The deviation from the thermal conductivity calculated using DFT is within 1% at 200 to 500 K for Si and within 5.4% at 200 to 1000 K for GaN.

metadata.title: Efficient anharmonic lattice dynamics calculations of thermal transport in crystalline and disordered solids
metadata.abstract: Understanding heat transport in semiconductors and insulators is of fundamental importance because of its technological impact in electronics and renewable energy harvesting and conversion. Anharmonic Lattice Dynamics provides a powerful framework for the description of heat transport at the nanoscale. One of the advantages of this method is that it naturally includes quantum effects due to atoms vibrations, which are needed to compute the thermal properties of semiconductors widely used in nanotechnology, like silicon and carbon, even at room temperature. While the heat transport picture substantially differs between amorphous and crystalline semiconductors from a microscopic standpoint, a unified approach to simulate both crystals and glasses has been devised. Here we introduce a unified workflow, which implements both the Boltzmann Transport equation (BTE) and the Quasi Harmonic Green-Kubo (QHGK) methods. We discuss how the theory can be optimized to exploit modern parallel architectures, and how it is implemented in $\kappa ALDo$: a versatile and scalable open-source software to compute phonon transport in solids. This approach is applied to crystalline and partially disordered silicon-based systems, including bulk silicon and clathrates, and on silicon-germanium alloy clathrates with largely reduced thermal conductivity.

tldr.text: The results clearly point out the importance of lattice thermal conductivity engineering in bulk and nanostructures to produce high-performance thermoelectric materials.

journal.name: Science and Technology of Advanced Materials

metadata.abstract: Various theoretical and experimental methods are utilized to investigate the thermal conductivity of nanostructured materials; this is a critical parameter to increase performance of thermoelectric devices. Among these methods, equilibrium molecular dynamics (EMD) is an accurate technique to predict lattice thermal conductivity. In this study, by means of systematic EMD simulations, thermal conductivity of bulk Si-Ge structures (pristine, alloy and superlattice) and their nanostructured one dimensional forms with square and circular cross-section geometries (asymmetric and symmetric) are calculated for different crystallographic directions. A comprehensive temperature analysis is evaluated for selected structures as well. The results show that one-dimensional structures are superior candidates in terms of their low lattice thermal conductivity and thermal conductivity tunability by nanostructuring, such as by diameter modulation, interface roughness, periodicity and number of interfaces. We find that thermal conductivity decreases with smaller diameters or cross section areas. Furthermore, interface roughness decreases thermal conductivity with a profound impact. Moreover, we predicted that there is a specific periodicity that gives minimum thermal conductivity in symmetric superlattice structures. The decreasing thermal conductivity is due to the reducing phonon movement in the system due to the effect of the number of interfaces that determine regimes of ballistic and wave transport phenomena. In some nanostructures, such as nanowire superlattices, thermal conductivity of the Si/Ge system can be reduced to nearly twice that of an amorphous silicon thermal conductivity. Additionally, it is found that one crystal orientation, 100, is better than the 111 crystal orientation in one-dimensional and bulk SiGe systems. Our results clearly point out the importance of lattice thermal conductivity engineering in bulk and nanostructures to produce high-performance thermoelectric materials. Graphical Abstract

paper-544f173743e30f899ed765ea02113da1c1.displayLabel: Thermal conductivity of intrinsic semiconductor at elevated temperature: role of four-phonon scattering and electronic heat conduction

s2Metadata.title: Thermal conductivity of intrinsic semiconductor at elevated temperature: role of four-phonon scattering and electronic heat conduction
s2Metadata.abstract: While using first-principles-based Boltzmann transport equation approach to predict the thermal conductivity of crystalline semiconductor materials has been a routine, the validity of the approach is seldom tested for high-temperature conditions. Most previous studies only focused on the phononic contribution, and neglected the electronic part. Meanwhile, the treatment on phonon transport is not rigorous as a few ingredients, such as four-phonon scatterings, phonon renormalization and thermal expansion, are ignored. In this paper, we present a Boltzmann transport equation study on high-temperature thermal conduction in bulk silicon by considering the effects of both phonons and electrons, and explore the role of the missing parts in the previous studies on the thermal conductivity at elevated temperature. For the phonon transport, four-phonon scattering is found to considerably reduce the thermal conductivity when the temperature is larger than 700 K, while the effects of phonon renormalization and thermal expansion on phononic thermal conductivity are negligible. Bipolar contribution to the electronic thermal conductivity calculated from first-principles is implemented for the first time. More than 25% of heat is shown to be conducted by electrons at 1500 K. The computed total thermal conductivity of silicon faithfully reproduces the measured data. The approach presented in this paper is expected to be applied to other high-temperature functional materials, and the results could serve as benchmarks and help to explain the high-temperature phonon and electron transport phenomena.

paper-fbf7170d0b720a69a2492581b23dc34f88.displayLabel: First-principles phonon physics using the Pheasy code

s2Metadata.title: First-principles phonon physics using the Pheasy code
s2Metadata.abstract: Parameter-free calculations of lattice dynamics from first principles have achieved significant progress in the past decades, with a wealth of applications in thermodynamics, phase transitions, and transport properties of materials. Current approaches to derive the interatomic force constants (IFCs) of lattice potential become challenging and sometimes infeasible when going beyond third-order anharmonicity, due to the combinatorial explosion in the number of higher-order IFCs. In this work, we present a robust and user-friendly program, , which reliably reconstructs the prescribed potential energy surface of crystalline solids via a Taylor expansion of arbitrarily high order. Given force-displacement datasets, the program enables an efficient and accurate extraction of IFCs using advanced machine-learning algorithms, and further calculates a wide range of harmonic and anharmonic phonon related properties. We show in three prototypical examples how the obtained IFCs have been successfully applied to study anharmonic lattice dynamics and thermal transport. Through these detailed benchmarks, we have also identified the optimal approach for IFC extractions and offered general guidelines for high-fidelity lattice-dynamical simulations, addressing the large uncertainties in the IFCs extracted from existing various schemes. Overall, the project aims to create a phonon code ecosystem that connects diverse phonon simulation platforms and offers access to the broad research community.

paper-5889a9cd0d2389bfce4a7bc1ec9052ec19.displayLabel: Significant reduction of lattice thermal conductivity by the electron-phonon interaction in silicon with high carrier concentrations: a first-principles study.

s2Metadata.title: Significant reduction of lattice thermal conductivity by the electron-phonon interaction in silicon with high carrier concentrations: a first-principles study.
s2Metadata.abstract: The electron-phonon interaction is well known to create major resistance to electron transport in metals and semiconductors, whereas fewer studies are directed to its effect on phonon transport, especially in semiconductors. We calculate the phonon lifetimes due to scattering with electrons (or holes), combine them with the intrinsic lifetimes due to the anharmonic phonon-phonon interaction, all from first principles, and evaluate the effect of the electron-phonon interaction on the lattice thermal conductivity of silicon. Unexpectedly, we find a significant reduction of the lattice thermal conductivity at room temperature as the carrier concentration goes above 10(19)  cm(-3) (the reduction reaches up to 45% in p-type silicon at around 10(21)  cm(-3)), a range of great technological relevance to thermoelectric materials.

paper-c1db9aa7a1e6d91e3dafea40ce6a6eaef0.displayLabel: Efficient anharmonic lattice dynamics calculations of thermal transport in crystalline and disordered solids

s2Metadata.title: Efficient anharmonic lattice dynamics calculations of thermal transport in crystalline and disordered solids
s2Metadata.abstract: Understanding heat transport in semiconductors and insulators is of fundamental importance because of its technological impact in electronics and renewable energy harvesting and conversion. Anharmonic Lattice Dynamics provides a powerful framework for the description of heat transport at the nanoscale. One of the advantages of this method is that it naturally includes quantum effects due to atoms vibrations, which are needed to compute the thermal properties of semiconductors widely used in nanotechnology, like silicon and carbon, even at room temperature. While the heat transport picture substantially differs between amorphous and crystalline semiconductors from a microscopic standpoint, a unified approach to simulate both crystals and glasses has been devised. Here we introduce a unified workflow, which implements both the Boltzmann Transport equation (BTE) and the Quasi Harmonic Green-Kubo (QHGK) methods. We discuss how the theory can be optimized to exploit modern parallel architectures, and how it is implemented in $\kappa ALDo$: a versatile and scalable open-source software to compute phonon transport in solids. This approach is applied to crystalline and partially disordered silicon-based systems, including bulk silicon and clathrates, and on silicon-germanium alloy clathrates with largely reduced thermal conductivity.

paper-9bcafe72a9aa8b0945e900ce108fb6ad25.displayLabel: Transport simulations in hierarchically disordered nanostructures for thermoelectric material design

s2Metadata.title: Transport simulations in hierarchically disordered nanostructures for thermoelectric material design
s2Metadata.abstract: Hierarchically nanostructured materials, where disorder is introduced in various length scales (at the atomic scale, the nanoscale, and the mesoscale) is one of the most promising directions to achieve extremely low thermal conductivities and improve thermoelectric performance. Here we theoretically investigate one such system, a nanocrystalline material with nanopores that are introduced between the crystalline regions. We use the Nonequilibrium Green's Function method for electronic transport and Molecular Dynamics for phonon transport.

paper-5440f8458754c69b941910a03a7f0e1e40.displayLabel: A Comprehensive Review of Heat Transfer in Thermoelectric Materials and Devices

s2Metadata.title: A Comprehensive Review of Heat Transfer in Thermoelectric Materials and Devices
s2Metadata.abstract: Solid-state thermoelectric devices are currently used in applications ranging from thermocouple sensors to power generators in satellites, to portable air-conditioners and refrigerators. With the ever-rising demand throughout the world for energy consumption and CO2 reduction, thermoelectric energy conversion has been receiving intensified attention as a potential candidate for waste-heat harvesting as well as for power generation from renewable sources. Efficient thermoelectric energy conversion critically depends on the performance of thermoelectric materials and devices. In this review, we discuss heat transfer in thermoelectric materials and devices, especially phonon engineering to reduce the lattice thermal conductivity of thermoelectric materials, which requires a fundamental understanding of nanoscale heat conduction physics.

paper-7768b8b467adf08a976e6e61b49bc31604.displayLabel: Computational prediction of lattice thermal conductivity: A comparison of molecular dynamics and Boltzmann transport approaches

s2Metadata.title: Computational prediction of lattice thermal conductivity: A comparison of molecular dynamics and Boltzmann transport approaches
s2Metadata.abstract: The predictive modeling of lattice thermal conductivity is of fundamental importance for the understanding and design of materials for a wide range of applications. Two major approaches, namely molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and calculations solving approximately the Boltzmann transport equation (BTE), have been developed to compute the lattice thermal conductivity. We present a detailed direct comparison of these two approaches, using as prototypical cases MgO and PbTe. The comparison, carried out using empirical potentials, takes into account the effects of fourth order phonon scattering, temperature-dependent phonon frequencies (phonon renormalization), and investigates the effects of quantum vs. classical statistics. We clarify that equipartition, as opposed to Maxwell Boltzmann, govern the statistics of phonons in MD simulations. We find that lattice thermal conductivity values from MD and BTE show an apparent, satisfactory agreement; however such an agreement is the result of error cancellations. We also show that the primary effect of statistics on thermal conductivity is via the scattering rate dependence on phonon populations.

paper-1b4f174685bbc26dd19180ecfcf7cb0b15.displayLabel: Simulating lattice thermal conductivity in semiconducting materials using high-dimensional neural network potential

s2Metadata.title: Simulating lattice thermal conductivity in semiconducting materials using high-dimensional neural network potential
s2Metadata.abstract: We demonstrate that a high-dimensional neural network potential (HDNNP) can predict the lattice thermal conductivity of semiconducting materials with an accuracy that is comparable to that of density functional theory (DFT) calculation. After a training procedure based on force, the root mean square error between the forces predicted by HDNNP and DFT is less than 40 meV Å−1. As typical examples, we present the results of Si and GaN bulk crystals. The deviation from the thermal conductivity calculated using DFT is within 1% at 200 to 500 K for Si and within 5.4% at 200 to 1000 K for GaN.

paper-292b26cc817258dac7b29d83cd91513ced.displayLabel: Uncertainty quantification in first-principles predictions of phonon properties and lattice thermal conductivity

s2Metadata.title: Uncertainty quantification in first-principles predictions of phonon properties and lattice thermal conductivity
s2Metadata.abstract: We present a framework for quantifying the uncertainty that results from the choice of exchange-correlation (XC) functional in predictions of phonon properties and thermal conductivity that use density functional theory (DFT) to calculate the atomic force constants. The energy ensemble capabilities of the BEEF-vdW XC functional are first applied to determine an ensemble of interatomic force constants, which are then used as inputs to lattice dynamics calculations and a solution of the Boltzmann transport equation. The framework is applied to isotopically-pure silicon. We find that the uncertainty estimates bound property predictions (e.g., phonon dispersions, specific heat, thermal conductivity) from other XC functionals and experiments. We distinguish between properties that are correlated with the predicted thermal conductivity [e.g., the transverse acoustic branch sound speed ($R^2=0.89$) and average Gruneisen parameter ($R^2=0.85$)] and those that are not [e.g., longitudinal acoustic branch sound speed ($R^2=0.23$) and specific heat ($R^2=0.00$)]. We find that differences in ensemble predictions of thermal conductivity are correlated with the behavior of phonons with mean free paths between $100$ and $300$ nm. The framework systematically accounts for XC uncertainty in phonon calculations and should be used whenever it is suspected that the choice of XC functional is influencing physical interpretations.

content.text: Method-to-method κ differences can usually be explained by which scattering mechanisms are included or missing (plus any artificial scattering from the simulation setup).
**Supporting evidence:**

- First-principles Si PBTE shows adding 4-phonon scattering lowers κ at 300 K by ~8% (3ph-only overestimates); and 4ph importance grows with T, with stated scaling τ_3ph ~ T^-1 and τ_4ph ~ T^-2, producing increasing high-T corrections.  <paper entityId="paper-544f173743e30f899ed765ea02113da1c166774b" annotationId="ann_001" corpusId="211987717" artifactId="extraction-result-6#uuid-e6.0">Gu et al., 2020</paper>

- First-principles Si PBTE (Pheasy+ShengBTE iterative for 3ph; FourPhonon RTA for 4ph) reports κ_3ph(300 K) ≈125.4 W/mK and κ_3+4ph(300 K) ≈115.4 W/mK (7.9% drop), demonstrating an omitted channel changes κ systematically.  <paper entityId="paper-fbf7170d0b720a69a2492581b23dc34f886f655c" annotationId="ann_002" corpusId="280421449" artifactId="extraction-result-4#uuid-e4.0">Lin et al., 2025</paper>

- Electron–phonon interaction (EPI) in Si at 300 K can reduce lattice κ by up to ~45% at extreme carrier concentrations (~1e21 cm^-3), showing that adding an additional scattering channel can strongly reduce κ when relevant (doped case).  <paper entityId="paper-5889a9cd0d2389bfce4a7bc1ec9052ec19aa910b" annotationId="ann_003" corpusId="5754250" artifactId="extraction-result-3#uuid-e3.0">Liao et al., 2014</paper>

- Empirical Tersoff-IFCs used in ALD/BTE for bulk diamond Si yield κ_Q(300 K)=305 W/mK versus DFT-PBTE inversion κ(300 K)=147 W/mK, consistent with a method/potential that effectively yields weaker scattering and/or higher velocities (i.e., different effective collision operator/spectrum).  <paper entityId="paper-c1db9aa7a1e6d91e3dafea40ce6a6eaef0f2a40a" annotationId="ann_004" corpusId="221507928" artifactId="extraction-result-10#uuid-e10.1">Barbalinardo et al., 2020</paper>

- A SW force-matched potential used in EMD-GK MD for pristine bulk Si gives κ(300 K)=207±12 W/mK and the authors attribute overprediction vs experimental literature primarily to the potential choice, illustrating method bias due to effective spectrum/scattering differences set by the force field.  <paper entityId="paper-9bcafe72a9aa8b0945e900ce108fb6ad250221e9" annotationId="ann_005" corpusId="57762337" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.0">Oliveira et al., 2018</paper>

- First-principles PBTE literature/review emphasizes that empirical potentials can deviate due to dispersion/anharmonicity errors; MD has finite-size issues and classical statistics; PBTE differs by RTA vs iterative solution choices—explicitly linking method discrepancies to spectrum/scattering/operator approximations.  <paper entityId="paper-544f173743e30f899ed765ea02113da1c166774b" annotationId="ann_006" corpusId="211987717" artifactId="extraction-result-6#uuid-e6.2">Gu et al., 2020</paper> <paper entityId="paper-5440f8458754c69b941910a03a7f0e1e40ec515e" annotationId="ann_007" corpusId="111146233" artifactId="extraction-result-7#uuid-e7.0">Tian et al., 2014</paper> <paper entityId="paper-7768b8b467adf08a976e6e61b49bc31604b121fe" annotationId="ann_008" corpusId="119231887" artifactId="extraction-result-1#uuid-e1.0">Puligheddu et al., 2019</paper>

- Si PBTE direct inversion vs RTA differs by ~5% at 300 K (147 vs 140 W/mK), showing that even within PBTE, solver approximations change the effective collision-operator treatment and κ.  <paper entityId="paper-c1db9aa7a1e6d91e3dafea40ce6a6eaef0f2a40a" annotationId="ann_009" corpusId="221507928" artifactId="extraction-result-10#uuid-e10.0">Barbalinardo et al., 2020</paper>

- ALD/PBTE with DFT forces vs HDNNP forces yields nearly identical κ(300 K) for Si (112.1 vs 110.4 W/mK) within the same PBTE-RTA workflow, indicating that if the force/IFC source preserves the scattering operator and spectrum, κ agreement follows—supporting the MESO focus on operator/spectrum fidelity rather than implementation brand.  <paper entityId="paper-1b4f174685bbc26dd19180ecfcf7cb0b152de2be" annotationId="ann_010" corpusId="160009739" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.0">Minamitani et al., 2019</paper>

content.title: High-T divergence law: omission of 4ph causes increasing κ overprediction with T

content.text: Leaving out four-phonon scattering makes κ too high, and the error grows as temperature increases.
**Supporting evidence:**

- First-principles Si PBTE study reports τ_3ph ~ T^-1 and τ_4ph ~ T^-2; inclusion of 4ph becomes significant above ~500–700 K and 3ph-only at 900 K gives κ≈43 W/mK and is ~20% larger than measurement, i.e., omission yields growing high-T overprediction.  <paper entityId="paper-544f173743e30f899ed765ea02113da1c166774b" annotationId="ann_011" corpusId="211987717" artifactId="extraction-result-6#uuid-e6.0">Gu et al., 2020</paper>

- Independent first-principles PBTE study shows at 300 K 4ph already reduces κ by ~7.9% (125.4→115.4 W/mK), establishing a nonzero correction that is expected to grow with T.  <paper entityId="paper-fbf7170d0b720a69a2492581b23dc34f886f655c" annotationId="ann_012" corpusId="280421449" artifactId="extraction-result-4#uuid-e4.0">Lin et al., 2025</paper>

- Review-level discussion notes four-phonon scattering can be comparable to three-phonon even for low-anharmonicity materials like Si and Ge near/above ΘD, implying increasing relevance at high T and thus growing bias if omitted.  <paper entityId="paper-7768b8b467adf08a976e6e61b49bc31604b121fe" annotationId="ann_013" corpusId="119231887" artifactId="extraction-result-1#uuid-e1.0">Puligheddu et al., 2019</paper>

content.title: Empirical-force-field bias law: κ inflation via (v, τ) co-bias in bulk Si

content.text: If the force field makes phonons too fast or too long-lived (or both), κ comes out too large, sometimes by about a factor of two.
**Supporting evidence:**

- Tersoff-based ALD/BTE for diamond Si yields κ_Q(300 K)=305 W/mK (and κ_classical=260 W/mK) while DFT-PBTE inversion yields κ_Q,Inv(300 K)=147 W/mK (and DFT classical limit ≈123 W/mK), demonstrating large κ inflation from Tersoff-derived lattice dynamics.  <paper entityId="paper-c1db9aa7a1e6d91e3dafea40ce6a6eaef0f2a40a" annotationId="ann_014" corpusId="221507928" artifactId="extraction-result-10#uuid-e10.1">Barbalinardo et al., 2020</paper>

- Pristine Si EMD-GK using a force-matched SW potential yields κ(300 K)=207±12 W/mK and authors state overprediction vs experimental reference is mainly due to the interatomic potential, supporting the idea that force-field choice changes effective spectrum/scattering and thus κ.  <paper entityId="paper-9bcafe72a9aa8b0945e900ce108fb6ad250221e9" annotationId="ann_015" corpusId="57762337" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.0">Oliveira et al., 2018</paper>

- First-principles uncertainty study shows κ(300 K) is strongly sensitive to phonon properties like TA sound speed and Grüneisen parameters (correlations R^2 up to 0.89), consistent with the mechanism that biases in velocities/anharmonicity produce large κ shifts; it also shows XC functional choice shifts κ from ~122 (LDA) to ~171 (BEEF-vdW) W/mK at 300 K for isotopically pure Si (3ph-only), indicating multiplicative sensitivity to spectrum/anharmonicity descriptors.  <paper entityId="paper-292b26cc817258dac7b29d83cd91513ced10ed7e" annotationId="ann_016" corpusId="218674110" artifactId="extraction-result-5#uuid-e5.0">Parks et al., 2020</paper>

- For bulk diamond Si at 300 K, a well-converged MD (EMD or homogeneous NEMD with finite-size handled) using Tersoff-1989 will predict κ larger than an ab initio PBTE benchmark that includes at least isotope scattering (and especially if it includes 4ph), with κ_Tersoff/κ_DFT likely >1.3; a factor near ~2 is plausible if the MD result reflects the same Tersoff spectral/anharmonic biases seen in Tersoff-ALD/BTE.
- For bulk Si at ~1100 K, if the ab initio reference includes 4ph scattering, a Tersoff-1989 MD prediction is likely to be higher by >30% unless NEMD setup artifacts (strong gradients/short length) artificially suppress κ.
- For Si PBTE workflows, swapping DFT forces for a high-quality surrogate trained to DFT (e.g., HDNNP) while keeping the same ALD/BTE settings will preserve κ(T) within a few percent over the training-valid range (e.g., 200–500 K), as long as the surrogate reproduces both harmonic and cubic IFCs accurately.

- In bulk Si1-xGex near x≈0.5 at 300–500 K, the spread between empirical-potential MD and first-principles DFPT+VCA/Tamura PBTE may shrink in relative terms compared to pure Si because alloy disorder dominates scattering; however, if force-constant disorder/localization is strong, explicit-disorder methods (large-supercell QHGK/MD) could predict substantially lower κ than VCA/Tamura PBTE.
- For Ge, empirical-potential bias sign may be less consistent than for Si because TA branch features are sensitive to force-constant range; potentials that misplace TA(X) could either increase or decrease κ relative to ab initio even if they are reasonable for Si.

- Compute Tersoff-1989 vs DFT mode-resolved group velocities and anharmonic indicators (e.g., Grüneisen parameters or 3ph phase space) for bulk Si; if Tersoff does not systematically increase v and/or increase τ (via reduced anharmonicity) yet still yields much larger κ, then the “(v,τ) co-bias” mechanism is incomplete and implementation/solver effects dominate.
- Run size- and time-converged EMD and homogeneous NEMD for bulk Si with the same Tersoff-1989 potential; if both converge to κ within ~10–20% of DFT-PBTE (3ph+isotope or 3ph+4ph+isotope), then the theory’s claim that the potential’s effective operator/spectrum is the dominant bias source for Tersoff must be revised (suggesting ALD/BTE extraction or other workflow differences are the main source).
- For Si PBTE, compare κ from iterative PBTE vs RTA across 200–500 K for the same IFCs; if differences become large (>15–20%) already at 300 K, then MESO must weight solver-induced operator errors more strongly than currently assumed for Si.

- No direct bulk Tersoff-1989 MD κ values for *bulk* Si at 300 K and 1100 K are provided in the evidence set; thus quantitative calibration for the specific 'GPUMD homogeneous NEMD' scenario is not directly supported here (only indirect evidence from Tersoff-ALD/BTE and other potentials).

paper-c1db9aa7a1e6d91e3dafea40ce6a6eaef0.displayLabel: Efficient anharmonic lattice dynamics calculations of thermal transport in crystalline and disordered solids

s2Metadata.title: Efficient anharmonic lattice dynamics calculations of thermal transport in crystalline and disordered solids
s2Metadata.abstract: Understanding heat transport in semiconductors and insulators is of fundamental importance because of its technological impact in electronics and renewable energy harvesting and conversion. Anharmonic Lattice Dynamics provides a powerful framework for the description of heat transport at the nanoscale. One of the advantages of this method is that it naturally includes quantum effects due to atoms vibrations, which are needed to compute the thermal properties of semiconductors widely used in nanotechnology, like silicon and carbon, even at room temperature. While the heat transport picture substantially differs between amorphous and crystalline semiconductors from a microscopic standpoint, a unified approach to simulate both crystals and glasses has been devised. Here we introduce a unified workflow, which implements both the Boltzmann Transport equation (BTE) and the Quasi Harmonic Green-Kubo (QHGK) methods. We discuss how the theory can be optimized to exploit modern parallel architectures, and how it is implemented in $\kappa ALDo$: a versatile and scalable open-source software to compute phonon transport in solids. This approach is applied to crystalline and partially disordered silicon-based systems, including bulk silicon and clathrates, and on silicon-germanium alloy clathrates with largely reduced thermal conductivity.

paper-7768b8b467adf08a976e6e61b49bc31604.displayLabel: Computational prediction of lattice thermal conductivity: A comparison of molecular dynamics and Boltzmann transport approaches

s2Metadata.title: Computational prediction of lattice thermal conductivity: A comparison of molecular dynamics and Boltzmann transport approaches
s2Metadata.abstract: The predictive modeling of lattice thermal conductivity is of fundamental importance for the understanding and design of materials for a wide range of applications. Two major approaches, namely molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and calculations solving approximately the Boltzmann transport equation (BTE), have been developed to compute the lattice thermal conductivity. We present a detailed direct comparison of these two approaches, using as prototypical cases MgO and PbTe. The comparison, carried out using empirical potentials, takes into account the effects of fourth order phonon scattering, temperature-dependent phonon frequencies (phonon renormalization), and investigates the effects of quantum vs. classical statistics. We clarify that equipartition, as opposed to Maxwell Boltzmann, govern the statistics of phonons in MD simulations. We find that lattice thermal conductivity values from MD and BTE show an apparent, satisfactory agreement; however such an agreement is the result of error cancellations. We also show that the primary effect of statistics on thermal conductivity is via the scattering rate dependence on phonon populations.

paper-5440f8458754c69b941910a03a7f0e1e40.displayLabel: A Comprehensive Review of Heat Transfer in Thermoelectric Materials and Devices

s2Metadata.title: A Comprehensive Review of Heat Transfer in Thermoelectric Materials and Devices
s2Metadata.abstract: Solid-state thermoelectric devices are currently used in applications ranging from thermocouple sensors to power generators in satellites, to portable air-conditioners and refrigerators. With the ever-rising demand throughout the world for energy consumption and CO2 reduction, thermoelectric energy conversion has been receiving intensified attention as a potential candidate for waste-heat harvesting as well as for power generation from renewable sources. Efficient thermoelectric energy conversion critically depends on the performance of thermoelectric materials and devices. In this review, we discuss heat transfer in thermoelectric materials and devices, especially phonon engineering to reduce the lattice thermal conductivity of thermoelectric materials, which requires a fundamental understanding of nanoscale heat conduction physics.

paper-544f173743e30f899ed765ea02113da1c1.displayLabel: Thermal conductivity of intrinsic semiconductor at elevated temperature: role of four-phonon scattering and electronic heat conduction

s2Metadata.title: Thermal conductivity of intrinsic semiconductor at elevated temperature: role of four-phonon scattering and electronic heat conduction
s2Metadata.abstract: While using first-principles-based Boltzmann transport equation approach to predict the thermal conductivity of crystalline semiconductor materials has been a routine, the validity of the approach is seldom tested for high-temperature conditions. Most previous studies only focused on the phononic contribution, and neglected the electronic part. Meanwhile, the treatment on phonon transport is not rigorous as a few ingredients, such as four-phonon scatterings, phonon renormalization and thermal expansion, are ignored. In this paper, we present a Boltzmann transport equation study on high-temperature thermal conduction in bulk silicon by considering the effects of both phonons and electrons, and explore the role of the missing parts in the previous studies on the thermal conductivity at elevated temperature. For the phonon transport, four-phonon scattering is found to considerably reduce the thermal conductivity when the temperature is larger than 700 K, while the effects of phonon renormalization and thermal expansion on phononic thermal conductivity are negligible. Bipolar contribution to the electronic thermal conductivity calculated from first-principles is implemented for the first time. More than 25% of heat is shown to be conducted by electrons at 1500 K. The computed total thermal conductivity of silicon faithfully reproduces the measured data. The approach presented in this paper is expected to be applied to other high-temperature functional materials, and the results could serve as benchmarks and help to explain the high-temperature phonon and electron transport phenomena.

paper-d67306ef6ca27d99aaf1063dc4a4e1b72c.displayLabel: Thermal conductivity engineering of bulk and one-dimensional Si-Ge nanoarchitectures

s2Metadata.title: Thermal conductivity engineering of bulk and one-dimensional Si-Ge nanoarchitectures
s2Metadata.abstract: Various theoretical and experimental methods are utilized to investigate the thermal conductivity of nanostructured materials; this is a critical parameter to increase performance of thermoelectric devices. Among these methods, equilibrium molecular dynamics (EMD) is an accurate technique to predict lattice thermal conductivity. In this study, by means of systematic EMD simulations, thermal conductivity of bulk Si-Ge structures (pristine, alloy and superlattice) and their nanostructured one dimensional forms with square and circular cross-section geometries (asymmetric and symmetric) are calculated for different crystallographic directions. A comprehensive temperature analysis is evaluated for selected structures as well. The results show that one-dimensional structures are superior candidates in terms of their low lattice thermal conductivity and thermal conductivity tunability by nanostructuring, such as by diameter modulation, interface roughness, periodicity and number of interfaces. We find that thermal conductivity decreases with smaller diameters or cross section areas. Furthermore, interface roughness decreases thermal conductivity with a profound impact. Moreover, we predicted that there is a specific periodicity that gives minimum thermal conductivity in symmetric superlattice structures. The decreasing thermal conductivity is due to the reducing phonon movement in the system due to the effect of the number of interfaces that determine regimes of ballistic and wave transport phenomena. In some nanostructures, such as nanowire superlattices, thermal conductivity of the Si/Ge system can be reduced to nearly twice that of an amorphous silicon thermal conductivity. Additionally, it is found that one crystal orientation, 100, is better than the 111 crystal orientation in one-dimensional and bulk SiGe systems. Our results clearly point out the importance of lattice thermal conductivity engineering in bulk and nanostructures to produce high-performance thermoelectric materials. Graphical Abstract

content.title: Statistics-convergence law: quantum vs classical κ discrepancy shrinks with T

content.text: Classical methods are most wrong at low temperature; they get closer to quantum results at high temperature.
**Supporting evidence:**

- DFT PBTE study reports κ_Q,Inv(300 K)=147 W/mK and κ_Cl,Inv(300 K)=123 W/mK and notes quantum and classical results converge as T increases (Fig. 2 trend).  <paper entityId="paper-c1db9aa7a1e6d91e3dafea40ce6a6eaef0f2a40a" annotationId="ann_001" corpusId="221507928" artifactId="extraction-result-10#uuid-e10.0">Barbalinardo et al., 2020</paper>

- Review discussion emphasizes classical MD uses equipartition and requires quantum corrections at low T; prior quantum-correction attempts can fail, highlighting a statistics-driven method discrepancy at low T.  <paper entityId="paper-7768b8b467adf08a976e6e61b49bc31604b121fe" annotationId="ann_002" corpusId="119231887" artifactId="extraction-result-1#uuid-e1.0">Puligheddu et al., 2019</paper> <paper entityId="paper-5440f8458754c69b941910a03a7f0e1e40ec515e" annotationId="ann_003" corpusId="111146233" artifactId="extraction-result-7#uuid-e7.0">Tian et al., 2014</paper>

content.title: Solver-fidelity law: RTA underestimates κ relative to inversion/iterative PBTE when mode coupling matters

content.text: RTA is usually a little low for Si at room temperature and can be more wrong at low temperature.
**Supporting evidence:**

- For diamond Si at 300 K, inversion gives 147 W/mK while RTA gives 140 W/mK (~5% lower), demonstrating solver-dependent κ differences in Si.  <paper entityId="paper-c1db9aa7a1e6d91e3dafea40ce6a6eaef0f2a40a" annotationId="ann_004" corpusId="221507928" artifactId="extraction-result-10#uuid-e10.0">Barbalinardo et al., 2020</paper>

- The Si 3ph-only PBTE study notes literature indicating iterative vs RTA differences <4% for Si at room temperature, consistent with modest solver bias at RT.  <paper entityId="paper-544f173743e30f899ed765ea02113da1c166774b" annotationId="ann_005" corpusId="211987717" artifactId="extraction-result-6#uuid-e6.0">Gu et al., 2020</paper>

- For the Si136 clathrate, authors report RTA corrections beyond RTA are <1%, illustrating a boundary condition where RTA error is very small due to collision-operator structure in that material.  <paper entityId="paper-c1db9aa7a1e6d91e3dafea40ce6a6eaef0f2a40a" annotationId="ann_006" corpusId="221507928" artifactId="extraction-result-10#uuid-e10.2">Barbalinardo et al., 2020</paper>

- If a PBTE κ(T) curve for bulk Si is recomputed with inversion/iterative instead of RTA using identical IFCs and scattering mechanisms, κ will increase by only a few percent near 300 K but by a larger fraction at lower T (e.g., <200 K).
- Two workflows with identical scattering physics but different harmonic dispersion fidelity (e.g., different potentials) will show κ differences that correlate with acoustic sound speeds and TA-branch features (SSC predicts stronger correlation than with details like IFC extraction algorithm).

- For Ge, if a potential reproduces acoustic sound speeds but mispredicts TA(X), SSC predicts that κ differences will show up primarily through changes in phase space and lifetimes rather than group-velocity magnitude alone; this could invert the sign of κ bias depending on how phase space shifts.
- In Si1-xGex, SSC predicts the temperature at which classical and quantum κ converge depends on alloy-induced spectral broadening; strong disorder may make classical MD appear ‘closer’ to quantum PBTE at lower T than in pure Si because high-frequency modes are already suppressed.

- Compare κ(T) from PBTE using DFT IFCs with κ(T) from classical-limit PBTE using the same IFCs; if the difference does not decrease with T, SSC’s statistics-convergence premise is violated for the tested regime.
- For Si, test whether κ differences across XC functionals correlate with TA sound speed and Grüneisen parameter as reported; if correlations fail in an expanded dataset, SSC’s spectrum-dominance claim needs revision.

- The provided evidence set includes many nanowire/superlattice κ values dominated by boundary/interface scattering; SSC is formulated for bulk crystalline comparisons and does not attempt to explain these boundary-dominated results.  <paper entityId="paper-d67306ef6ca27d99aaf1063dc4a4e1b72c44aafe" annotationId="ann_007" corpusId="5718073" artifactId="extraction-result-11#uuid-e11.1">Kandemir et al., 2017</paper>

content.title: Long-range randomness can suppress generalized diffusivity far beyond periodic substituted-cell predictions

content.text: A truly random alloy can conduct heat far worse than a small repeating ‘ordered alloy pattern’, mainly because long-range randomness destroys how vibrations carry energy across the structure.
**Supporting evidence:**

- For nominally identical composition Si0.85Ge0.15 (clathrate), a periodically replicated substituted-cell model yields κ≈31 W/mK (QHGK on a 5×5×5 replicated supercell of the 136-atom substituted cell), while a truly random 17000-atom alloy realization yields κ≈1.7 W/mK; the authors attribute the large difference mainly to strong suppression of generalized diffusivity/velocities (especially for <3 THz modes), with DOS and lifetimes not changing comparably.  <paper entityId="paper-c1db9aa7a1e6d91e3dafea40ce6a6eaef0f2a40a" annotationId="ann_001" corpusId="221507928" artifactId="extraction-result-10#uuid-e10.4">Barbalinardo et al., 2020</paper>

- The same study reports that the periodically substituted 15% Ge case has κ≈33 W/mK from BTE-RTA on the 136-atom substituted cell, and κ≈31 W/mK from QHGK on its periodic replica, indicating that the very low κ (1.7 W/mK) is specifically tied to long-range randomness rather than solver choice for the periodic model.  <paper entityId="paper-c1db9aa7a1e6d91e3dafea40ce6a6eaef0f2a40a" annotationId="ann_002" corpusId="221507928" artifactId="extraction-result-10#uuid-e10.3">Barbalinardo et al., 2020</paper>

content.title: In strong-disorder alloys, disorder-model uncertainty can exceed solver-choice uncertainty

content.text: For strongly alloyed SiGe, whether you model real atomic randomness (and force-constant disorder) matters more than whether you compute κ with GK, NEMD, or BTE.
**Supporting evidence:**

- A review/discussion of Si/Ge/SiGe methods notes: (i) pure Si and Ge can show consistency between GK-MD and BTE in prior work, but (ii) BTE becomes problematic for Si–Ge alloys, pointing to alloy/disorder treatment—not merely solver choice—as a key divergence source.  <paper entityId="paper-7768b8b467adf08a976e6e61b49bc31604b121fe" annotationId="ann_003" corpusId="119231887" artifactId="extraction-result-1#uuid-e1.0">Puligheddu et al., 2019</paper>

- Another review discussion states that empirical-potential NEMD studies can show large discrepancies with experiment for SiGe alloys, while DFPT+VCA/Tamura-type approaches (e.g., Garg et al.) can reproduce experiments, highlighting disorder-model adequacy as a controlling factor in alloys.  <paper entityId="paper-5440f8458754c69b941910a03a7f0e1e40ec515e" annotationId="ann_004" corpusId="111146233" artifactId="extraction-result-7#uuid-e7.2">Tian et al., 2014</paper> <paper entityId="paper-d67306ef6ca27d99aaf1063dc4a4e1b72c44aafe" annotationId="ann_005" corpusId="5718073" artifactId="extraction-result-11#uuid-e11.5">Kandemir et al., 2017</paper>

- In explicit-disorder calculations (QHGK) at fixed composition, switching only the disorder realization from periodic substituted to truly random changes κ from ~31 W/mK to ~1.7 W/mK, dwarfing the difference between BTE-RTA and QHGK for the periodic substituted model (~33 vs ~31 W/mK).  <paper entityId="paper-c1db9aa7a1e6d91e3dafea40ce6a6eaef0f2a40a" annotationId="ann_006" corpusId="221507928" artifactId="extraction-result-10#uuid-e10.3">Barbalinardo et al., 2020</paper>

- Classical MD with explicit alloying (Tersoff EMD) reports very strong κ suppression and in some strongly suppressed nanowire/superlattice cases nearly temperature-independent κ over 200–500 K, consistent with a regime where detailed solver refinements are less influential than the presence of strong disorder/interface scattering; while these are nanostructured cases, they illustrate the broader ‘strong scattering reduces solver sensitivity’ mechanism.  <paper entityId="paper-d67306ef6ca27d99aaf1063dc4a4e1b72c44aafe" annotationId="ann_007" corpusId="5718073" artifactId="extraction-result-11#uuid-e11.0">Kandemir et al., 2017</paper>

- For bulk diamond Si1-xGex near x≈0.5, keeping the same interatomic model (e.g., one empirical potential or one DFT/ML force model), κ computed for (i) a periodic small-cell substitution pattern (or its periodic replicas) will exceed κ computed for (ii) a large explicitly random alloy supercell with converged disorder correlations, even when using the same transport solver.
- If two studies use the same solver (e.g., PBTE-RTA) but one uses VCA+mass-disorder (Tamura/Abeles) and the other uses an explicit-disorder supercell including force-constant disorder, the explicit-disorder result will generally produce lower κ at intermediate compositions, with the largest deviation coming from low-to-mid frequency contributions.

- In diamond SiGe, there exists a temperature/composition window where force-constant disorder (beyond mass disorder) changes κ by >2× relative to mass-only models; the window shifts with T because increasing anharmonic broadening partially masks disorder-induced diffusivity suppression.
- A convergence criterion based on a disorder correlation length (from pair/multisite correlations of alloy configurations) will predict when periodic alloy models approach random-alloy κ; for SiGe at 300 K this length may exceed typical MD-accessible cells, implying many published MD results are effectively ‘short-correlation’ disorder models.

- Compute κ for a sequence of SiGe explicit-alloy models with increasing supercell size and increasingly randomized correlations (e.g., SQS-like to fully random) using identical solver and identical force model; if κ converges quickly to the periodic-substitution value rather than decreasing toward a lower random-alloy value, DRD’s long-range-randomness dominance is weakened for diamond SiGe.
- For the same harmonic spectrum, compare PBTE(VCA+Tamura mass disorder) to an explicit-disorder PBTE/QHGK that includes force-constant disorder; if they agree closely across x at 300 K (within ~10–20%), then DRD overstates the importance of force-constant/long-range disorder for diamond SiGe (even if it remains true for clathrates).

- The clearest quantitative evidence for the ‘periodic substituted vs truly random’ order-of-magnitude κ gap is for a SiGe clathrate alloy rather than diamond SiGe; the magnitude of the effect could be smaller in diamond-structure SiGe alloys.  <paper entityId="paper-c1db9aa7a1e6d91e3dafea40ce6a6eaef0f2a40a" annotationId="ann_008" corpusId="221507928" artifactId="extraction-result-10#uuid-e10.4">Barbalinardo et al., 2020</paper>

paper-c1db9aa7a1e6d91e3dafea40ce6a6eaef0.displayLabel: Efficient anharmonic lattice dynamics calculations of thermal transport in crystalline and disordered solids

s2Metadata.title: Efficient anharmonic lattice dynamics calculations of thermal transport in crystalline and disordered solids
s2Metadata.abstract: Understanding heat transport in semiconductors and insulators is of fundamental importance because of its technological impact in electronics and renewable energy harvesting and conversion. Anharmonic Lattice Dynamics provides a powerful framework for the description of heat transport at the nanoscale. One of the advantages of this method is that it naturally includes quantum effects due to atoms vibrations, which are needed to compute the thermal properties of semiconductors widely used in nanotechnology, like silicon and carbon, even at room temperature. While the heat transport picture substantially differs between amorphous and crystalline semiconductors from a microscopic standpoint, a unified approach to simulate both crystals and glasses has been devised. Here we introduce a unified workflow, which implements both the Boltzmann Transport equation (BTE) and the Quasi Harmonic Green-Kubo (QHGK) methods. We discuss how the theory can be optimized to exploit modern parallel architectures, and how it is implemented in $\kappa ALDo$: a versatile and scalable open-source software to compute phonon transport in solids. This approach is applied to crystalline and partially disordered silicon-based systems, including bulk silicon and clathrates, and on silicon-germanium alloy clathrates with largely reduced thermal conductivity.

paper-1b4f174685bbc26dd19180ecfcf7cb0b15.displayLabel: Simulating lattice thermal conductivity in semiconducting materials using high-dimensional neural network potential

s2Metadata.title: Simulating lattice thermal conductivity in semiconducting materials using high-dimensional neural network potential
s2Metadata.abstract: We demonstrate that a high-dimensional neural network potential (HDNNP) can predict the lattice thermal conductivity of semiconducting materials with an accuracy that is comparable to that of density functional theory (DFT) calculation. After a training procedure based on force, the root mean square error between the forces predicted by HDNNP and DFT is less than 40 meV Å−1. As typical examples, we present the results of Si and GaN bulk crystals. The deviation from the thermal conductivity calculated using DFT is within 1% at 200 to 500 K for Si and within 5.4% at 200 to 1000 K for GaN.

paper-fbf7170d0b720a69a2492581b23dc34f88.displayLabel: First-principles phonon physics using the Pheasy code

s2Metadata.title: First-principles phonon physics using the Pheasy code
s2Metadata.abstract: Parameter-free calculations of lattice dynamics from first principles have achieved significant progress in the past decades, with a wealth of applications in thermodynamics, phase transitions, and transport properties of materials. Current approaches to derive the interatomic force constants (IFCs) of lattice potential become challenging and sometimes infeasible when going beyond third-order anharmonicity, due to the combinatorial explosion in the number of higher-order IFCs. In this work, we present a robust and user-friendly program, , which reliably reconstructs the prescribed potential energy surface of crystalline solids via a Taylor expansion of arbitrarily high order. Given force-displacement datasets, the program enables an efficient and accurate extraction of IFCs using advanced machine-learning algorithms, and further calculates a wide range of harmonic and anharmonic phonon related properties. We show in three prototypical examples how the obtained IFCs have been successfully applied to study anharmonic lattice dynamics and thermal transport. Through these detailed benchmarks, we have also identified the optimal approach for IFC extractions and offered general guidelines for high-fidelity lattice-dynamical simulations, addressing the large uncertainties in the IFCs extracted from existing various schemes. Overall, the project aims to create a phonon code ecosystem that connects diverse phonon simulation platforms and offers access to the broad research community.

paper-292b26cc817258dac7b29d83cd91513ced.displayLabel: Uncertainty quantification in first-principles predictions of phonon properties and lattice thermal conductivity

s2Metadata.title: Uncertainty quantification in first-principles predictions of phonon properties and lattice thermal conductivity
s2Metadata.abstract: We present a framework for quantifying the uncertainty that results from the choice of exchange-correlation (XC) functional in predictions of phonon properties and thermal conductivity that use density functional theory (DFT) to calculate the atomic force constants. The energy ensemble capabilities of the BEEF-vdW XC functional are first applied to determine an ensemble of interatomic force constants, which are then used as inputs to lattice dynamics calculations and a solution of the Boltzmann transport equation. The framework is applied to isotopically-pure silicon. We find that the uncertainty estimates bound property predictions (e.g., phonon dispersions, specific heat, thermal conductivity) from other XC functionals and experiments. We distinguish between properties that are correlated with the predicted thermal conductivity [e.g., the transverse acoustic branch sound speed ($R^2=0.89$) and average Gruneisen parameter ($R^2=0.85$)] and those that are not [e.g., longitudinal acoustic branch sound speed ($R^2=0.23$) and specific heat ($R^2=0.00$)]. We find that differences in ensemble predictions of thermal conductivity are correlated with the behavior of phonons with mean free paths between $100$ and $300$ nm. The framework systematically accounts for XC uncertainty in phonon calculations and should be used whenever it is suspected that the choice of XC functional is influencing physical interpretations.

paper-544f173743e30f899ed765ea02113da1c1.displayLabel: Thermal conductivity of intrinsic semiconductor at elevated temperature: role of four-phonon scattering and electronic heat conduction

s2Metadata.title: Thermal conductivity of intrinsic semiconductor at elevated temperature: role of four-phonon scattering and electronic heat conduction
s2Metadata.abstract: While using first-principles-based Boltzmann transport equation approach to predict the thermal conductivity of crystalline semiconductor materials has been a routine, the validity of the approach is seldom tested for high-temperature conditions. Most previous studies only focused on the phononic contribution, and neglected the electronic part. Meanwhile, the treatment on phonon transport is not rigorous as a few ingredients, such as four-phonon scatterings, phonon renormalization and thermal expansion, are ignored. In this paper, we present a Boltzmann transport equation study on high-temperature thermal conduction in bulk silicon by considering the effects of both phonons and electrons, and explore the role of the missing parts in the previous studies on the thermal conductivity at elevated temperature. For the phonon transport, four-phonon scattering is found to considerably reduce the thermal conductivity when the temperature is larger than 700 K, while the effects of phonon renormalization and thermal expansion on phononic thermal conductivity are negligible. Bipolar contribution to the electronic thermal conductivity calculated from first-principles is implemented for the first time. More than 25% of heat is shown to be conducted by electrons at 1500 K. The computed total thermal conductivity of silicon faithfully reproduces the measured data. The approach presented in this paper is expected to be applied to other high-temperature functional materials, and the results could serve as benchmarks and help to explain the high-temperature phonon and electron transport phenomena.

paper-9bcafe72a9aa8b0945e900ce108fb6ad25.displayLabel: Transport simulations in hierarchically disordered nanostructures for thermoelectric material design

s2Metadata.title: Transport simulations in hierarchically disordered nanostructures for thermoelectric material design
s2Metadata.abstract: Hierarchically nanostructured materials, where disorder is introduced in various length scales (at the atomic scale, the nanoscale, and the mesoscale) is one of the most promising directions to achieve extremely low thermal conductivities and improve thermoelectric performance. Here we theoretically investigate one such system, a nanocrystalline material with nanopores that are introduced between the crystalline regions. We use the Nonequilibrium Green's Function method for electronic transport and Molecular Dynamics for phonon transport.

journal.name: 2018 IEEE 13th Nanotechnology Materials and Devices Conference (NMDC)

paper-7768b8b467adf08a976e6e61b49bc31604.displayLabel: Computational prediction of lattice thermal conductivity: A comparison of molecular dynamics and Boltzmann transport approaches

s2Metadata.title: Computational prediction of lattice thermal conductivity: A comparison of molecular dynamics and Boltzmann transport approaches
s2Metadata.abstract: The predictive modeling of lattice thermal conductivity is of fundamental importance for the understanding and design of materials for a wide range of applications. Two major approaches, namely molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and calculations solving approximately the Boltzmann transport equation (BTE), have been developed to compute the lattice thermal conductivity. We present a detailed direct comparison of these two approaches, using as prototypical cases MgO and PbTe. The comparison, carried out using empirical potentials, takes into account the effects of fourth order phonon scattering, temperature-dependent phonon frequencies (phonon renormalization), and investigates the effects of quantum vs. classical statistics. We clarify that equipartition, as opposed to Maxwell Boltzmann, govern the statistics of phonons in MD simulations. We find that lattice thermal conductivity values from MD and BTE show an apparent, satisfactory agreement; however such an agreement is the result of error cancellations. We also show that the primary effect of statistics on thermal conductivity is via the scattering rate dependence on phonon populations.

content.title: Room-temperature bulk Si: Tersoff IFC-based transport overestimates κ by ~2× vs DFT PBTE (anchor law)

content.text: Around 300 K, using Tersoff for bulk silicon tends to give about twice the thermal conductivity that DFT-based BTE gives.
**Supporting evidence:**

- DFT PBTE (direct inversion, quantum statistics) for diamond Si reports κ(300 K)=147 W/mK; the same study reports Tersoff-based ALD/BTE κ_Q(300 K)=305 W/mK (and κ_classical=260 W/mK), i.e., ≈2.1× higher than DFT inversion at 300 K.  <paper entityId="paper-c1db9aa7a1e6d91e3dafea40ce6a6eaef0f2a40a" annotationId="ann_001" corpusId="221507928" artifactId="extraction-result-10#uuid-e10.0">Barbalinardo et al., 2020</paper>

- The same DFT PBTE study shows RTA vs inversion differences are modest at 300 K (quantum: 140 vs 147 W/mK; ~5%), implying the ≈2× Tersoff-vs-DFT gap is not explainable by RTA vs inversion alone.  <paper entityId="paper-c1db9aa7a1e6d91e3dafea40ce6a6eaef0f2a40a" annotationId="ann_002" corpusId="221507928" artifactId="extraction-result-10#uuid-e10.0">Barbalinardo et al., 2020</paper>

- A separate first-principles PBTE/DFT workflow (phono3py, RTA) gives κ(300 K)=112.1 W/mK for Si, further indicating that first-principles PBTE values cluster far below ~300 W/mK at 300 K; Tersoff ≈305 W/mK is therefore an outlier high relative to multiple DFT-based PBTE pipelines.  <paper entityId="paper-1b4f174685bbc26dd19180ecfcf7cb0b152de2be" annotationId="ann_003" corpusId="160009739" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.2">Minamitani et al., 2019</paper>

- Another first-principles PBTE/DFT study for bulk Si (iterative 3ph with isotopes; optional 4ph) reports κ_3ph(300 K)≈125.4 W/mK and κ_3+4ph(300 K)≈115.4 W/mK, again far below ~300 W/mK and consistent with Tersoff-based transport being high relative to DFT-based transport at 300 K.  <paper entityId="paper-fbf7170d0b720a69a2492581b23dc34f886f655c" annotationId="ann_004" corpusId="280421449" artifactId="extraction-result-4#uuid-e4.0">Lin et al., 2025</paper>

- A first-principles uncertainty-quantification study reports a range of DFT-PBTE κ(300 K) values depending on XC functional (e.g., PBE 154, PBEsol 128, LDA 122 W/mK; BEEF-vdW best-fit 171 W/mK for isotopically pure Si with only 3ph). Even the high end of these DFT predictions is well below 260–305 W/mK from Tersoff transport, supporting the conclusion that Tersoff is systematically high at 300 K versus DFT PBTE.  <paper entityId="paper-292b26cc817258dac7b29d83cd91513ced10ed7e" annotationId="ann_005" corpusId="218674110" artifactId="extraction-result-5#uuid-e5.0">Parks et al., 2020</paper>

content.title: High-temperature amplification: 4-phonon-aware DFT references reduce κ faster with T than Tersoff-1989 is expected to (categorical forecast at ~1100 K)

content.text: At ~1100 K, a DFT reference that includes four-phonon scattering drops κ strongly; Tersoff-1989 MD is therefore expected to come out noticeably higher (often >30% higher) unless the NEMD setup artificially lowers κ.
**Supporting evidence:**

- A first-principles Si study spanning 100–1500 K reports that omitting 4ph overestimates κ by ~8% at 300 K and that 4ph becomes increasingly important above ~500–700 K; at 900 K, 3ph-only κ is reported as 43 W/mK and is ~20% larger than measurement, implying that 4ph-inclusive κ is substantially lower at high T than 3ph-only.  <paper entityId="paper-544f173743e30f899ed765ea02113da1c166774b" annotationId="ann_006" corpusId="211987717" artifactId="extraction-result-6#uuid-e6.0">Gu et al., 2020</paper>

- The same first-principles high-T study states (as a mechanistic scaling rule) that 3ph lifetimes scale roughly ~T^-1 while 4ph lifetimes scale roughly ~T^-2, indicating an accelerating relative importance of 4ph with increasing temperature.  <paper entityId="paper-544f173743e30f899ed765ea02113da1c166774b" annotationId="ann_007" corpusId="211987717" artifactId="extraction-result-6#uuid-e6.0">Gu et al., 2020</paper>

- Independent first-principles PBTE for Si at 300 K shows 4ph reduces κ from ~125.4 to ~115.4 W/mK (~7.9%), consistent with the claim that 4ph corrections are non-negligible already at 300 K and grow with T.  <paper entityId="paper-fbf7170d0b720a69a2492581b23dc34f886f655c" annotationId="ann_008" corpusId="280421449" artifactId="extraction-result-4#uuid-e4.0">Lin et al., 2025</paper>

- Tersoff-based ALD/BTE for diamond Si at 300 K strongly overpredicts κ relative to DFT inversion (305 vs 147 W/mK), supporting the premise that the potential can yield insufficient effective resistive scattering and/or inflated transport quantities; this provides the abductive anchor that the bias remains upward unless canceled by NEMD artifacts.  <paper entityId="paper-c1db9aa7a1e6d91e3dafea40ce6a6eaef0f2a40a" annotationId="ann_009" corpusId="221507928" artifactId="extraction-result-10#uuid-e10.0">Barbalinardo et al., 2020</paper>

- General methodological discussion notes empirical-potential MD results can be strongly affected by interatomic potential quality and MD finite-size effects, consistent with the stated caveat that NEMD artifacts can move comparisons toward apparent agreement.  <paper entityId="paper-544f173743e30f899ed765ea02113da1c166774b" annotationId="ann_010" corpusId="211987717" artifactId="extraction-result-6#uuid-e6.2">Gu et al., 2020</paper>

- This statement was logically inferred (abduction) by combining: (i) evidence that Tersoff produces large upward bias at 300 K in bulk Si transport (Tersoff ALD/BTE vs DFT PBTE), and (ii) evidence that DFT PBTE κ decreases more strongly with T when 4ph scattering is included (increasingly important at high T).

- H5 @300 K: For size-converged bulk Si, κ_Tersoff-1989(homogeneous NEMD)/κ_almaBTE(3ph/4ph+isotopes as implemented) will be >1.0; a plausible prior range is ~1.3–2.1, with the upper end corresponding to the ≈2× Tersoff-vs-DFT transport anchor (305 vs 147 W/mK).
- H5 @1100 K: If the almaBTE reference includes strong high-T resistive physics (especially 4ph), then the comparison category is most likely “Tersoff higher by more than 30%”, unless NEMD length/gradient artifacts reduce κ_Tersoff.

- If a carefully converged homogeneous NEMD calculation with Tersoff-1989 at 1100 K produces κ within 30% of a 4ph-inclusive DFT PBTE reference, it would imply a strong, temperature-dependent cancellation between (i) Tersoff’s intrinsic overconductivity and (ii) NEMD finite-size/nonequilibrium artifacts, suggesting that method agreement can be accidental rather than indicating correct physics.
- If replacing Tersoff-1989 with a DFT-trained ML potential (or force-matched empirical potential) and then running homogeneous NEMD yields κ close to 4ph-inclusive DFT PBTE at 1100 K, it would support the claim that the dominant error source is the potential’s anharmonic coefficients rather than NEMD methodology itself.

- Perform homogeneous NEMD with Tersoff-1989 for bulk Si at 300 K and 1100 K while systematically increasing sample length and cross-section; if κ converges to within ±30% of the DFT PBTE reference at both temperatures, the claimed intrinsic Tersoff overconductivity prior is weakened.
- Compute ALD/PBTE for bulk diamond Si using Tersoff-1989 IFCs but compare RTA vs full inversion; if full inversion reduces κ by a factor comparable to the observed ~2× gap to DFT, then solver approximation (not potential) would be the main driver—contradicting the theory’s emphasis on potential-derived scattering/dispersion errors.
- Extract effective Grüneisen parameters and phonon lifetimes from Tersoff-1989 (via ALD) and from DFT IFCs and test whether Tersoff systematically yields longer lifetimes for heat-carrying acoustic modes; absence of such lifetime inflation would undermine the “underdamped phonon gas” mechanism.

- No direct bulk diamond Si κ(T) dataset from Tersoff-1989 MD (EMD or homogeneous NEMD) is provided in the evidence; the anchor is Tersoff ALD/BTE at 300 K, not MD, and not specifically labeled as Tersoff-1989 in that source entry.  <paper entityId="paper-c1db9aa7a1e6d91e3dafea40ce6a6eaef0f2a40a" annotationId="ann_011" corpusId="221507928" artifactId="extraction-result-10#uuid-e10.1">Barbalinardo et al., 2020</paper>

- An SW force-matched potential used with EMD-GK for pristine Si yields κ(300 K)=207±12 W/mK, showing that not all empirical potentials underpredict scattering; however, this theory is about Tersoff-1989 specifically and does not model SW behavior.  <paper entityId="paper-9bcafe72a9aa8b0945e900ce108fb6ad250221e9" annotationId="ann_012" corpusId="57762337" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.0">Oliveira et al., 2018</paper>

s2Metadata.title: A Comprehensive Review of Heat Transfer in Thermoelectric Materials and Devices
s2Metadata.abstract: Solid-state thermoelectric devices are currently used in applications ranging from thermocouple sensors to power generators in satellites, to portable air-conditioners and refrigerators. With the ever-rising demand throughout the world for energy consumption and CO2 reduction, thermoelectric energy conversion has been receiving intensified attention as a potential candidate for waste-heat harvesting as well as for power generation from renewable sources. Efficient thermoelectric energy conversion critically depends on the performance of thermoelectric materials and devices. In this review, we discuss heat transfer in thermoelectric materials and devices, especially phonon engineering to reduce the lattice thermal conductivity of thermoelectric materials, which requires a fundamental understanding of nanoscale heat conduction physics.

The energy ensemble capabilities of the BEEF-vdW XC functional are first applied to determine an ensemble of interatomic force constants, which are then used as inputs to lattice dynamics calculations and a solution of the Boltzmann transport equation. The framework is applied to isotopically-pure silicon. We find that the uncertainty estimates bound property predictions (e.g., phonon dispersions, specific heat, thermal conductivity) from other XC functionals and experiments. We distinguish between properties that are correlated with the predicted thermal conductivity [e.g., the transverse acoustic branch sound speed ($R^2=0.89$) and average Gruneisen parameter ($R^2=0.85$)] and those that are not [e.g., longitudinal acoustic branch sound speed ($R^2=0.23$) and specific heat ($R^2=0.00$)]. We find that differences in ensemble predictions of thermal conductivity are correlated with the behavior of phonons with mean free paths between $100$ and $300$ nm. The framework systematically accounts for XC uncertainty in phonon calculations and should be used whenever it is suspected that the choice of XC functional is influencing physical interpretations.

s2Metadata.title: First-principles phonon physics using the Pheasy code
s2Metadata.abstract: Parameter-free calculations of lattice dynamics from first principles have achieved significant progress in the past decades, with a wealth of applications in thermodynamics, phase transitions, and transport properties of materials. Current approaches to derive the interatomic force constants (IFCs) of lattice potential become challenging and sometimes infeasible when going beyond third-order anharmonicity, due to the combinatorial explosion in the number of higher-order IFCs. In this work, we present a robust and user-friendly program, , which reliably reconstructs the prescribed potential energy surface of crystalline solids via a Taylor expansion of arbitrarily high order. Given force-displacement datasets, the program enables an efficient and accurate extraction of IFCs using advanced machine-learning algorithms, and further calculates a wide range of harmonic and anharmonic phonon related properties. We show in three prototypical examples how the obtained IFCs have been successfully applied to study anharmonic lattice dynamics and thermal transport. Through these detailed benchmarks, we have also identified the optimal approach for IFC extractions and offered general guidelines for high-fidelity lattice-dynamical simulations, addressing the large uncertainties in the IFCs extracted from existing various schemes. Overall, the project aims to create a phonon code ecosystem that connects diverse phonon simulation platforms and offers access to the broad research community.

content.title: SMRTA/RTA bias: κ_RTA ≤ κ_iter/inv, with a temperature-dependent gap

content.text: Using RTA instead of a full PBTE solution usually makes κ a bit too small; the difference is small near room temperature for Si but gets larger at lower temperatures.
**Supporting evidence:**

- For bulk diamond Si at 300 K, a DFT PBTE calculation reports κ_Q,Inv = 147 W/mK (direct inversion with quantum statistics) and κ_Q,RTA = 140 W/mK, i.e., RTA is ~5% lower than inversion at the same IFC level.  <paper entityId="paper-c1db9aa7a1e6d91e3dafea40ce6a6eaef0f2a40a" annotationId="ann_001" corpusId="221507928" artifactId="extraction-result-10#uuid-e10.0">Barbalinardo et al., 2020</paper>

- A separate first-principles Si study (including 3ph, 4ph, isotopes) states that prior literature indicates the iterative vs RTA difference is <4% for Si at room temperature (consistent with a modest systematic underestimation from RTA near 300 K).  <paper entityId="paper-544f173743e30f899ed765ea02113da1c166774b" annotationId="ann_002" corpusId="211987717" artifactId="extraction-result-6#uuid-e6.0">Gu et al., 2020</paper>

- A review of first-principles PBTE notes that iterative solutions can differ from RTA and that RTA neglect of coupling between modes can cause quantitative differences; this frames the mechanism as general across PBTE implementations.  <paper entityId="paper-5440f8458754c69b941910a03a7f0e1e40ec515e" annotationId="ann_003" corpusId="111146233" artifactId="extraction-result-7#uuid-e7.0">Tian et al., 2014</paper>

content.title: Finite-displacement IFC range/supercell inadequacy can bias κ downward via dispersion and scattering errors

content.text: If the force-constant supercell or cutoff is too small, the phonon dispersion and scattering will be wrong and κ often comes out too low.
**Supporting evidence:**

- A phono3py PBTE study explicitly reports that small IFC supercell sizes can underestimate κ (discussed for GaN: using a 32-atom cell vs 108-atom in a prior study, with underestimation attributed to supercell size). This provides direct evidence that IFC supercell inadequacy can depress κ in finite-displacement PBTE workflows.  <paper entityId="paper-1b4f174685bbc26dd19180ecfcf7cb0b152de2be" annotationId="ann_004" corpusId="160009739" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.2">Minamitani et al., 2019</paper>

- Uncertainty-quantification work notes that predicting TA branch frequencies near the X-point is challenging for both Si and Ge and that the discrepancy has been ascribed to the number of neighbor shells included in harmonic force-constant calculations—linking IFC range/cutoff choices mechanistically to dispersion errors that can shift κ.  <paper entityId="paper-292b26cc817258dac7b29d83cd91513ced10ed7e" annotationId="ann_005" corpusId="218674110" artifactId="extraction-result-5#uuid-e5.1">Parks et al., 2020</paper>

- A first-principles uncertainty study for isotopically pure Si shows κ at 300 K depends strongly on DFT functional and correlates with TA[100] sound speed and TA X-point frequency (R^2=0.77 for TA X-point frequency correlation), supporting the claim that errors in TA-branch characteristics (which can arise from underconverged IFC range) propagate into κ variability.  <paper entityId="paper-292b26cc817258dac7b29d83cd91513ced10ed7e" annotationId="ann_006" corpusId="218674110" artifactId="extraction-result-5#uuid-e5.0">Parks et al., 2020</paper>

- A first-principles PBTE study for Si emphasizes careful convergence practices (large supercells, q-grids up to 30x30x30) and highlights that insufficient convergence (supercell/q-grid) can affect κ; while not isolating supercell-size error numerically for Si, it supports the general necessity of converged IFC extraction to avoid κ bias.  <paper entityId="paper-fbf7170d0b720a69a2492581b23dc34f886f655c" annotationId="ann_007" corpusId="280421449" artifactId="extraction-result-4#uuid-e4.0">Lin et al., 2025</paper>

- For bulk Si near 300 K, a PBTE workflow that switches from SMRTA/RTA to iterative or direct inversion while holding the same IFCs fixed will increase κ by a few percent (order 3–6%), consistent with the 147 vs 140 W/mK evidence gap.
- At temperatures below ~200 K in high-purity bulk Si (where normal processes are more influential), the relative increase κ_iter/inv − κ_RTA will be larger than at 300 K (directionally: RTA becomes progressively less accurate).
- If two DFT-PBTE workflows differ mainly by underconverged IFC real-space range (smaller supercells/cutoffs) versus converged IFC range, the underconverged workflow will tend to predict lower κ for Si/Ge, with the discrepancy correlating with errors in TA branch features (e.g., TA X-point frequency).

- For bulk Ge, correcting harmonic IFC range (more neighbor shells / larger supercell) will change κ more strongly than for Si (because of potentially greater TA-edge sensitivity), possibly changing the ordering of which DFT functional appears 'best' against experiment once convergence is enforced.
- In explicit-supercell PBTE modeling of Si1-xGex (not VCA), insufficient supercell size will not only depress κ but also alter the apparent composition dependence by artificially suppressing long-wavelength contributions, potentially shifting the κ(x) minimum away from x≈0.5 in a size-dependent way.

- For a fixed bulk-Si DFT IFC set, compute κ(T) using both SMRTA/RTA and direct inversion/iterative PBTE across a temperature sweep. If κ_RTA exceeds κ_iter/inv at any temperature with identical inputs, the assumed systematic directionality (RTA underestimation) would be called into question (suggesting inconsistent scattering implementation or numerical issues).
- Within a finite-displacement PBTE workflow for Si or Ge, vary harmonic/anharmonic IFC supercell sizes and neighbor cutoffs while keeping q-mesh convergence tight. If κ is invariant within ~1% across these changes and TA(X) frequencies are also stable, the proposed IFC-range-driven κ underestimation mechanism is likely negligible for that workflow/material.

- No provided evidence gives a direct numerical example (for bulk Si or Ge) where a too-small IFC supercell quantitatively lowers κ; the explicit documented magnitude example is for GaN, so the size of this bias for Si/Ge remains uncertain from the current evidence set.  <paper entityId="paper-1b4f174685bbc26dd19180ecfcf7cb0b152de2be" annotationId="ann_008" corpusId="160009739" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.2">Minamitani et al., 2019</paper>
